title: Geometric Heat Pumping On A Quantum Processor
authors: Ger\'onimo J. Caselli, Luis O. Manuel, Liliana Arrachea, Pablo S. Cornaglia
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09062v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Geometric heat pumping is the transfer of energy between reservoirs at equal temperature where the heat exchanged in an adiabatic cycle depends only on the driving contour in parameter space. We implement this mechanism on a superconducting quantum processor using a collision model, where a driven qubit interacts repeatedly with two ancilla qubits that are prepared in thermal states and emulate the reservoirs. Energy measurements before and after each interaction provide a calorimetric record of the heat exchanged with each reservoir. By reversing the driving contour, we extract a heat contribution associated with pumping. Its dependence on the period and on the contour follows exact simulations of the collision model, without adjustable parameters, and approaches in the slow-driving regime the geometric limit of the corresponding Lindblad dynamics.
tldr: The paper experimentally implements geometric heat pumping on a superconducting quantum processor using a collision model with thermal ancilla qubits, observing contour-dependent heat exchange that matches exact simulations and approaches the Lindblad geometric limit.
motivation: Geometric heat pumping enables energy transfer between reservoirs at equal temperature, with the exchanged heat determined solely by the driving contour in parameter space. Realizing this in a controllable quantum platform can test quantum thermodynamic predictions and provide a building block for quantum thermal machines.
method: A driven qubit repeatedly interacts with two ancilla qubits prepared in thermal states to emulate reservoirs. Energy measurements before and after each collision yield a calorimetric record, and reversing the driving contour isolates the heat contribution associated with geometric pumping.
result: The extracted pumped heat depends on the driving period and contour in agreement with parameter-free exact simulations of the collision model, and in the slow-driving regime it approaches the geometric limit predicted by the corresponding Lindblad dynamics.
conclusion: The experiment demonstrates geometric heat pumping on a quantum processor, validating collision-model thermodynamics and offering a platform for studying non-equilibrium quantum thermodynamics and geometric effects in quantum thermal machines.

title: Efficiently Computable Bounds On The Energy-constrained Quantum Reading Capacity
authors: Vishal Singh, Zixin Huang, Mark M. Wilde
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08945v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In quantum reading, classical messages are encoded in sequences of quantum channels and recovered by probing the channels and processing their outputs. We study the reading capacity of a finite family of finite-dimensional channels under an average constraint on the probing energy, allowing arbitrary adaptive operations between channel uses. Using an input-dependent chain rule for the Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy, we derive a converse bound expressed as an optimization involving channel Choi operators and the operator relative entropy. This formulation admits semidefinite approximations and reduces, without an energy constraint, to a channel information radius. To obtain achievable rates, we construct bilinear semidefinite lower approximations to a standard non-adaptive reading bound. Alternating optimization produces feasible probe states and encoding distributions, whose Holevo information gives a directly evaluable achievable rate. For jointly classical-quantum channels, we derive a separate converse based on the Umegaki relative entropy. Without an energy constraint, this converse matches a non-adaptive achievable rate, recovering a recent result of Pascual Abraldes and Winter: non-adaptive protocols suffice to achieve the unconstrained reading capacity of jointly classical-quantum channels.
tldr: This paper derives efficiently computable converse and achievable bounds on the energy-constrained quantum reading capacity using Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy and semidefinite approximations.
motivation: Quantum reading capacity characterizes classical communication through quantum channels under energy constraints, but tight bounds allowing adaptive protocols are challenging to compute.
method: The authors use an input-dependent chain rule for the Belavkin-Staszewski relative entropy to derive a converse bound, and construct bilinear semidefinite lower approximations with alternating optimization for achievable rates.
result: They obtain a semidefinite-representable converse, recover a channel information radius without energy constraint, and for jointly classical-quantum channels the converse matches non-adaptive achievable rates, rederiving a recent result.
conclusion: The work provides computable bounds on energy-constrained quantum reading capacity and clarifies the power of non-adaptive protocols for jointly classical-quantum channels.

title: Correspondence Between Asymptotic Quantum Many-Body Scars In Closed Systems And Diffusive Nambu-Goldstone Modes In Open Systems
authors: Masaya Kunimi, Taiki Haga, Masaya Nakagawa
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09662v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hydrodynamic relaxation in open quantum many-body systems can be understood in terms of diffusive Nambu--Goldstone (NG) modes associated with strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB). Here, we find a common structure underlying weak ergodicity breaking in closed quantum systems and diffusive hydrodynamics in open quantum systems. We establish a spectral correspondence between the parent Hamiltonian of rainbow quantum many-body scar (RQMBS) states in closed systems and the effective Lindbladian of strongly dissipative open systems with strong [MATH] symmetry and local charge-dephasing Lindblad operators. For broad classes of spin, fermionic, and bosonic systems, we construct asymptotic RQMBS (ARQMBS) states. Within the enlarged scar subspace, the parent Hamiltonian admits a local Rokhsar--Kivelson-type frustration-free decomposition. A single-mode variational construction gives an [MATH] upper bound on its lowest excitation energy and yields states satisfying the defining ARQMBS criteria: orthogonality, vanishing energy variance, and characteristic entanglement scaling. Under vectorization, RQMBS states are mapped to maximally mixed infinite-temperature states in fixed-charge sectors, which exhibit long-range SWSSB order under finite-density conditions. Assuming uniformly bounded positive transition rates, the effective Lindbladian has the same local projectors as the parent Hamiltonian but with positive transition-dependent weights, yielding two-sided spectral bounds and the same system-size scaling of their gaps. For uniform rates, the two operators are proportional to each other and their eigenmodes coincide. Therefore, an exact quadratic parent-Hamiltonian branch maps directly to a diffusive NG mode. Our results connect different mechanisms of slow relaxation in closed and open quantum many-body systems.
tldr: The paper establishes a spectral correspondence between rainbow quantum many-body scar states in closed systems and diffusive Nambu-Goldstone modes in open systems via a parent Hamiltonian/Lindbladian mapping.
motivation: To uncover a common structure underlying weak ergodicity breaking in closed quantum systems and diffusive hydrodynamics in open quantum many-body systems.
method: Constructs asymptotic rainbow quantum many-body scar states for spin, fermionic, and bosonic systems, and maps the parent Hamiltonian to an effective Lindbladian using a Rokhsar-Kivelson-type frustration-free decomposition, variational bounds, and vectorization.
result: Shows that the effective Lindbladian shares local projectors with the parent Hamiltonian, giving two-sided spectral bounds and matching gap scaling; uniform rates yield proportional operators and an exact mapping from a quadratic parent-Hamiltonian branch to a diffusive Nambu-Goldstone mode.
conclusion: The results connect different mechanisms of slow relaxation in closed and open quantum many-body systems, linking quantum many-body scars to hydrodynamic Nambu-Goldstone modes through strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking.

title: Stimulated Emission For A Three-level Artificial Atom In Waveguide Quantum Electrodynamics
authors: O. A. Chuikin, Ya. S. Greenberg, V. V. Taravkova, O. V. Kibis
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work is devoted to a theoretical study of the interaction of a quantum three-level ladder system with a continuous electromagnetic field in a one-dimensional open waveguide. We consider a situation closely resembling stimulated emission - the scattering of a single-photon exponential pulse by an excited three-level emitter. Using the real-space formalism, we obtain an analytical expression for the wavefunction of our system. We show that, for the low anharmonicity of a three-level system inherent to a transmon (the most common type of artificial atom), the influence of the third level can have a significant effect on the system's behavior. Namely, the presence of the third level largely suppresses the stimulated emission effect if the relative anharmonicity is lower than [MATH]. However, for a three-level system, it is possible to obtain correlation effects such as photon bunching in the reflected field, which can also be 'switched off' by tuning the incident photon parameters.
tldr: Theoretical study of stimulated emission and photon correlations when a single-photon pulse scatters off a three-level transmon-like artificial atom in a one-dimensional waveguide.
motivation: To understand how the third level and low anharmonicity of a transmon affect stimulated emission and photon statistics in waveguide quantum electrodynamics.
method: Real-space formalism is used to solve the scattering of an exponential single-photon pulse by an excited three-level ladder emitter, yielding an analytical wavefunction for the system.
result: For low relative anharmonicity, the third level largely suppresses stimulated emission; however, photon bunching can appear in the reflected field and can be switched off by tuning the incident photon parameters.
conclusion: The three-level nature of transmon artificial atoms qualitatively changes stimulated emission and enables controllable correlation effects in waveguide QED.

The authors employ the real-space formalism to derive an analytical expression for the full wavefunction of the system, treating the emitter as a three-level system with a ladder configuration. The study is motivated by the physics of transmon qubits, which are weakly anharmonic artificial atoms where the third level is not negligible. The central finding is that the presence of the third level can drastically alter the scattering outcome: for relative anharmonicity |α_r| < 4%, the stimulated emission effect is largely suppressed. Additionally, the authors show that photon bunching in the reflected field can arise due to the three-level structure, and this correlation effect can be tuned on or off by adjusting the incident photon parameters. The work provides a detailed analytical and numerical analysis of the scattering dynamics, including the populations of the emitter levels and the properties of the outgoing photon field.

title: High-Fidelity Inter-Species Rydberg Gates With Two-Photon Driving
authors: Kevin Singh Shuan Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recently, neutral atom arrays have become known for their promising potential in quantum information processing. High-fidelity entangling operations are typically achieved by exciting atoms to high-lying Rydberg states through two-photon processes. To improve the performance of these systems at the hardware level, dual-species strategies have been applied to enhance readout, error correction, and reloading in neutral atom systems. However, the influence of laser crosstalk arising from two-photon excitation for dual-species systems has remained largely unexplored in the literature. Here, we develop a model that incorporates the influence of crosstalk in inter-species Rydberg gates with two-photon driving. We demonstrate that the influence of this crosstalk can be suppressed to arbitrarily small levels through appropriate gate design, with gate fidelities greater than [MATH] achievable with conservative experimental parameters in the near-detuned case of an [MATH]Rb/[MATH]Rb system. We also outline how this fidelity can be further enhanced through improvements to the Rydberg excitation.

title: Geodesic-based Optimal Control For Leakage Suppression In Superconducting Qubits
authors: Adonai Hil\'ario Da Silva, Tanmoy Pandit, Francesco Cosco
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Superconducting qubits are often based on the first two energy levels of a physical anharmonic LC oscillator. Since the anharmonicity of such systems is usually much lower than the involved energy gaps, population can easily leak to higher energy states. This is what characterizes leakage errors, and it can have multiple sources: from coherent error induced by the control platform to incoherent thermal dissipation. In this work, we adapt an optimal control method based on sub-Riemannian geodesic search in the unitary group for a system consisting of two superconducting qubits with leakage levels. We use the [MATH] rotation for single-qubit operation analysis, and the [MATH]SWAP operation for two-qubit analysis. For the former, we find considerable performance improvement in average gate fidelity as well as in the reduction of leakage errors when comparing the obtained optimal pulses with Gaussian and DRAG pulses, especially for short duration pulses. For the [MATH]SWAP gate, although leakage error remains roughly the same, we manage to obtain considerably higher fidelities with the cost of requiring a slightly longer time evolution.
tldr: Adapts sub-Riemannian geodesic optimal control to suppress leakage and improve gate fidelity in two superconducting qubits.
motivation: Superconducting qubits suffer population leakage to higher energy states due to low anharmonicity, which limits gate fidelity and requires improved control pulses.
method: The authors formulate optimal control as a sub-Riemannian geodesic search in the unitary group for a two-transmon system including leakage levels, analyzing π rotations and √SWAP gates and comparing with Gaussian and DRAG pulses.
result: For single-qubit operations, the geodesic pulses yield considerable improvements in average gate fidelity and leakage reduction, especially for short durations; for the √SWAP gate, leakage remains similar but fidelity is considerably higher at the cost of slightly longer evolution time.
conclusion: Geodesic-based optimal control is an effective approach for leakage suppression and fidelity enhancement in superconducting qubit gates.

title: Efficient Detection Of Spectral Cluster States
authors: M. Kalash, U. -N. Han, C. Roh, M. H. M. Passos, Y. -S. Ra, M. V. Chekhova
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09745v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimode entangled states of light are key resources for high-dimensional photonic quantum technologies, particularly for continuous-variable quantum computing and quantum information processing. Exploiting their full capabilities requires detection strategies that can efficiently and simultaneously access a large number of modes and their quantum correlations. Multimode optical parametric amplification (MOPA) provides a promising approach by amplifying multiple quadratures prior to detection, rendering the measurement robust against subsequent optical losses while enabling broadband operation. Here, we demonstrate the spectral multimode capability of MOPA by simultaneously characterizing a broadband 60-node dual-rail continuous-variable cluster state. We reconstruct the cluster-state nullifiers across the spectral modes and observe nearly uniform squeezing ranging from -7.2 to -6.5 dB. Furthermore, by evaluating the van Loock-Furusawa criterion across all relevant bipartitions, we verify genuine multipartite entanglement throughout the 60-node state. These results establish MOPA as a promising platform for scalable high-dimensional quantum information processing in the spectral domain.
tldr: The paper demonstrates efficient detection of a broadband 60-node dual-rail continuous-variable cluster state using multimode optical parametric amplification (MOPA) and verifies genuine multipartite entanglement.
motivation: Multimode entangled states are key resources for high-dimensional photonic quantum technologies, but efficiently detecting many modes and their quantum correlations remains a central challenge.
method: MOPA amplifies multiple quadratures before detection, enabling reconstruction of cluster-state nullifiers across spectral modes; the van Loock-Furusawa criterion is evaluated over all relevant bipartitions.
result: Nearly uniform squeezing from -7.2 to -6.5 dB is observed across the 60 nodes, and genuine multipartite entanglement is verified throughout the state.
conclusion: MOPA is established as a promising platform for scalable high-dimensional quantum information processing in the spectral domain.

title: Automated Reduction Of Fault-tolerant Circuits
authors: Hyeongjun Jeon, Jeonghoon Lee, Taehyun Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an automated method for reducing fault-tolerant circuits through fault-equivalent rewrites. Starting from a known fault-tolerant circuit, the search applies non-reducing enabling rules to expose Bell-pair reductions, each of which removes an ancilla preparation and a CNOT gate. Because every search transition preserves fault equivalence, the resulting circuits inherit the fault-tolerance properties of the input circuit. Candidate circuits are evaluated using circuit-level Monte Carlo simulation. For Shor-style syndrome extraction with the [MATH] code, our method reduces one syndrome-measurement round from 30 to 18 ancilla preparations and from 54 to 42 CNOT gates. At a physical two-qubit error rate of [MATH], the optimized circuit lowers the logical error rate by approximately 21% for both logical basis states. The reduction ranges from 13% to 23% over a range of [MATH] spanning two orders of magnitude. We also apply the method to Steane-based dynamic syndrome extraction constructed from Goto's verified logical-[MATH] preparation, in which the verification qubit serves as a flag. The search selects a circuit using four ancillas and 14 CNOT gates, matching the resource counts of the previous design but with an improved CNOT depth. Under depolarizing idle noise at [MATH] the selected circuit lowers the logical error rate by approximately 15% for both logical basis states, and by approximately [MATH] at [MATH]. These results demonstrate that automated fault-equivalent rewriting can identify circuits with lower resource costs or improved logical performance without separately verifying the fault tolerance of every candidate.

abstract: ArXiv:2610.08953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the effects of initial states on the dynamics of a quantum spin-boson model using an efficient variational polaron master equation approach. The transformation of a factorized system-environment initial state into the variational polaron frame introduces inhomogeneous terms in the master equation, essential for accurately describing non-Markovian dynamics beyond the weak coupling regime. To efficiently account for these effects, we formulate the dynamics in an extended auxiliary Liouville space, converting the resulting integro-differential equations into coupled ordinary differential equations. We further introduce a simplified variational polaron technique for computing the time evolution of expectation values of general observables, including those that do not commute with the polaron transformation, overcoming a major limitation of previous approaches and enabling the unified treatment of coherence and population dynamics. The effects of transformed initial states generated from arbitrary factorized initial states are systematically characterized through expectation values and trace-distance analysis, providing insight into the associated bath-relaxation dynamics over a broad range of tunneling amplitudes, temperatures, and coupling strengths. Comparison with the weak-coupling master equation reveals a delay phenomenon associated with multi-bath-quanta processes, pronounced at intermediate coupling strengths and tunneling amplitudes. We further show that coherent superposition initial states induce stronger nonequilibrium effects than localized states, with inhomogeneous terms playing a crucial role in the short-time dynamics. The proposed formalism applies to both undriven and resonantly driven spin-boson models, providing a computationally efficient framework for open quantum-system dynamics with arbitrary factorized initial states and general physical observables.
tldr: The paper develops an efficient variational polaron master equation for non-Markovian spin-boson dynamics that handles transformed initial states and general observables via an extended auxiliary Liouville space.
motivation: Accurate description of non-Markovian open quantum dynamics beyond weak coupling requires properly accounting for initial system-environment correlations and transformed initial states.
method: They formulate the variational polaron master equation in an extended auxiliary Liouville space, converting integro-differential equations into coupled ordinary differential equations, and introduce a simplified technique for computing expectation values of general observables.
result: The approach characterizes bath-relaxation dynamics across tunneling amplitudes, temperatures, and coupling strengths, reveals a delay phenomenon from multi-bath-quanta processes, and shows coherent superposition initial states induce stronger nonequilibrium effects than localized states.
conclusion: The formalism provides a computationally efficient framework for open quantum-system dynamics with arbitrary factorized initial states and general physical observables, applicable to both undriven and resonantly driven spin-boson models.

title: Phonon-Enabled Collective Strong Coupling Of Color Centers In A Plasmonic Cavity
authors: Bharti Garg, Prabhdeep Singh, Masoud Taleb, Nahid Talebi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09716v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum emitters in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are promising building blocks for solid-state quantum photonics because of their bright room-temperature emission. These emitters strongly interact with lattice vibrations, which partially underpins their excitation efficiency. Here, using complementary cathodoluminescence (CL) and photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy, we demonstrate cavity-mediated interactions between hBN quantum emitters coupled to the same plasmonic Au void cavity at the room temperature. Cathodoluminescence measurements reveal that a vibronic transition of the 443 nm emitter hybridizes with the cavity mode, giving rise to a spectrally resolved splitting, while the neighboring 537 nm emitter remains in the weak-coupling regime despite spectral overlap. The energy split of the CL peak is at the order of 36.2 meV, whereas the PL-resolved peak is approximately 24.1 meV, which is due to the collective excitations of multiple emitters per electron excitation and their mutual interactions. Maxwell-Bloch simulations reproduce the experimental spectra and identify the observed splitting as the result of cavity-induced hybridization. Excitation-dependent PL further shows that the hybridized state can be accessed through phonon-assisted excitations below the zero-phonon transition. These results demonstrate that vibronic transitions provide an effective pathway for controlling interactions between multiple quantum emitters in hybrid plasmonic nanophotonic systems.
tldr: Room-temperature cavity-mediated collective strong coupling is demonstrated between hexagonal boron nitride color centers in a plasmonic Au void cavity, enabled by vibronic transitions.
motivation: hBN quantum emitters are promising for solid-state quantum photonics, but their strong interaction with lattice vibrations is usually treated as a loss channel; this work explores whether phonon-assisted transitions can instead mediate useful cavity-emitter interactions.
method: Complementary cathodoluminescence (CL) and photoluminescence (PL) spectroscopy are used to probe hBN emitters coupled to the same plasmonic cavity, with Maxwell-Bloch simulations reproducing the observed spectra.
result: A vibronic transition of the 443 nm emitter hybridizes with the cavity mode, producing a spectrally resolved splitting of about 36.2 meV in CL and 24.1 meV in PL, whereas the neighboring 537 nm emitter remains weakly coupled despite spectral overlap.
conclusion: Vibronic transitions provide an effective pathway for controlling interactions among multiple quantum emitters in hybrid plasmonic nanophotonic systems.

title: Visualizing Two Qubits
authors: Simon Grosse-Holz
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08897v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I propose a simple visualization for pure two-qubit states, constructed from three components: two Bloch balls for the marginal qubits (the mixed states obtained by ignoring the other qubit, respectively) and an entanglement component consisting of a rotoreflection and a contraction. I prove that this picture accurately captures the local and global structure of the relevant state space without gaps or degeneracies: the underlying parametrization is a global diffeomorphism onto the state space. Finally, I use this picture to visualize conditional states, the entanglement degree(s) of freedom, and single qubit rotations.
tldr: A geometric visualization of pure two-qubit states as two marginal Bloch balls plus an entanglement component (rotoreflection and contraction), proven to be a global diffeomorphism onto the state space.
motivation: Two-qubit states are fundamental in quantum information, but their state space is high-dimensional and hard to visualize. A faithful low-dimensional picture could aid intuition about local and global structure, conditional states, and entanglement degrees of freedom.
method: The author constructs a parametrization of pure two-qubit states from two Bloch vectors for the marginals and an entanglement component consisting of a rotoreflection and a contraction. He proves that this map is a global diffeomorphism onto the relevant state space and uses it to visualize conditional states, entanglement parameters, and single-qubit rotations.
result: The proposed picture provides a complete, gap-free, and non-degenerate representation of pure two-qubit states. It captures both local marginal structure and global entanglement structure, and allows visualization of conditional states and single-qubit operations.
conclusion: This visualization offers a rigorous and intuitive tool for understanding two-qubit entanglement and state-space geometry, potentially useful for pedagogical and qualitative analyses in quantum information.

deep_read.detailed_summary:
The paper proposes a geometric visualization for pure two-qubit states based on a decomposition into two marginal Bloch balls and an entanglement component. The marginal Bloch balls represent the reduced density matrices of each qubit, while the entanglement component is a rotoreflection (a rotation combined with a reflection) and a contraction that encodes the non-local correlations. The author proves that this parametrization is a global diffeomorphism onto the space of pure two-qubit states, meaning it provides a one-to-one, smooth, and invertible mapping without gaps or degeneracies. This ensures that every pure two-qubit state corresponds uniquely to a point in the product of the two Bloch balls and the entanglement parameters.

The visualization is then used to illustrate conditional states, the degrees of freedom associated with entanglement, and single-qubit rotations. Conditional states, obtained by measuring one qubit, are shown as points within the other qubit's Bloch ball, with the entanglement component determining how these conditional states are related. The entanglement degrees of freedom are parameterized by the rotoreflection and contraction, which together have three real parameters (since a rotoreflection in 3D is defined by an axis and an angle, plus a contraction factor). The paper emphasizes that this picture captures both local and global structure of the state space, providing an intuitive yet rigorous tool for understanding two-qubit entanglement.

The work is primarily expository and pedagogical, aiming to offer a clear geometric interpretation of pure two-qubit states. It does not introduce new physical results but rather provides a novel visualization that could aid in teaching and in building intuition about entanglement. The proof of the global diffeomorphism is a technical contribution that validates the visualization's completeness. The paper is concise and focuses on the mathematical construction and its implications for visualizing quantum correlations.
key_contributions: Proposes a geometric visualization of pure two-qubit states using two marginal Bloch balls and an entanglement component (rotoreflection + contraction).
Proves that the parametrization is a global diffeomorphism onto the pure two-qubit state space, ensuring no gaps or degeneracies.
Demonstrates how conditional states and single-qubit rotations can be visualized within this framework.
Provides an intuitive representation of the entanglement degrees of freedom, separating local and non-local properties.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology is based on a mathematical decomposition of pure two-qubit states. The author starts with the Schmidt decomposition, which expresses any pure two-qubit state as a sum of two product states with Schmidt coefficients. The marginal states are then obtained by partial trace, yielding two Bloch vectors. The entanglement is encoded in a rotoreflection and a contraction, which can be derived from the Schmidt coefficients and the relative phase between the Schmidt bases. The proof of the global diffeomorphism involves showing that the map from the state parameters (two Bloch vectors, a rotation axis, an angle, and a contraction factor) to the state space is bijective and smooth with a smooth inverse. This is done by constructing the inverse map explicitly and verifying its smoothness. The approach is rigorous and relies on standard tools from differential geometry and quantum information theory.
deep_read.results_analysis: The main result is the proof that the proposed parametrization is a global diffeomorphism. This means that the space of pure two-qubit states is diffeomorphic to the product of two Bloch balls (each a 3D ball) and a 3D parameter space for the entanglement component (a rotoreflection and a contraction). The total dimension is 3+3+3=9, but pure two-qubit states have 6 real dimensions (since the state space is CP^3, which is 6-dimensional). The apparent discrepancy is resolved because the marginal Bloch vectors are not independent; they are constrained by the entanglement parameters. Specifically, the lengths of the Bloch vectors are determined by the Schmidt coefficients, and their orientations are related by the rotoreflection. Thus, the effective degrees of freedom are 6. The paper does not provide numerical values but rather a qualitative geometric picture. The visualization shows that entanglement corresponds to a contraction of the Bloch balls and a relative rotation/reflection between them.

Rigorous proof of the global diffeomorphism ensures the visualization is complete and without degeneracies.
The decomposition into local and entanglement components is natural and aligns with the Schmidt decomposition.
The visualization can be used to illustrate conditional states and single-qubit rotations, making it pedagogically valuable.
limitations: The paper is purely expository and does not present new physical results or applications.
The visualization is limited to pure two-qubit states; extension to mixed states or more qubits is not addressed.
The entanglement component (rotoreflection + contraction) may be less intuitive than other entanglement measures like concurrence.

title: Witnessing Quantum Bayesian Inference Beyond Classical Learning
authors: Francesco Buscemi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can an agent's predictions reveal whether its reasoning is based on a classical or a quantum model? Using known results on matrix factorizations, here we show that quantum Bayesian retrodiction can produce one-step-ahead forecasts incompatible with every classical Bayesian explanation based on learning about a fixed but unknown sampling law from conditionally independent observations. The separation has a sharp threshold in the number of outcomes: for any measurement with at most four outcomes, the quantum predictions admit a classical realization, irrespective of the prior state and the finite Hilbert-space dimension, whereas a five-outcome measurement on a single qubit already violates an explicit classical bound. This bound holds for arbitrary classical latent states, prior probabilities, and sampling laws, and involves only the agent's initial and updated predictions. Thus, in this setting, quantum Bayesian retrodiction is strictly more expressive than classical Bayesian learning, and this difference can be witnessed without observing or specifying the agent's internal description.
tldr: The paper shows that quantum Bayesian retrodiction can produce one-step-ahead predictions that are impossible to reproduce by any classical Bayesian learning model, with a sharp threshold of five measurement outcomes on a single qubit.
motivation: To determine whether an agent's predictions can reveal whether its underlying reasoning is classical or quantum, and to establish an operational separation between quantum and classical Bayesian inference.
method: Using known results on matrix factorizations, the author derives classical-realizability bounds for quantum Bayesian retrodiction and identifies a minimal measurement setting that violates these bounds.
result: Any measurement with at most four outcomes admits a classical realization, but a five-outcome measurement on a single qubit already violates an explicit classical bound that holds for all classical latent states, priors, and sampling laws.
conclusion: Quantum Bayesian retrodiction is strictly more expressive than classical Bayesian learning in this setting, and this separation can be witnessed using only the agent's initial and updated predictions without access to its internal description.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper investigates whether an agent's one-step-ahead predictions can distinguish between classical and quantum Bayesian reasoning. The authors consider a scenario where an agent makes predictions about future observations based on past data, and ask whether these predictions are compatible with a classical Bayesian model that learns a fixed but unknown sampling law from conditionally independent observations. Using known results on matrix factorizations, they prove that quantum Bayesian retrodiction can produce forecasts that cannot be realized by any classical Bayesian explanation. The key result is a sharp threshold: for any measurement with at most four outcomes, the quantum predictions always admit a classical realization, regardless of the prior state or Hilbert-space dimension. However, a five-outcome measurement on a single qubit already violates an explicit classical bound. This bound is derived for arbitrary classical latent states, prior probabilities, and sampling laws, and depends only on the agent's initial and updated predictions. Thus, quantum Bayesian retrodiction is strictly more expressive than classical Bayesian learning in this setting, and the difference can be witnessed without access to the agent's internal description.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a mathematical approach rooted in matrix factorization theory to compare the predictive capabilities of quantum Bayesian retrodiction and classical Bayesian learning. They formalize the classical scenario as an agent that learns a fixed but unknown sampling law from conditionally independent observations, leading to predictions that satisfy certain factorization constraints. Quantum Bayesian retrodiction, in contrast, involves updating a quantum state via a measurement channel and then predicting future outcomes. By analyzing the matrix factorization properties of the resulting prediction matrices, they derive necessary and sufficient conditions for classical realizability. The sharp threshold at four outcomes is proven by showing that any quantum prediction matrix with up to four outcomes can be factored in a way consistent with a classical latent variable model, while a five-outcome example on a qubit yields a matrix that violates the classical bound. The bound itself is expressed in terms of the agent's initial and updated predictions, making it experimentally accessible without detailed knowledge of the quantum state or measurement.
deep_read.results_analysis: The central result is the identification of a sharp threshold: for measurements with at most four outcomes, quantum Bayesian retrodiction predictions are always classically realizable, irrespective of the prior state and Hilbert-space dimension. This is a strong statement, as it implies that no classical-quantum separation can be observed with such measurements. However, for five outcomes on a single qubit, the authors provide an explicit violation of the classical bound. The bound is derived analytically and holds for arbitrary classical latent states, prior probabilities, and sampling laws. The violation is witnessed solely by the agent's initial and updated predictions, meaning that an experimenter can test the classicality of the agent's reasoning without accessing its internal quantum state or measurement. The paper does not provide numerical values for the violation, but the threshold at four outcomes is exact and dimension-independent.

The classical bound is derived under very general assumptions, making it robust and widely applicable.

The use of matrix factorization techniques offers a novel and rigorous mathematical foundation for comparing classical and quantum Bayesian inference.
limitations: The paper focuses on one-step-ahead predictions and conditionally independent observations; it is unclear how the results extend to more complex temporal dependencies or multi-step predictions.

The practical implications for quantum advantage in learning tasks are not discussed; the separation is information-theoretic rather than computational.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work lies at the intersection of quantum foundations, quantum information theory, and Bayesian inference, which are core areas in quantum physics. It addresses fundamental questions about the distinguishability of classical and quantum models of reasoning, a topic relevant to quantum cognition and quantum machine learning. The use of matrix factorization and the sharp threshold result may inspire further research into the expressive power of quantum models in prediction tasks, and the operational testability of the separation could lead to experimental proposals in quantum information processing.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant and novel contribution to the understanding of quantum versus classical Bayesian inference. The sharp threshold at four outcomes is a striking result that clarifies the boundary of classical realizability. The mathematical approach is rigorous and the operational nature of the bound makes it experimentally appealing. While the scope is limited to one-step-ahead predictions and conditionally independent observations, the work opens up new avenues for exploring quantum advantages in predictive tasks. Overall, it is a high-quality theoretical paper that will likely stimulate further research in quantum foundations and quantum information.

title: Teleportation Of A Programmable Gate
authors: Mark Hillery Nada Ali
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09022v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Alice and Bob each have a qubit, and they would like to perform a two-qubit gate on them with the assistance of Charlie. The action of this gate depends on a parameter, which either Charlie knows, will receive later as classical information, or is encoded in a program state. We discuss both the case in which Alice and Bob send Charlie their qubits, which he entangles with his state, and the case where Alice and Bob use teleportation to entangle their states with Charlie's state. All of these procedures depend on the ability of Alice and Bob to apply local correction operations that depend on the results of measurements that Charlie makes, and we discuss under what conditions such operations are possible.
tldr: The paper proposes protocols for Alice and Bob to apply a parameterized two-qubit gate on their qubits with assistance from Charlie, using either direct entanglement or teleportation and measurement-dependent local corrections.
motivation: Distributed quantum computation requires methods for implementing non-local gates when the gate parameter may be known, communicated later, or kept secret. The paper addresses these scenarios by proposing protocols that use entanglement and classical communication to achieve the desired gate.

title: Interaction-Assisted Spin Coherence In A Multimode Trapped Atomic Ensemble
authors: Ebubechukwu O. Ilo-Okeke Aleksandre Merabishvili
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09073v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a thermally occupied multimode trapped ensemble, mode-dependent detunings can strongly suppress Ramsey contrast even when the underlying dynamics remains coherent. We develop a weak-axis-resolved Hamiltonian theory in which collective mode spins experience longitudinal detunings and overlap-dependent exchange interactions. Without exchange, the distribution of detunings across thermally occupied modes produces coherent phase mixing and an algebraically decaying Ramsey-contrast envelope in the many-mode continuum regime. At the mean-field level, exchange generates a self-consistent restoring field that reduces phase dispersion and restores collective contrast. The crossover is governed by the competition between the collective exchange scale and the thermally induced detuning spread: when the late-time contrast is expressed in terms of their ratio, results at different temperatures collapse onto a common trend, and the crossover coupling follows the predicted inverse-square thermal scaling, with a numerical exponent of 2.06. Weak irreversible pure dephasing limits, but does not eliminate, this recovery, demonstrating that exchange refocuses coherent inhomogeneous phase mixing but cannot reverse irreversible phase noise.

motivation: Mode-dependent detunings in thermally occupied multimode trapped ensembles can suppress Ramsey contrast even when dynamics remain coherent, motivating a better understanding of how interactions might mitigate this loss.
method: The authors develop a weak-axis-resolved Hamiltonian theory for collective mode spins with longitudinal detunings and overlap-dependent exchange interactions, analyzing the crossover between exchange and thermal dephasing.
result: Exchange generates a self-consistent restoring field that reduces phase dispersion and restores contrast; the crossover follows inverse-square thermal scaling with a numerical exponent of 2.06, and weak irreversible pure dephasing limits but does not eliminate recovery.
conclusion: Exchange interactions can refocus coherent inhomogeneous phase mixing but cannot reverse irreversible phase noise, providing a quantitative picture of interaction-assisted spin coherence in trapped atomic ensembles.

title: When The Coupler Is The Channel: An And Condition On Cavity Photon-number Means
authors: Yueying Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can two cavities have equal mean photon numbers whenever at least one of two binary controls is off, and unequal means only when both controls are on? We give an elementary construction using a two-pump beam-splitter interaction whose strength is proportional to the product of the controls. A phase-coherent single-excitation state yields mean occupations [MATH] for inputs [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH], and [MATH] for input [MATH]. This realizes the desired AND condition exactly at the level of population means. It also makes the communication resource explicit: the interaction acts after the inputs are supplied and changes local statistics with the remote input. For any no-signalling distribution with finite means, the corresponding exact-mean score is at most [MATH] under uniform inputs. We give a robust consistency inequality, a finite-sample counting protocol, and a coherent-state realization showing that this mean response does not require entanglement. The construction provides a concrete example for distinguishing controlled interactions from nonlocal-game resources.

title: Cross-Validation Of Open-Source Quantum Network Simulators
authors: Joaquin Chung (argonne National Laboratory, University Of Chicago), Michal Hajdu\v{s}ek (keio University), Naphan Benchasattabuse (keio University), Robert J. Hayek (argonne National Laboratory, Northwestern University), Alexander Kolar (argonne National Laboratory, University Of Chicago), Ansh Singal (argonne National Laboratory, Northwestern University), Kento Samuel Soon (keio University), Kentaro Teramoto (mercari Inc), Allen Zang (argonne National Laboratory, University Of Chicago), Caitao Zhan (argonne National Laboratory), Raj Kettimuthu (argonne National Laboratory, University Of Chicago), Rodney van Meter
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09322v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a comparative analysis of two open-source quantum network simulators, QuISP and SeQUeNCe, focusing on cross-validation of basic networking tasks to ensure consistency and accuracy in simulation outputs. Although both simulators are designed to study quantum network management policies and their dynamics under complex noise models, their differing underlying assumptions can lead to variations in simulation results. We highlight the discrepancies in how the two simulators handle connections, internal network node processing time, and classical communication, resulting in significant quantitative and qualitative differences in the time required to perform basic network tasks such as entanglement generation, purification, and swapping. We simulate common scenarios between the simulators to compare both the latency of resource distribution and the fidelity of the distributed resources. Our findings indicate that while the simulators differ in the time required to complete network tasks---a constant factor difference attributable to their respective connection models---they agree on the fidelity of the distributed resources under identical error parameters. This work demonstrates a crucial first step towards enhancing the reliability and reproducibility of quantum network simulations, as well as leading to full protocol development. Furthermore, our benchmarking methodology establishes a foundational set of tasks for the cross-validation of simulators to study future quantum networks.

title: Structure-preserving Full- And Low-rank Exponential Methods For The Optimal Control Of Lindblad Equations
authors: Alfio Borzi Hao Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimal control of open quantum systems governed by the Lindblad master equation requires the repeated solution of forward and adjoint evolution equations. For large Hilbert spaces, these computations demand numerical methods that are structure-preserving, accurate, and computationally efficient, while remaining compatible with nonsmooth optimization techniques. In this work, a unified framework for optimal control of Lindblad equations is presented. The continuous optimality system is derived from the Pontryagin maximum principle and solved by a sequential quadratic Hamiltonian (SQH) method. Its numerical realization is based on second-order exponential midpoint propagators for the forward and adjoint Lindblad equations with time-dependent Hamiltonians. Full-rank schemes preserving the Hermitian and positive-semidefinite structure of the density matrix are developed together with low-rank formulations that substantially reduce storage requirements and computational cost. Rigorous error estimates are established for the full- and low-rank forward and adjoint propagators. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence rates, demonstrate the effectiveness of the low-rank approximations, and illustrate the performance of the proposed FREM-SQH and LREM-SQH algorithms for optimal control problems with smooth and nonsmooth control costs.
tldr: A unified numerical framework for optimal control of Lindblad master equations using structure-preserving full- and low-rank exponential integrators combined with sequential quadratic Hamiltonian optimization.
motivation: Optimal control of open quantum systems governed by the Lindblad equation requires repeated forward and adjoint solves that must preserve the density matrix structure and remain computationally feasible for large Hilbert spaces.
method: The continuous optimality system is derived via the Pontryagin maximum principle and solved with a sequential quadratic Hamiltonian (SQH) method, using second-order exponential midpoint propagators for forward and adjoint Lindblad equations with full-rank and low-rank formulations, including rigorous error estimates.
result: Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence rates, demonstrate the effectiveness of the low-rank approximations, and illustrate the performance of FREM-SQH and LREM-SQH for optimal control problems with smooth and nonsmooth control costs.
conclusion: The proposed structure-preserving exponential methods provide accurate and efficient optimal control for Lindblad equations, with low-rank variants substantially reducing storage and computational cost.

title: Time-Bin Properties Of Photon Pairs From A 2GHz Waveguide Resonator
authors: Kaisa Laiho Stefan Kazmaier
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We produce degenerate photon pairs called signal and idler via parametric down-conversion (PDC) in a Fabry-P\'erot waveguide resonator having close to a 2GHz bandwidth in the telecom C-band. Our PDC source is based on a type-II periodically-poled Lithium Niobate waveguide with high-reflecting end facets forming the resonator. We measure the strength of the photon-pair correlation between signal and idler after selecting a single resonator mode from the multimode PDC emission. Thereafter, we investigate their sub-nanosecond long pulse shapes, in other words the time bins, with standard photon counting. We find that the time-bin durations vary significantly from each other, which can be predicted by the different optical losses of the cross-polarized signal and idler. Further, we simulate the temporal properties of signal and idler via the Fourier transform of their joint spectral characteristics. Our results deliver empiric insight about the time bins of photon pairs and are relevant for driving future quantum networks at the edge to narrow bandwidths but nevertheless in the pulsed regime.

result: The time-bin durations of signal and idler vary significantly, which can be explained by their different optical losses; the measured pulse shapes are sub-nanosecond.
conclusion: These empirical insights into photon-pair time bins are relevant for developing narrow-bandwidth, pulsed quantum network sources.

title: Quantum Readout Complexity For Normalized Linear Functionals
authors: Roi Vence-Nogueira
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum numerical algorithms often encode a positive solution [MATH] in the amplitudes of a quantum state, while the required scientific output is a normalized linear functional of [MATH]. Basis measurements produce probabilities determined by squared solution values, while the functional uses the solution values themselves. We study the complexity of this output-interface problem for [MATH] and identify a target-dependent susceptibility [MATH] that governs the amount of copies of the solution state needed. For a fixed positive reference state and a neighborhood around it, the optimal number of unknown-state copies is [MATH], where [MATH] is the absolute error tolerance and [MATH] is the allowed failure probability. We show that two fixed single-copy measurements attain the same rate. We then analyze how this baseline changes when the interface retains classical information, uses adaptive allocation, supplies coherent access, or restricts the allowed solution family. Therefore [MATH] quantifies a central cost of using a solution encoded in an [MATH]-normalized quantum state to estimate an [MATH]-normalized linear observable.
tldr: The paper analyzes the copy complexity of estimating a normalized linear functional from a quantum state that encodes a solution in its amplitudes, identifying a target-dependent susceptibility that governs the optimal sample scaling.
motivation: Quantum numerical algorithms often encode the solution in amplitudes, but the desired scientific output is a normalized linear functional of the solution, while basis measurements only yield squared amplitudes, creating an output-interface problem.
method: The authors formulate the readout complexity for an M-normalized quantum state and derive the optimal number of unknown-state copies as a function of error tolerance and failure probability, then compare various measurement and access models.
result: They find that the optimal number of copies scales with a target-dependent susceptibility χ, and that two fixed single-copy measurements attain the same rate; they also analyze how the baseline changes with classical information retention, adaptive allocation, coherent access, and restricted solution families.
conclusion: The susceptibility χ quantifies a central cost of using an amplitude-encoded solution and provides a benchmark for readout complexity in quantum numerical algorithms.

title: Non-Orthogonal Amplitude Amplification For Hybrid Cv-dv Quantum Processors
authors: Jiyuan Liu, Joel Bierman, Yuan Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a non-orthogonal amplitude amplification (NOAA) method for hybrid continuous-variable- discrete-variable (CV-DV) quantum processors, where the available CV-assisted projector is not perfectly se- lective for the target state. We establish a bound on the achievable target-state fidelity, which is determined by the initial target-state amplitude and the selectivity of the accessible reflection operator. This bound limits the performance of NOAA in hybrid CV-DV systems. To mitigate this limitation, we propose using a squeezed CV ancilla to reduce the overlap between relevant CV states and a hybrid quantum signal processing (HQSP) filter to suppress errors arising from imperfect knowledge of the target eigenenergy. Numerical simulations show that, for small initial target-state amplitudes, our protocol achieves higher fidelity and efficiency than the repeat-until-success (RUS) method despite the presence of non-orthogonality. For large initial amplitudes, RUS is already efficient, and amplitude amplification provides little additional advantage.
tldr: Introduces a non-orthogonal amplitude amplification method for hybrid CV-DV quantum processors and bounds the achievable target-state fidelity due to imperfect reflection selectivity.
motivation: Amplitude amplification typically assumes orthogonal projectors, but hybrid CV-DV processors have non-orthogonal reflections that limit target-state fidelity.
method: The authors derive a fidelity bound and propose using a squeezed CV ancilla to reduce CV-state overlap plus a hybrid quantum signal processing filter to suppress errors from uncertain target eigenenergy, supported by numerical simulations.
result: For small initial target-state amplitudes, the protocol achieves higher fidelity and efficiency than repeat-until-success despite non-orthogonality; for large initial amplitudes, RUS is already efficient and amplification offers little advantage.
conclusion: The NOAA protocol mitigates non-orthogonality in hybrid CV-DV systems, but its benefit is mainly limited to the small-amplitude regime.

title: Matrix Product State Representatives Of Symmetry-Protected Phases
authors: Thomas Jackson
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide a simple ansatz for finding integer spin [MATH]-invariant matrix product states representing a phase for each triple of [MATH] topological indices studied in the literature by Tasaki and Ogata (corresponding to time-reversal and reflection symmetries) . Every combination of trivial and non-trivial indices has a spin-[MATH] [MATH], time-reversal, and site-reflection symmetric MPS representative with injectivity length [MATH]. We provide some exact examples for spin-[MATH] and a Fortran program which will find representatives of any triple for any integer spin, as well as some data from random sampling for small spin. The existence of such states agrees with the classification of Chen, Gu, and Wen , and with the recent results of Tasaki equating the hidden-order and one of Ogata's indices, wherein the Ogata index is that associated to the dihedral [MATH] symmetry.
tldr: The paper constructs explicit matrix product state representatives for symmetry-protected topological phases characterized by time-reversal and reflection indices.
motivation: Symmetry-protected topological phases are classified by topological indices, but explicit tensor network representatives for all index combinations are lacking.
method: The author provides an ansatz for integer spin MPS invariant under time-reversal and site-reflection symmetries, with a Fortran program to find representatives for any triple of indices.
result: Every combination of trivial and non-trivial topological indices has an MPS representative with injectivity length 2, and exact examples are given for spin-1.
conclusion: The existence of these MPS representatives agrees with the Chen-Gu-Wen classification and Tasaki's recent results relating to the classification of symmetry-protected topological phases.

title: Physics-Aware Power Optimization For Rydberg Quantum Arrays Via Barankin Bound Minimization
authors: Yixiao Li, Jiayi Zhang, Bokai Xu, Yin Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09421v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rydberg-atom quantum uniform linear arrays (RAQ-ULAs) offer a promising sensing architecture for direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation in terahertz (THz) beam alignment. Existing studies often model the quantum receiver as a macroscopic linear block and rely on the Cramer-Rao bound (CRB) for array evaluation or power allocation. However, as a local variance bound, the CRB cannot capture threshold breakdown caused by spatial ambiguities in low-signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) regimes. This paper proposes a physics-aware power optimization framework for RAQ-ULAs based on stochastic Barankin bound minimization. We derive a closed-form stochastic multipoint Barankin bound (BRB) matrix under a low-SNR integrability condition and introduce an arcsine-prior calibration to characterize bounded-domain error saturation. By incorporating a Lindblad-guided electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) readout model, we couple the ambiguity-sensitive BRB with photon shot noise, power broadening, and laser Rabi frequencies. A CRB-optimized analytical baseline is further derived to expose the limitation of local-SNR-based allocation. To solve the resulting nonconvex problem, we develop a backtracking majorization-minimization (MM) algorithm with a Lipschitz-based quadratic surrogate. The algorithm ensures monotonic decrease and converges to a feasible stationary point. Simulations show that the proposed framework predicts threshold breakdown more accurately than the CRB and enlarges the reliable operating region under severe THz attenuation.
tldr: The paper proposes a physics-aware power optimization framework for Rydberg-atom quantum uniform linear arrays in terahertz direction-of-arrival sensing, based on minimizing a stochastic Barankin bound.
motivation: Existing CRB-based evaluations fail to capture threshold breakdown from spatial ambiguities in low-SNR regimes, limiting reliable power allocation for Rydberg-array quantum receivers.
method: It derives a closed-form stochastic multipoint Barankin bound matrix, incorporates an arcsine-prior calibration and Lindblad-guided EIT readout model, and solves the resulting nonconvex problem via a backtracking majorization-minimization algorithm.
result: Simulations show the proposed framework predicts threshold breakdown more accurately than the CRB and enlarges the reliable operating region under severe THz attenuation.
conclusion: Barankin-bound minimization enables physics-aware power optimization that improves the practical operating range of Rydberg-atom arrays for THz beam alignment.

title: Improving The Constant In The Aharonov--Regev Theorem
authors: Shuhong Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Aharonov-Regev proof that [MATH] lies in [MATH] uses a verifier that tests dual lattice vectors; its proof gives [MATH]. We study this verifier through a linear program in which a certificate is modeled as a sample from a probability distribution on the dual lattice. This viewpoint gives an exact analysis of the close-target tests: adding gradient and Hessian checks increases the certified close radius from [MATH] to [MATH], and higher derivatives cannot improve it within this framework. With Gaussian certificates for far targets, we obtain $[MATH][MATH]c>2/(\pi\sqrt3)\approx0.3676$. An appendix gives a finite-bit implementation of the verifier. We also show that the Gaussian certificate is not always optimal and solve the unbounded-support program exactly for targets of order two, where its value is determined by the spectral capacity of an odd dual coset.
tldr: The paper improves the constant in the Aharonov-Regev theorem by analyzing the quantum verifier for the closest vector problem via a linear program and Gaussian certificates, achieving c > 2/(π√3) ≈ 0.3676.
motivation: The Aharonov-Regev theorem proved that the closest vector problem lies in QMA, but the constant in the proof was not tight; improving it may sharpen the completeness-soundness gap of the verifier.
method: The verifier is studied through a linear program where a certificate is modeled as a sample from a probability distribution on the dual lattice, using gradient and Hessian checks and Gaussian certificates for far targets.
result: Adding gradient and Hessian checks increases the certified close radius, Gaussian certificates yield c > 2/(π√3) ≈ 0.3676, and the Gaussian certificate is not always optimal; for order-two targets the unbounded-support program is solved exactly via the spectral capacity of an odd dual coset.
conclusion: The improved constant and exact analysis provide a better understanding of the Aharonov-Regev verifier, though higher derivatives cannot improve the bound within this framework.

title: Optimal (Parallel) Spooky Pebbling On Binary Trees
authors: Mingyu Lee, Sanghyun Lee, Kabgyun Jeong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pebble games model computations under a fixed space budget. Spooky pebbling allows quantum memory to be released by measurement, with the resulting phases corrected later. We study two-input computations with binary-tree dependencies and determine the optimal work and parallel depth for complete binary trees. Our key idea is to clean up the tree in blocks, reducing repeated recomputation of intermediate values. For the complete tree [MATH] with [MATH] vertices and every space budget [MATH], we give an algorithm with asymptotically optimal work [MATH]. At the minimum budget [MATH], this improves the [MATH] bound of Kornerup, Sadun, and Soloveichik to [MATH], resolving their time-optimality question. We also construct a parallel schedule with optimal depth \[ \Theta\!\left(h+\frac ns \max\!\left\{{\log(s+1)},\,1+\log^*h\right\}\right). \] Our lower bounds hold for every full binary tree. We also show that achieving optimal parallel depth can require asymptotically more work than minimizing work alone. Applying our schedule to the RNS point-addition trees in the public implementation of Chevignard, Fouque, and Schrottenloher reduces their Toffoli/AND gate count by [MATH] for a P-224 instance and [MATH] for a P-256 instance, using the same arithmetic circuits and peak workspace.
tldr: The paper determines optimal work and parallel depth for spooky pebbling on complete binary trees, improving prior bounds and applying the results to reduce gate counts in RNS point-addition implementations.
motivation: Pebble games model space-constrained computations, and spooky pebbling extends this to quantum memory release via measurement; previous bounds for binary trees were suboptimal and left time-optimality questions unresolved.
method: The authors design algorithms that clean up the tree in blocks to reduce repeated recomputation, prove matching lower bounds for every full binary tree, and construct a parallel schedule with optimal depth.
result: They achieve asymptotically optimal work for every space budget, improve the minimum-budget bound of Kornerup, Sadun, and Soloveichik, and reduce Toffoli/AND gate counts in public RNS point-addition implementations for P-224 and P-256 instances.
conclusion: Achieving optimal parallel depth can require asymptotically more work than minimizing work alone, and their schedule yields concrete improvements in quantum circuit gate counts for elliptic curve arithmetic.

title: Full Molecular Dynamics Simulations Of A Single Trapped Ion In A Neutral Bath
authors: Saajid Chowdhury, Ruiren Shi, Jes\'us P\'erez-R\'ios
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09268v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present full molecular dynamics simulations that explicitly incorporate the simultaneous interactions between a trapped ion and a bath of neutral atoms. In contrast to conventional molecular dynamics treatments, this framework enables a systematic assessment of how the atomic-gas density influences both the ion's cooling dynamics and its steady-state mean kinetic energy. Our results show that the gas density measurably modifies the ion's average kinetic energy, albeit only weakly, in qualitative disagreement with predictions obtained from standard molecular dynamics simulations. In addition, the calculations indicate that short-range features of the atom-ion interaction potential become increasingly consequential as the atomic density increases. Simulations including many atoms yield higher mean kinetic energies than standard molecular dynamics, a trend we attribute to the transient formation of molecular-ion complexes. Finally, we observe that for a fixed ion, lighter atomic baths lead to a smaller final ion average kinetic energy than heavier atomic baths.
tldr: Full molecular dynamics simulations reveal that a neutral atom bath weakly modifies a trapped ion's cooling dynamics and steady-state kinetic energy, with higher densities leading to molecular-ion complex formation and different behavior from standard MD.
motivation: To systematically assess how the density of a neutral atomic gas influences the cooling dynamics and steady-state mean kinetic energy of a trapped ion, going beyond conventional molecular dynamics treatments.
method: Full molecular dynamics simulations that explicitly incorporate simultaneous interactions between a trapped ion and a bath of neutral atoms, including many-atom simulations and varying bath atomic masses.
result: The gas density weakly modifies the ion's average kinetic energy, in qualitative disagreement with standard MD; many-atom simulations yield higher mean kinetic energies due to transient molecular-ion complexes, and lighter baths lead to lower final ion kinetic energy than heavier baths.
conclusion: Short-range features of the atom-ion interaction potential become increasingly important at higher densities, and explicit many-body effects must be accounted for in modeling trapped ion dynamics in neutral baths.

title: Pareto-optimal Quantum Kernel Selection For Unsupervised Anomaly Detection On Real Malware Beaconing Data
authors: Boaz Micah, Nadia Milazzo, Maissa Beji, Borja Aizpurua, Lloren\c{c} Espinosa-Portal\'es, Esteban Payares, Ghada Ben Slama, Luc Andrea, Michel Kurek, Thomas Cope, Olivier Salomon
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09717v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum kernel methods are leading candidates for a practical quantum advantage in machine learning, but assessing that potential requires two quantities usually reported separately: how well a kernel performs on the task, and how far its geometry departs from the classical kernels available for the same problem. We introduce a fully unsupervised, multi-objective protocol that optimises simultaneously the normalised pseudo discrepancy (NPD), a label-free proxy for anomaly detection quality, and the geometric difference (GD) to a tuned classical reference kernel, selecting models from the resulting Pareto front. We apply it to malware beaconing detection in real network traffic, using a one-class support vector machine with fidelity and projected quantum kernels over four data encodings, on simulators and on IQM's 20-qubit Garnet processor. NPD-guided selection alone finds a fidelity kernel that beats the tuned classical baseline, but with a geometric difference too small to certify the gain as quantum. Projected kernels reach far larger geometric differences; the Pareto-selected one only marginally exceeds the baseline (AUC [MATH] versus [MATH], [MATH] relative to that reference kernel), still below the NPD-selected fidelity kernel ([MATH]).
tldr: This paper introduces a multi-objective protocol for selecting quantum kernels in unsupervised anomaly detection, applied to malware beaconing data, but finds no certified quantum advantage.
motivation: Quantum kernel methods are promising for practical quantum advantage in machine learning, but performance and geometric departure from classical kernels are usually assessed separately.
method: The authors optimize normalized pseudo discrepancy (NPD) and geometric difference (GD) simultaneously, selecting models from the Pareto front, using one-class SVM with fidelity and projected quantum kernels over four encodings on simulators and a 20-qubit IQM processor.
result: NPD-guided selection finds a fidelity kernel that beats the tuned classical baseline but with too small a geometric difference to certify quantumness; projected kernels achieve larger GD but only marginally exceed the baseline in AUC.
conclusion: The study highlights the challenge of certifying quantum advantage in kernel-based anomaly detection and suggests that geometric difference alone may not suffice for practical quantum gains.

title: Task-Sufficient Contraction: Source Selection For Machine Information Interfaces
authors: Joss Armstrong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08884v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A declared task can sometimes certify a reduced source before a downstream encoder, codebook, rate, distortion target, or optimizer is chosen. This paper studies when one such reduction preserves the complete downstream problem family, a property termed Task-Sufficient Contraction. The reduced source is fixed by the task before the later operating point is selected. An exact contraction allows the later problem to be solved on that source with the same result as if the full source had been retained. For a machine with a fixed set of possible actions and a fixed loss, the paper identifies a consumer-specific source by merging states only when every available action has the same regret in both. For finite action sets, replacing the richer source by this reduced source preserves the complete one-step rate-regret curve, even though the reduction is fixed before the distortion target is chosen. A second result gives an exact characterization for quadratic loss on affine feasible-action sets: the canonical reduced source is the projection onto the directions in which feasible actions can differ. Under a fixed energy budget, this becomes centered load, while retaining only the optimal water-filled action is too coarse. Earlier Information Bottleneck, semantic rate-distortion, and goal-oriented quantization results are then used to distinguish exact, architecture-conditioned, approximate, failed, and corrected contractions. The framework suggests a way for heterogeneous machines to exchange what a receiving task needs without first aligning their full internal representations.
tldr: This paper introduces task-sufficient contraction, a method for selecting a reduced source that preserves the full downstream rate–regret problem family before any encoder or distortion target is chosen.
motivation: Heterogeneous machines need to exchange only task-relevant information without aligning their full internal representations, motivating a principled reduction of source data based on the receiving task.
method: The paper defines exact task-sufficient contraction and derives state-merging rules: for a fixed action set and loss, states are merged only when every action has the same regret; for quadratic loss on affine feasible-action sets, the canonical reduced source is the projection onto directions of action differences.
result: For finite action sets, the reduced source preserves the complete one-step rate–regret curve exactly, and under a fixed energy budget the centered load is sufficient while keeping only the optimal water-filling action is too coarse.
conclusion: The framework distinguishes exact, architecture-conditioned, approximate, failed, and corrected contractions, offering a way for machines to exchange task-specific information without full representation alignment.

title: Quantum Approximation Complexity Of Classical Optimization Problems
authors: Stuart Hadfield
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical approximation complexity asks what solution quality can be guaranteed with polynomial-time computation. The classes APX, PTAS, and FPTAS distinguish a fixed approximation ratio, approximation to any fixed accuracy, and approximation schemes whose running time is also polynomial in inverse accuracy. Their randomized counterparts are R-APX, R-PTAS, and R-FPTAS. We define bounded-error quantum counterparts BQ-APX, BQ-PTAS, and BQ-FPTAS. Membership requires a uniform quantum algorithm that, on every input, returns a feasible classical solution achieving at least the claimed approximation ratio with probability at least 2/3. Scores (objective values) must be efficiently classically computable. Running time includes parameter selection, preparation, measurement, decoding, and repetition. Many quantum optimization methods are used heuristically, and high benchmark scores alone do not establish these guarantees. We further establish a conditional hierarchy for logarithmic, polynomial, and exponential approximation factors. Assuming NP [MATH] BQP, the quantum classes form a strict hierarchy. Problems based on prime factorization and discrete logarithms give conditional quantum-classical separations. Certified Maximum Order has an exact quantum algorithm, while any randomized polynomial-time algorithm guaranteeing at least an inverse-polynomial approximation ratio on every input would yield efficient factoring. Discrete-Logarithm Fitting has an exact quantum algorithm and a deterministic one-half approximation, but any fixed improvement over one half would give a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for the safe-prime discrete logarithm problem. Our results show, under explicit complexity assumptions, that quantum computation can improve worst-case approximation guarantees. A quantum-classical gap for common problems such as MaxCut or MaxSAT remains open.
tldr: Defines bounded-error quantum counterparts of classical approximation complexity classes (BQ-APX, BQ-PTAS, BQ-FPTAS) and derives conditional hierarchies and quantum-classical separations for optimization problems.
motivation: Classical approximation complexity (APX, PTAS, FPTAS) does not capture what quantum polynomial-time algorithms can guarantee, yet quantum optimization heuristics are often claimed to succeed without such worst-case guarantees.
method: Introduces uniform quantum approximation classes requiring a quantum algorithm to output feasible classical solutions with approximation ratio guarantees at probability ≥ 2/3, then establishes a conditional hierarchy for logarithmic, polynomial, and exponential factors assuming NP ⊄ BQP, and constructs problems from factoring and discrete logarithm.
result: Assuming NP ⊄ BQP the quantum classes form a strict hierarchy; Certified Maximum Order and Discrete-Logarithm Fitting admit exact quantum algorithms with hardness of classical approximation, giving conditional quantum-classical separations, while gaps for MaxCut/MaxSAT remain open.
conclusion: Quantum computation can provably improve worst-case approximation guarantees under explicit complexity assumptions, but common problems like MaxCut and MaxSAT still lack a demonstrated quantum-classical gap.

title: Heat Transport Of The $\beta$-Fermi--Pasta--Ulam--Tsingou Chain In The Long-wave Limit
authors: Henrique Santos Lima, Matheus M. R. Poltronieri Martins, Lucas Reis E Silva
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Resolving the anomalous conductivity exponent of the symmetric [MATH]-Fermi--Pasta--Ulam--Tsingou chain by molecular dynamics can require very large systems because of long finite-size crossovers and thermal-contact resistance. Motivated by this computational challenge, we derive a long-wavelength continuum description and investigate whether the kinetic-theory scaling [MATH] becomes accessible with a moderate number of numerical degrees of freedom. The nonlinear elastic field retains the cubic stress of the microscopic interaction and exchanges heat with Langevin reservoirs. A flux-conservative spatial discretization constructs the force and energy current from the same stress, providing a consistent interior transport estimator. For [MATH], corresponding to approximately [MATH] mesh nodes and above at the reference resolution, the fitted exponent is [MATH]. Mesh refinement supports the stability of this exponent between the two finer resolutions, although the conductivity amplitude remains resolution-dependent. The main result is thus an accessible finite-size regime near [MATH], rather than convergence of the absolute conductivity as the mesh spacing vanishes. This formulation provides a practical route to studying anomalous transport in anharmonic systems and a conservative continuum framework for investigating energy flow in nonlinear elastic media.
