tldr: The paper derives a long-wavelength continuum description of heat transport in the classical β-Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou chain to access anomalous conductivity scaling at moderate system sizes.
motivation: Molecular-dynamics simulations of anomalous heat transport in the β-FPUT chain require very large systems due to long finite-size crossovers and thermal-contact resistance, motivating a continuum approach.
method: A nonlinear elastic field retaining the cubic stress of the microscopic interaction exchanges heat with Langevin reservoirs, and a flux-conservative spatial discretization provides a consistent interior transport estimator.
result: For system sizes corresponding to approximately 10^4 mesh nodes and above, the fitted conductivity exponent stabilizes at finer resolutions in a finite-size regime, although the conductivity amplitude remains resolution-dependent.
conclusion: The formulation offers a practical continuum route to study anomalous transport in anharmonic systems rather than relying solely on direct molecular dynamics.

title: Divide Et Impera Quantum Neural Networks For Modular Hybrid Computing Architectures
authors: Emanuele Casciaro, Fabio Mascherpa, Alfonso Amendola, Filippo Caruso
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum machine learning is rapidly emerging as a promising and potentially more sustainable approach that can complement traditional, energy-hungry HPC, AI, and GPU resources-particularly for the demanding global challenges the world urgently needs to address. In recent years, the first prototypes of quantum processors have reached the market, are sometimes available via the cloud, and distributed quantum computing is beginning to move from a largely theoretical concept to a demonstrated reality. However, these devices are still noisy and qubit-limited. Therefore, it is desirable to design quantum machine learning models with a reduced quantum register and a limited number of quantum gates, avoiding overly deep and wide quantum circuits. Here, we explore this idea by proposing a novel divide-et-impera-based training protocol that splits quantum neural networks into smaller components and better governs their optimization. We benchmark our approach on real data and real-world prediction tasks in intertwined energy and environmental domains, such as the status of charging stations for electric vehicles and the global air quality index. Our results suggest a design principle for quantum machine learning algorithms across a wide range of applications, which can be more feasibly tested on state-of-the-art quantum processors or within modular quantum architectures being developed for future hybrid infrastructures interconnected via high-speed communication links.
tldr: The paper proposes a divide-and-conquer training protocol for quantum neural networks that splits large models into smaller trainable components to better suit noisy, qubit-limited quantum processors.
motivation: Quantum machine learning is seen as a sustainable complement to energy-hungry HPC and AI, but current quantum devices remain noisy and qubit-limited, so shallow and narrow circuits are needed.
method: The authors introduce a divide-et-impera training strategy that decomposes quantum neural networks into smaller modules and benchmarks it on real-world prediction tasks in energy and environmental domains, including electric vehicle charging station status and global air quality index.
result: The results suggest improved optimization control and feasibility for state-of-the-art quantum processors or modular hybrid quantum architectures interconnected by high-speed communication links.
conclusion: The work proposes a design principle for quantum machine learning algorithms that can be more feasibly tested on near-term quantum hardware and future modular quantum infrastructures.

title: Second-Order Image Characterization With Distortion And Secrecy
authors: Cao Daming
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09472v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Image-size characterization connects coding constraints to the probability carried by source cells and their output images. At second order, this connection must retain the joint fluctuations of all active constraints and distinguish encoder-observable source variation from unobserved channel noise. We extend the single-output posterior characterization to simultaneous posterior and conditional-composition image bounds. The bounds preserve the actual coupling of multiple outputs, quantify conditional likelihood losses for irregular cells, and admit actual-distortion marks. Two further extensions replace disjoint counting by weighted reconstruction-policy images and replace output cardinality by posterior-mass constraints for secrecy. Direct applications yield matching second-order regions for compatible multi-source helper intersections, one lossy reconstruction with several informed lossless reconstructions, Gaussian common/private descriptions, and privacy amplification from a prescribed conditional type. The Gaussian description result also gives joint rate--distortion offsets. For general helper sections, genuinely lossy informed reconstruction, Gaussian Wyner--Ziv coding, and reconciliation followed by extraction, the same image methods give explicit rate bounds with their remaining losses identified. The resulting rate corrections reflect both the image constraints and the observations available to each terminal.
tldr: The paper develops second-order image-size characterizations for multi-output lossy coding with distortion and secrecy, extending posterior and conditional-composition bounds to joint fluctuations.
motivation: Second-order rate characterizations require retaining joint fluctuations of all active constraints and distinguishing encoder-observable source variation from unobserved channel noise.
method: It extends single-output posterior characterization to simultaneous posterior and conditional-composition image bounds, using weighted reconstruction-policy images and posterior-mass constraints for secrecy.
result: It yields matching second-order regions for multi-source helper intersections, one lossy reconstruction with several informed lossless reconstructions, Gaussian common/private descriptions, and privacy amplification from a prescribed conditional type, along with joint rate–distortion offsets.
conclusion: The same image methods give explicit rate bounds and identify remaining losses for general helper sections, genuinely lossy informed reconstruction, Gaussian Wyner–Ziv coding, and reconciliation followed by extraction.

title: Cost Of Delay For Post-Quantum Migration: Putting Classical And Harvest-Now-Decrypt-Later Risk On One Ordered List
authors: Animesh Shaw
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Organisations deciding which assets to migrate to post-quantum cryptography first, and how that work competes with a backlog of classical findings, lack a common unit: post-quantum scores are dimensionless and quantum-only, while classical risk is annualised loss. We express both threats as a cost of delay in currency per year on the same asset. The quantum term is the rate at which deferring migration commits irreversible harvest-now-decrypt-later loss, computed from required confidentiality duration, recordable traffic share and data turnover, using a quantum-arrival law fitted in closed form to published expert anchors. A competing-risks factor couples the two terms so the same loss is not counted twice. We prove that the construction is not a weighted sum of a classical and a quantum score, give a dominance threshold on the classical hazard that is independent of asset value, and show that the induced order is optimal for sequencing work under constant loss rates. We verify the implementation by simulation, adaptive quadrature and a second implementation. On four public systems with parameters assumed from public documentation, the quantum term reorders the asset list beyond input uncertainty for one system only (signal-to-noise 1.36 against 0.14-0.46), moves specific long-lived, quiet, recordable assets decisively, and otherwise changes magnitudes. Asset value and turnover explain 73-91% of the uncertainty in the quantum term; the arrival date explains 3-17%. The case studies are illustrative and are not validated against outcomes.
tldr: The paper proposes expressing classical and harvest-now-decrypt-later post-quantum migration risk as a common cost-of-delay in currency per year to prioritize remediation on one ordered list.
motivation: Organizations lack a common unit to compare the urgency of post-quantum cryptography migration against a backlog of classical security findings.
method: It derives a quantum cost-of-delay term from confidentiality duration, recordable traffic share, data turnover, and a fitted quantum-arrival law, then couples it with classical risk via a competing-risks factor and validates the construction through simulation and a second implementation.
result: On four illustrative public systems, the quantum term reorders assets decisively only for one system, moves long-lived quiet recordable assets, and its uncertainty is explained mostly by asset value and turnover rather than quantum arrival date.
conclusion: The framework offers a principled way to sequence post-quantum migration and classical remediation on one list, but the case studies are illustrative and not validated against real outcomes.

title: On Optimal Encodings And Systematicity In Function-Correcting Codes
authors: Charul Rajput, Kanchana Lokshmii Jagatti, B. Sundar Rajan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Function-correcting codes (FCCs) protect the value of a function [MATH] of the message against [MATH] errors. In the original formulation of Lenz et al. (2023), the encoding is systematic, and the lower bound of [MATH] on the redundancy relies on this form. Recently, D. Ho (arXiv, 2026) showed, for linear functions and linear encodings, that systematicity can cost redundancy. We begin with the OR function to show that the cost is not confined to the linear setting: a non-systematic encoding attains redundancy [MATH] while every systematic encoding needs [MATH]. For a linear function [MATH] and a fixed linear code [MATH], let [MATH] denote the minimum distance between codewords of messages with different function values. Different generator matrices of [MATH] assign different codewords to the messages and can give different values of [MATH]. We study which generator matrix of [MATH] gives the largest [MATH]. We give an algorithm that constructs an optimal generator matrix and determines the optimal value as the weight of a codeword in a greedy basis of [MATH]. We then characterize, in terms of information sets, when a generator matrix in systematic form attains this optimum, and give a necessary condition that is checked on the low-weight codewords of [MATH] alone. For two-valued functions, we drop both linearity and systematicity. Using the minimality of initial segments of the simplicial order with respect to Hamming neighbourhoods, we show that a non-systematic [MATH]-FCC of length [MATH] exists if and only if a condition depending on [MATH] only through the size of its smaller preimage holds. For [MATH], redundancy [MATH] is sufficient for every nonconstant two-valued function on [MATH] with [MATH]. For general [MATH], redundancy [MATH] suffices for all two-valued functions once [MATH] is large enough, and for each [MATH] we give an upper bound on the threshold in [MATH] beyond which redundancy [MATH] suffices.
tldr: This paper studies function-correcting codes, showing that systematic encodings can be suboptimal even beyond the linear setting and providing algorithms and characterizations for optimal non-systematic encodings.
motivation: Function-correcting codes protect the value of a function of the message, and the original systematic encoding formulation may incur extra redundancy; the paper investigates when and how non-systematic encodings can improve redundancy.
method: The authors use the OR function, analyze generator matrices of linear codes, introduce a greedy basis and information set characterization, and leverage initial segments of the simplicial order for two-valued functions.
result: They show a non-systematic encoding attains better redundancy than any systematic encoding for OR, give an algorithm to construct an optimal generator matrix, characterize when systematic form is optimal, and provide a characterization for two-valued functions.

title: Function-Correcting Lee-distance Codes For Symbol-Pair Read Channels
authors: B. Sundar Rajan Hareesh K.
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09491v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Function-correcting codes (FCCs) protect specified function evaluations of messages against errors while reducing the redundancy required for reliable communication. We study FCCs for symbol-pair read channels, motivated by high-density storage systems that read overlapping symbol pairs. Phase-shift keying (PSK) modulation is well-suited to such systems due to its bandwidth efficiency and noise robustness. While FCCs for symbol-pair read channels have been studied under the Hamming metric, the Lee metric is a more appropriate error model for [MATH]-ary PSK and, hence for [MATH]-ary symbol-pair read channels. We generalize the symbol-pair Lee distance, previously defined only over [MATH], to [MATH], [MATH], and introduce function-correcting symbol-pair Lee-distance codes (FCSPLCs) over [MATH], specializing to [MATH], [MATH], for [MATH]-ary PSK constellations. We investigate their redundancy requirements by introducing irregular-pair Lee-distance codes and relating the optimal redundancy of FCSPLCs to the shortest length of such codes. We derive Plotkin-type and Gilbert--Varshamov-type bounds on the optimal redundancy through lower and upper bounds on the shortest length of irregular-pair Lee-distance codes. For bijective functions, we obtain corresponding Plotkin-type and Gilbert--Varshamov-type bounds for classical Lee metric codes for symbol-pair read channels over [MATH], which, to the best of our knowledge, are the first such bounds for the Lee metric symbol-pair setting. We then specialize the FCSPLC framework to pair-locally bounded functions, the Pair-Lee weight function, and the Pair-Lee weight distribution function, giving explicit constructions and corresponding bounds on the optimal redundancy. Finally, for linear functions, we derive a Plotkin-type lower bound on the optimal redundancy.
tldr: The paper introduces function-correcting symbol-pair Lee-distance codes for PSK-based symbol-pair read channels and derives bounds on their optimal redundancy.
motivation: High-density storage systems read overlapping symbol pairs, and the Lee metric is more appropriate for M-ary PSK; function-correcting codes reduce redundancy by protecting only specified function evaluations of messages.
method: The authors generalize symbol-pair Lee distance, define function-correcting symbol-pair Lee-distance codes, introduce irregular-pair Lee-distance codes, and derive Plotkin-type and Gilbert-Varshamov-type bounds on optimal redundancy.
result: They obtain bounds on the optimal redundancy of FCSPLCs, specialize to pair-locally bounded functions and Pair-Lee weight functions, and for bijective functions give the first Plotkin and Gilbert-Varshamov bounds for classical Lee metric codes in the symbol-pair setting.
conclusion: The framework extends function-correcting codes to symbol-pair Lee-metric channels, providing redundancy bounds and constructions, but remains entirely within classical coding theory without quantum extension.

title: Non-Hermitian Cooperation Induced Chern Insulator
authors: Weiwei Zhu, Bingbing Wang, Mengxiang Xie, Hong-Yu Zou, Yang Long, Hong-Xiang Sun, Haoran Xue, Jie Ren
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09413v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional Chern insulators rely on breaking time-reversal symmetry via magnetic fields or synthetic gauge fields. Here we introduce a fundamentally different paradigm: a static lattice without any gauge field becomes a Chern insulator solely through the cooperation of two non-Hermitian ingredients: on-site loss and non-reciprocal coupling. Neither effect alone suffices; only their synergy opens a topological gap and gives rise to robust chiral edge states with a nonzero Chern number. The underlying mechanism originates from a non-Hermitian chiral molecule formed by the lossy sites, whose dynamically dominant mode carries an orbital angular momentum that effectively generates a synthetic flux after the fast-decaying degrees of freedom are eliminated. Our results establish non-Hermitian cooperation as a versatile resource for inducing Chern topology without external fields or temporal modulations, opening a new route to topological phases in open classical and quantum systems.
tldr: A static non-Hermitian lattice combining on-site loss and non-reciprocal coupling realizes a Chern insulator with chiral edge states and nonzero Chern number, without any external magnetic field or synthetic gauge field.
motivation: Conventional Chern insulators require broken time-reversal symmetry via magnetic or synthetic gauge fields, motivating a search for alternative mechanisms that generate topological band gaps from intrinsic non-Hermitian ingredients instead of external fields.
method: The authors study a tight-binding lattice where on-site loss cooperates with non-reciprocal hopping; eliminating the fast-decaying degrees of freedom yields an effective description in which a non-Hermitian chiral molecule of lossy sites carries orbital angular momentum that acts as a synthetic flux.
result: Neither loss nor non-reciprocity alone is sufficient; only their synergy opens a topological gap and produces robust chiral edge states with a nonzero Chern number, demonstrating a non-Hermitian cooperation induced Chern insulator phase.
conclusion: Non-Hermitian cooperation is proposed as a versatile resource for inducing Chern topology in open classical and quantum platforms without external fields or temporal modulation, suggesting new routes to field-free topological phases.

title: Quantum Anomaly Detection In Real Scarce Data
authors: Emanuele Casciaro, Fabio Mascherpa, Alfonso Amendola, Filippo Caruso
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09635v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anomaly detection on small and unbalanced datasets remains very challenging in machine learning, although this scenario is common in several domains, including healthcare, cybersecurity, finance, and energy. Data augmentation and generative AI may mitigate training-data scarcity, but they often fall short because anomalies are, by definition, unpredictable, rare, and highly diverse events compared to high-probability normal data. Overfitting to pseudo-anomalies, model collapse, high-dimensional data, uninterpretable black-box models, and validation challenges are typical issues limiting their practical applicability. In this context, quantum machine learning may provide a promising and more sustainable avenue because it can enable more interpretable models with far fewer trainable parameters and smaller datasets, implementable on energy-efficient quantum hardware. Here, we propose a novel two-step hybrid classical--quantum architecture for sequential data and test it on a realistic scenario in the global energy-transition domain, i.e., automated anomaly detection in large-scale photovoltaic plants. The achieved generalization capability and competitive prediction accuracy may pave the way for new hybrid learning models able to exploit the continuously increasing power of cloud-available and more sustainable quantum accelerators integrated with more traditional energy-hungry High Performance Computing resources.
tldr: A two-step hybrid classical-quantum machine learning architecture is proposed for anomaly detection on small, unbalanced sequential data and tested on automated fault detection in large-scale photovoltaic plants.
motivation: Anomaly detection with scarce, unbalanced data is challenging, and classical augmentation/generative approaches suffer from overfitting to pseudo-anomalies and model collapse; quantum machine learning is proposed as a more interpretable and energy-efficient alternative with fewer trainable parameters.
method: A hybrid classical-quantum pipeline tailored to sequential data is developed and applied to a realistic energy-transition use case, namely anomaly detection in photovoltaic-plant monitoring data.
result: The approach achieves competitive prediction accuracy and good generalization capability on the realistic photovoltaic anomaly-detection scenario using small datasets.
conclusion: Hybrid quantum-classical learning may enable sustainable anomaly-detection models exploiting cloud-available quantum accelerators alongside traditional HPC resources.

title: On The Complexity Of The Single-move Labeled Token Routing Problem
authors: Nicolas Bousquet, Remy El Sabeh, Amer E. Mouawad, Naomi Nishimura
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09084v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In neutral-atom quantum computers, atoms are moved to target positions along paths of empty positions, and a target position may be reserved for one species of atom. Motivated by this task, we introduce Single-Move Labeled Token Routing: every source and every target vertex of a graph is assigned a set of labels, and tokens occupy the sources. A solution consists of a matching that assigns each source to a compatible target (one whose label set intersects its own), a route for each matched pair, and a movement order in which, when a token is moved, its route contains no other token. The problem is known to be polynomial-time solvable when every source is compatible with every target, and [MATH]-complete on grid graphs when each source is compatible with exactly one target. We prove that the latter case remains [MATH]-complete on grids and on planar graphs of maximum degree four even when some solution has pairwise edge-disjoint routes. On trees, the problem is known to be [MATH]-complete even for maximum degree three. We study trees through the solution edge multiplicity, the largest number of routes of a solution sharing an edge, and the candidate edge multiplicity, the largest number of compatible pairs whose paths share an edge. We prove that on trees of maximum degree three, the problem is [MATH]-hard parameterized by a bound on the solution edge multiplicity, even when a movement order is given, and that on trees of unbounded degree, it is [MATH]-complete even when the candidate edge multiplicity is at most eight. We show that on trees the problem is fixed-parameter tractable parameterized by the maximum degree together with the candidate edge multiplicity, and also by the candidate vertex multiplicity, the same count at vertices. Unless [MATH], neither the maximum degree nor the candidate edge multiplicity can be omitted.
tldr: The paper studies the computational complexity of a single-move labeled token routing problem motivated by atom rearrangement in neutral-atom quantum computers, proving hardness and FPT results on grids, planar graphs, and trees.
motivation: In neutral-atom quantum computers, atoms must be moved along paths of empty sites to target positions that may be reserved for a specific species, motivating a combinatorial routing problem whose complexity is poorly understood.
method: The authors formalize Single-Move Labeled Token Routing, prove NP-completeness on grids/planar max-degree-4 graphs even with pairwise edge-disjoint routes, and analyze trees via solution and candidate edge/vertex multiplicity parameters to derive W-hardness and fixed-parameter tractability results.
result: The routing problem remains NP-complete under strong structural restrictions, is W[1]-hard parameterized by solution edge multiplicity even when a movement order is given, is NP-complete on unbounded-degree trees with candidate edge multiplicity at most eight, and is FPT in maximum degree plus candidate (edge/vertex) multiplicity.
conclusion: The work delineates the complexity landscape of atom-routing in neutral-atom architectures, showing that neither maximum degree nor candidate edge multiplicity can be dropped from the FPT parameterization unless standard complexity assumptions fail.

title: Vibrational Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization With Unitary-Cluster-Jastrow Ans\"atze On Ibm QPUs
authors: Kunal Kumar, Erik L\"otstedt, Yuri Kobayashi, Seiji Yunoki
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09532v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We extend sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) to anharmonic vibrational spectra and use it to benchmark how vibrational ans\"atze scale on present-day hardware under a direct one-hot encoding (up to 72 qubits). Five particle-conserving circuits are warm-started through vibrational coupled-cluster (VCC) t1, t2 amplitudes: UVCCSD, the compact heuristic circuit (CHC), and three unitary-cluster-Jastrow ans\"atze introduced here, VLUCJ, Vg-uCJ, and VIm-uCJ. A self-consistent configuration-recovery loop reconstructs correlated states from hardware samples in the low-retention regime where na\"ive post-selection breaks down, enabling the calculation of ground-state energies for H[MATH]O, CH[MATH]O, and CH[MATH]ClF (3-9 modes). We compare harmonic-oscillator and vibrational self-consistent-field (VSCF, "modal") reference bases. In the small-modal-basis regime relevant for near-term devices, the modal basis is typically more accurate than the harmonic-oscillator representation; empirically, it also yields substantially better-converged hardware sampling for deep circuits at these qubit counts. Across ans\"atze, we find a clear retention/accuracy tradeoff when scaling: the new VLUCJ circuit is the most hardware-robust, retaining the largest fraction of physically valid one-hot outcomes, whereas the more expressive uCJ variants and UVCCSD can recover more correlation when retention is sufficient. Finally, we extend the recovery protocol to excited states by targeting a chosen per-mode VSCF occupation and warm-starting it with a state-specific VCC calculation, and we demonstrate the calculation of one representative fundamental vibrational frequency per molecule on IBM QPUs.
tldr: The paper extends sample-based quantum diagonalization to anharmonic vibrational spectra and benchmarks vibrational ansätze on IBM quantum processors.
motivation: Near-term quantum devices may help compute molecular vibrational spectra, but existing ansätze face retention and accuracy tradeoffs on real hardware.
method: Five particle-conserving circuits are warm-started with vibrational coupled-cluster amplitudes and evaluated using a self-consistent configuration-recovery loop on up to 72 qubits.
result: The new VLUCJ circuit is most hardware-robust, while more expressive uCJ variants and UVCCSD recover more correlation when retention is sufficient; modal bases often outperform harmonic-oscillator bases.
conclusion: The work demonstrates proof-of-concept vibrational frequency calculations on IBM QPUs and highlights retention/accuracy tradeoffs for scaling vibrational ansätze.

title: Achieving A Long Lifetime Synchronized State In A Thermal Vapor Rydberg Time Crystal
authors: William J. Watterson, Dixith Manchaiah, Christopher L. Holloway
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time crystals are a unique and recently discovered state of matter in which time-translational symmetry is spontaneously broken. Although this state has been observed across a variety of quantum systems, understanding the nature between driving, dissipation, and noise and the effects of these forces on the state lifetime remains elusive. Here, we study phase diffusion and entrainment of the time crystalline oscillatory state of a thermal-vapor Rydberg atom ensemble. We apply a pulsed rf heterodyne driving field which can entrain the oscillation frequency during the on driving period. During the off period, the entrained ensemble phase diffuses on a 1/[MATH] timescale up to 2.3 ms -- significantly longer than the Rydberg state lifetime. We additionally study how the entrainment and phase diffusion timescales are affected by the strength and detuning of the rf driving field, and develop a classical Fokker-Planck model with an Adler-based driving term that reproduces the observed experimental findings. These results demonstrate the creation of a long-time synchronized time crystal Rydberg atom ensemble state, which could be utilized in applications requiring frequency and phase stability.
tldr: The paper realizes a long-lived synchronized time-crystalline state in a thermal Rydberg vapor by entraining its oscillation with pulsed rf driving and models phase diffusion with a classical Fokker-Planck equation.
motivation: Time crystals offer a platform to study spontaneous time-translation symmetry breaking, but the interplay of driving, dissipation, and noise on their lifetime and synchronization remains poorly understood.
method: A thermal-vapor Rydberg atom ensemble is subjected to pulsed rf heterodyne driving to entrain the time-crystal oscillation; phase diffusion during off periods is measured, and a classical Fokker-Planck model with an Adler driving term is developed.
result: The entrained ensemble phase diffuses on a timescale up to 2.3 ms, significantly longer than the Rydberg state lifetime, and the entrainment and phase diffusion timescales depend on rf driving strength and detuning, reproduced by the model.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a long-time synchronized time crystal in Rydberg atoms, potentially useful for applications requiring frequency and phase stability.

title: Compact Fully Integrated Alignment-Free And Linearly Polarized Ho$^{3+}$ Single-Frequency Waveguide Laser
authors: Jeswin Jacob, T Toney Fernandez, Dale Otten, Ori Henderson-Sapir, 3 Karen Privat, David Lancaster
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09435v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report, for the first time, a fully integrated Ho[MATH]-doped fluoride glass waveguide laser incorporating a femtosecond laser-inscribed waveguide and waveguide Bragg grating. The compact 12.4 mm cavity achieves stable single-frequency lasing at 2062.21 nm with a line width of better than 5 MHz. The laser emits linearly polarized light, which is efficiently delivered through an SM1950 single-mode fiber. This alignment-free architecture provides a compact and robust platform for integrated mid-infrared single-frequency laser sources.
tldr: A compact fully integrated Ho3+-doped fluoride glass waveguide laser achieves stable single-frequency linearly polarized lasing at 2062.21 nm with <5 MHz linewidth.
motivation: There is a need for compact robust mid-infrared single-frequency laser sources for applications such as sensing and spectroscopy.
method: The device integrates a femtosecond laser-inscribed waveguide and a waveguide Bragg grating in Ho3+-doped fluoride glass, forming a 12.4 mm cavity.
result: The laser emits at 2062.21 nm with a linewidth better than 5 MHz, linearly polarized output, and efficient delivery through SM1950 single-mode fiber.
conclusion: This alignment-free architecture provides a compact and robust platform for integrated mid-infrared single-frequency laser sources.

title: The Geometry Of Lee-Yang Tensors
authors: Jake Hofgard
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09485v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide a geometric description of Lee-Yang tensors, building upon several recent results of Bravyi, Gosset, Liu, and Wong. By applying tools from complex Perron-Frobenius theory, we generalize one of their key lemmas to bound the spectral ratio of non-normal operators with Lee-Yang radius greater than one. As a direct consequence, we provide a local-to-global principle for bounding spectral gaps of Suzuki-Fisher Hamiltonians, a family of [MATH]-local Hamiltonians, using only the Lee-Yang radius of each local operator to bound the gap from below. On the other hand, we develop a simple perturbative technique to show that the Gibbs states of [MATH]-local Hamiltonians, [MATH], cannot have Lee-Yang radius at least one for all inverse temperatures [MATH]. We apply this same method to conclude that Suzuki-Fisher Hamiltonians are precisely those Hamiltonians whose Gibbs states are Lee-Yang at all inverse temperatures [MATH].
tldr: The paper provides a geometric description of Lee-Yang tensors and applies complex Perron-Frobenius theory to bound spectral gaps of Suzuki-Fisher Hamiltonians and characterize their Gibbs states.
motivation: Recent results by Bravyi, Gosset, Liu, and Wong on Lee-Yang tensors motivate a deeper geometric understanding and generalization to non-normal operators and local Hamiltonians.
method: The author uses complex Perron-Frobenius theory to generalize a key lemma for bounding spectral ratios, and develops a perturbative technique for analyzing Gibbs states of local Hamiltonians.
result: A local-to-global principle bounds spectral gaps of Suzuki-Fisher Hamiltonians via local Lee-Yang radii, and it is shown that Suzuki-Fisher Hamiltonians have Gibbs states that are locally indistinguishable.

title: Sample-based Quantum Simulation Of Vibrational Structure Of Polyyne Chains
authors: Sarah Mostame, Tanvi P. Gujarati, Alberto Baiardi, Abhijit Mitra, Dimitar Trenev, Sumathy Raman
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting anharmonic vibrational spectra is a complex computational task, which becomes quickly infeasible as molecular size and the number of vibrational basis functions increase, leading to an exponential growth of the underlying Hilbert space. Here, we employ a sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) framework to compute anharmonic vibrational energies and spectra. The approach combines quantum state preparation and sampling with configuration recovery, diagonalization of the Hamiltonian projected in a subspace of basis configurations, and calculation of transition-dipole moments to obtain both vibrational energies and infrared spectra. We investigate two approaches for sampling, namely, vib-LUCJ and vib-SqDRIFT and apply the method to study the polyyne molecules C[MATH]H[MATH] and C[MATH]H[MATH], reaching representations requiring up to 104 qubits. Beyond energies, transition-dipole calculations reveal that infrared intensities and excited-state composition continue to evolve with basis size through anharmonic mixing and intensity redistribution, even when low-energy eigenvalues appear converged. These results show that sample-based quantum subspace methods can capture spectroscopic information in vibrational spaces far beyond the regime of full diagonalization. Moreover, our simulation identify multi-state recovery and scalable projected-space treatment as central challenges for further scaling sample-based approaches.
tldr: This paper applies a sample-based quantum diagonalization framework to compute anharmonic vibrational energies and infrared spectra of polyyne chains using up to 104 qubits.
motivation: Predicting anharmonic vibrational spectra becomes computationally infeasible as molecular size grows, motivating quantum-computing approaches that can handle exponentially large vibrational Hilbert spaces.
method: The authors combine quantum state preparation and sampling via vib-LUCJ and vib-SqDRIFT with configuration recovery, subspace Hamiltonian diagonalization, and transition-dipole moment calculations to obtain vibrational energies and IR intensities.
result: They compute spectra for C8H2 and C12H2, reaching 104-qubit representations, and find that IR intensities and excited-state composition continue to evolve with basis size even when low-energy eigenvalues appear converged.
conclusion: Sample-based quantum subspace methods can capture spectroscopic information beyond full diagonalization, but multi-state recovery and scalable projected-space treatment remain key challenges for further scaling.

title: Q-PhotoMarket: A Design Space Exploration Framework For Photonic Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks In Financial Market Prediction
authors: Alberto Marchisio, Hanzalah Mohamed Siraj, Muhammad Kashif, Nouhaila Innan, Muhammad Shafique
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photonic quantum computing has recently emerged as a promising platform for hybrid quantum machine learning due to its native realization of linear-optical circuits and the computational complexity of boson sampling. However, despite growing interest in quantum methods for finance, the influence of photonic circuit design choices on predictive performance remains largely unexplored. Existing studies typically evaluate a single architecture, leaving the broader photonic design space unexamined. In this work, we present Q-PhotoMarket, a systematic design space exploration (DSE) framework for photonic hybrid quantum neural networks (HQNNs) applied to financial market prediction. We explore over 5,000 valid photonic configurations spanning input photon states, circuit architectures, entangling models, and measurement strategies across their compatible computation spaces, for U.S., Indian, and cryptocurrency markets. To improve search efficiency, the exhaustive exploration is complemented with Bayesian optimization. We further incorporate threshold calibration and prediction-collapse diagnostics to enable reliable evaluation under increasingly imbalanced return thresholds. Experimental results show that systematic exploration of more than 5,000 photonic HQNN configurations reveals consistent architectural patterns across financial markets, identifies robust high-performing designs, and demonstrates competitive performance relative to classical machine learning baselines.
tldr: Q-PhotoMarket systematically explores over 5,000 photonic hybrid quantum neural network configurations for financial market prediction, using Bayesian optimization to identify robust architectures and competitive performance against classical baselines.
motivation: Photonic quantum computing is promising for hybrid quantum machine learning, but the impact of photonic circuit design choices on predictive performance in finance remains largely unexplored, with existing studies evaluating only single architectures.
method: The paper introduces a design space exploration framework spanning input photon states, circuit architectures, entangling models, and measurement strategies, complemented by Bayesian optimization, threshold calibration, and prediction-collapse diagnostics across U.S., Indian, and cryptocurrency markets.
result: Systematic exploration reveals consistent architectural patterns across markets, identifies robust high-performing designs, and demonstrates competitive performance relative to classical machine learning baselines.
conclusion: The framework provides a systematic approach to designing photonic hybrid quantum neural networks for financial prediction, though its primary contribution lies in applied quantum machine learning rather than quantum information theory or the researcher's listed directions.

title: A Minimal Bicomplex Extension Of The Complex Scalar Algebra Of Quantum Mechanics With An Ideal-Valued Sector
authors: Ralf Otte
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09747v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard quantum mechanics takes the complex numbers as its scalar algebra. We ask whether this complex structure is algebraically fundamental or may instead form a distinguished embedded sector of a larger commutative and associative scalar algebra. Requiring the ordinary complex sector to remain intact while admitting an additional stable complex-like analytic sector turns the latter into a proper ideal, makes zero divisors unavoidable in finite dimension, and implies a lower bound of four real dimensions. The bicomplex algebra realizes this minimum, and under an additional compatibility assumption the four-dimensional realization is unique up to isomorphism. The resulting algebra exhibits two distinct decompositions: the canonical decomposition into orthogonal idempotent ideals and a decomposition adapted to the embedded complex sector and the additional ideal-valued sector. The ordinary complex scalars therefore lie diagonally across the canonical idempotent decomposition. The ideal sector supports Taylor series, oscillatory exponentials, Fourier-type kernels, and Schr\"odinger-type expressions, and carries a formal ideal-valued eigenvalue structure. Restricting the Born rule to the embedded complex sector recovers its standard form. Whether this dual scalar architecture has physical significance beyond the algebraic framework remains an open question.
tldr: The paper proposes a minimal bicomplex extension of the complex scalar algebra of quantum mechanics, yielding an ideal-valued sector and studying its algebraic properties.
motivation: It questions whether the complex numbers are algebraically fundamental in quantum mechanics or whether they can be embedded in a larger commutative associative scalar algebra.
method: By requiring an intact complex sector and an additional stable complex-like analytic sector, the authors derive a proper ideal, zero divisors, and a four-dimensional minimum, realized by bicomplex numbers with uniqueness up to isomorphism under compatibility.
result: The bicomplex algebra admits two decompositions—canonical idempotent and the embedded complex/ideal decomposition—and supports Taylor series, oscillatory exponentials, Fourier-type kernels, Schrödinger-type expressions, and formal ideal-valued eigenvalues, while the Born rule reduces to standard form on the complex sector.
conclusion: The physical significance of this dual scalar architecture remains open; the work is purely algebraic/foundational and does not address mainstream quantum information or thermodynamics topics.

title: Numerical Bogoliubov Approximation Of Bosonic Many-body Quantum Dynamics
authors: Yoann Le H\'enaff, Christian Lubich, Peter Pickl
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an algorithm for the numerical solution of the time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation for N >> 1bosons interacting via a two-body interaction potential in the mean-field scaling regime. Unlike existing numerical algorithms for quantum dynamics, the proposed algorithm has a computational complexity that is independent of the number N of particles. It is based on an ansatz for the wave function inspired by the Bogoliubov theory, which is an asymptotic theory for large N. In a first part, we follow Bogoliubov theory in evolving the condensate function by the Hartree equation, but we use the Dirac--Frenkel time-dependent variational principle to derive nonlinear equations of motion for the excitation functions in the Bogoliubov ansatz. By carefully exploiting the bosonic symmetry, the so obtained approximate wave functions are shown to have derivatives bounded independently of N apart from a time-dependent global phase factor which rotates with a frequency proportional to N. In the second part, we numerically approximate the wave function (modulo the phase) by a composite algorithm, which employs an appropriate splitting of the equations of motion and uses a dynamical low-rank approximation of the fundamental two-particle excitation function by linear combinations of products of single-particle functions. The low-rank excitation function is evolved in time by a basis update and Galerkin (BUG) integrator that is robust to small singular values of the coefficient matrix and allows for rank adaptivity. Numerical results are provided to assess the performance of the proposed algorithm.
tldr: A numerical algorithm based on the Bogoliubov ansatz and dynamical low-rank approximation is proposed for simulating the time-dependent Schrödinger equation of many bosons with complexity independent of particle number N.
motivation: Simulating large bosonic many-body quantum dynamics is computationally challenging because standard numerical methods scale poorly with the number of particles N.
method: The condensate is evolved via the Hartree equation, excitation functions are derived using the Dirac-Frenkel time-dependent variational principle, and the resulting equations are integrated with a splitting scheme and a basis-update-and-Galerkin (BUG) low-rank integrator.
result: The approximate wavefunction has derivatives bounded independently of N (up to a global phase rotating with frequency proportional to N), and numerical tests assess the algorithm's performance.
conclusion: The proposed algorithm enables efficient numerical simulation of mean-field bosonic quantum dynamics with computational cost independent of N.

title: Distance Structure Of Insertion Kernels And Local Port Response In Non-Reciprocal Su--Schrieffer--Heeger Chains
authors: Bin Guo Xudong Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-reciprocal lattices offer a flexible setting for directional wave transport, raising the question of how enhanced internal scattering translates into transmission between fixed external ports. We address this question for non-reciprocal Su--Schrieffer--Heeger (SSH) chains with staggered gain and loss by relating the reference-dependent insertion kernel [MATH] to the coherent transmission intensity [MATH]. On a fixed finite graph, a strong-insertion expansion gives a contribution proportional to [MATH], whose coefficient is the signed sum of shortest directed paths of length [MATH]. When this sum is nonzero, it sets the leading behavior independently of fixed diagonal losses; when it cancels, those losses can enter the first surviving higher-order term. For a fixed cross-sublattice endpoint channel, transmission has a strictly negative slope at every nonzero differentiable stationary point of the kernel magnitude. In the weak-insertion regime, the reference-system coefficient [MATH] predicts the initial transmission change for symmetric SSH ports, and [MATH] together with a strictly stable baseline guarantees local stable enhancement. Finite-chain calculations and driven dynamics connect these results to observable response and distinguish asymptotic convergence from transient settling. A strictly dissipative short-chain example exhibits local enhancement without net power gain. Together, these results separate graph-path structure, coherent port response, and dynamical establishment, providing channel-specific criteria for interpreting internal scattering.
tldr: The paper relates insertion kernels to coherent transmission in non-reciprocal Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chains with gain and loss, providing graph-path-based criteria for local port response.
motivation: Non-reciprocal lattices enable directional wave transport, but it is unclear how enhanced internal scattering maps to transmission between fixed external ports.
method: The authors use a strong-insertion expansion, signed sums over shortest directed paths, stationary point analysis, and finite-chain plus driven dynamics calculations.
result: The leading transmission behavior is set by shortest directed path sums, a negative slope appears at stationary points of the kernel magnitude, and weak-insertion coefficients predict initial changes and local stable enhancement.
conclusion: The work separates graph-path structure, coherent port response, and dynamical establishment, offering channel-specific criteria for interpreting internal scattering and showing local enhancement without net power gain in a dissipative short-chain example.

title: Spurious Zero-dispersion Continua In Full $(2,q)$-positivity: A Linear Hierarchy-depth Lower Bound From An Exactly Solvable Counting Operator
authors: Maho Nakata
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational two-particle reduced-density-matrix methods impose hierarchies of semidefinite constraints. We ask whether a fixed level of such a hierarchy can recover even an elementary many-fermion spectrum, using the dispersion test, in which a value is accepted as an eigenvalue when the minimized dispersion vanishes. For an exactly solvable operator that counts fermions in one half of the spin orbitals, whose spectrum consists of integers, we determine the complete set of accepted values at every level of the full hierarchy of particle-hole semidefinite constraints. Besides the integers, this set contains an entire interval of noninteger values unless the hierarchy level grows linearly with the particle number, and we give the exact threshold. The proof constructs explicit pseudo reduced density matrices that are diagonal in the occupation basis, obtained by continuing the occupation probabilities of a fixed-particle-number state to a noninteger particle number. Classical semidefinite constraints on occupation correlations, supplemented by nonnegative occupation-pattern probabilities, suffice to establish fermionic positivity. For this counting model the two relaxations have the same dispersion zero set, not necessarily the same feasible states, and a converse argument shows that no other false eigenvalues occur. The limitation is specific to the hierarchy: two-body inequalities that encode the integer spectrum would remove every false value but are not generated at a fixed level. We also verify that the full semidefinite constraints and their complete projection onto two-particle reduced-density-matrix space are equivalent in finite dimensions, so that the result applies equally to the polar formulation.
tldr: The paper analyzes spurious zero-dispersion values in the full (2,q)-positivity hierarchy for fermionic reduced density matrices, proving a linear hierarchy-depth lower bound using an exactly solvable counting operator.
motivation: Variational two-particle reduced-density-matrix methods impose semidefinite hierarchies, and the authors ask whether a fixed hierarchy level can recover even elementary many-fermion spectra via the dispersion test.
method: They construct explicit pseudo reduced density matrices diagonal in the occupation basis by analytically continuing fixed-particle-number occupation probabilities to noninteger particle number, and compare the full semidefinite hierarchy with its classical occupation-correlation relaxation.
result: Besides the integer eigenvalues, the accepted set contains an entire interval of noninteger values unless the hierarchy level grows linearly with particle number, with an exact threshold; both relaxations share the same dispersion zero set and no other false eigenvalues occur.
conclusion: The limitation is intrinsic to fixed-level two-body inequalities, which fail to remove spurious values, whereas higher-level constraints encoding the integer spectrum would eliminate all false values.

title: Reconstruction Of Geometric And Structural Aspects Of Undeciphered Messages By Information-theoretic Methods
authors: Abicumaran Uthamacumaran Hector Zenil
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08861v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In previous work, we established sufficient conditions for recovering geometry and topology from non-random information, demonstrating reconstruction with the Arecibo message. Undeciphered historical records present a related problem: one-way communication without access to their makers' intentions or encoding conventions. Here we extend this framework to the Phaistos Disc, Andean khipu, Rongorongo, Indus inscriptions and the Voynich manuscript, using Egyptian layouts and Arecibo as controls. Algorithmic information dynamics (AID) guides structural perturbations, combining classical information measures, predictive coding, compression and algorithmic-probability-based estimates. Phaistos retains 0.714 bits of excess adjacent-sign mutual information after positional controls; its authentic segmentation lies within a broad information basin, and cross-face boundary prediction achieves AUCs of 0.76 and 0.86. Repetition explains its principal recurrence, while the tested spiral embeddings provide no evidence of additional cross-winding structure. Across several corpora, comparative transfer persists beyond exact shared local pairs. Khipu knot forms distinguish authentic attachments after controlling for degree, depth, fibre and twist (adjusted [MATH]); constrained assignment recovers 8.75\% of concealed parents against 7.87\% expected by chance. Row-alignment tests yield no comparable evidence after correction. Calibrated BDM recovers Arecibo's 23-column width (search-corrected [MATH]), while executable controls detect spatial dependence and eliminate it through interventions on the generator. These findings connect information-based structural reconstruction with interventional reasoning, distinguishing recoverable organisation from semantic decipherment.
tldr: The paper applies algorithmic information dynamics and classical information measures to reconstruct structural aspects of undeciphered historical messages such as the Phaistos Disc, khipu, Rongorongo, Indus inscriptions, and the Voynich manuscript.
motivation: Undeciphered records pose a one-way communication problem where encoding conventions and intentions are unknown, motivating information-theoretic methods to recover geometric and structural organization without semantic decipherment.
method: The authors extend their previous framework using algorithmic information dynamics (AID) to guide structural perturbations, combining classical information measures, predictive coding, compression, and algorithmic-probability-based estimates, with Egyptian layouts and the Arecibo message as controls.
result: They find excess mutual information and structural regularities in several corpora, including Phaistos Disc segmentation and cross-face prediction, khipu knot attachment distinctions, and recovery of Arecibo's 23-column width, while row-alignment tests yield no comparable evidence.
conclusion: The findings connect information-based structural reconstruction with interventional reasoning, distinguishing recoverable organization from semantic decipherment.

title: Shadow-Free Scattering With Complex Frequency Excitations
authors: Vitali Kozlov, Wei Wang, Seunghwi Kim, Arno Thielens, Andrea Alu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The optical theorem dictates that the wave scattering of an object in the forward direction is proportional to the total power extinguished from the excitation. For passive objects, this relationship is a by-product of the intuitive notion that scattering and absorption necessarily create shadows, and that zero forward scattering, i.e., no shadow, can only be obtained if the object is fully transparent, i.e., it neither scatters nor absorbs. Materials with gain can be in principle leveraged to suppress forward scattering while preserving a large scattering signature in other directions. However, sufficient optical gain is challenging to realize, and it inherently leads to instabilities and nonlinearities. Here, we experimentally demonstrate shadow-free \ scattering from a passive high-index dielectric sphere by exciting it with a complex frequency signal tailored to mimic the presence of material gain. We achieve as much as 26dB suppression of the forward scattering when compared with optimal monochromatic excitations, while preserving strong scattering in other directions. More broadly, our results demonstrate how complex frequencies offer a natural pathway to enhance control over the scattering signature of passive objects, with implications for a range of photonic applications.
tldr: The paper experimentally demonstrates shadow-free forward scattering from a passive high-index dielectric sphere using complex frequency excitations tailored to mimic material gain.
motivation: The optical theorem ties forward scattering to extinction, and for passive objects zero forward scattering seems to require full transparency; gain materials could break this but introduce instabilities.
method: They excite a passive high-index dielectric sphere with a complex frequency signal that mimics gain, measuring forward scattering suppression compared to optimal monochromatic excitations.
result: They achieve up to 26 dB suppression of forward scattering while maintaining strong scattering in other directions.
conclusion: Complex frequency excitations provide a natural pathway to control scattering signatures of passive objects, with potential photonic applications.

title: Electromagnetic Field Of An Oscillating Point Charge Measured By A Transversely Comoving Observer
authors: Shengwang Du Ruben Canora
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09445v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the electromagnetic field produced by a harmonically oscillating point charge and measured by a spatially separated observer undergoing the same motion. We evaluate the exact retarded field on the observer's worldline and project the electromagnetic field tensor onto the observer's local orthonormal tetrad. This construction yields the electric and magnetic fields, electromagnetic energy density, and Poynting vector measured as functions of the observer's proper time. Our formulation separates unambiguous local observables from the observer-dependent classification of a field as radiation and provides a concrete setting in which to examine how a charge that is spatially static in a non-inertial coordinate system can nevertheless produce time-dependent locally measured fields.
tldr: The paper computes the exact electromagnetic field of a harmonically oscillating point charge as measured by a spatially separated observer undergoing the same motion.
motivation: The authors aim to clarify how local electromagnetic observables and the classification of radiation depend on the observer's motion, especially for non-inertial observers.
method: They evaluate the retarded Liénard–Wiechert field on the observer's worldline and project the electromagnetic field tensor onto the observer's local orthonormal tetrad.
result: The construction yields the measured electric and magnetic fields, electromagnetic energy density, and Poynting vector as functions of the observer's proper time.
conclusion: The formulation separates unambiguous local observables from observer-dependent radiation classification and illustrates how a charge static in a non-inertial frame can still produce time-dependent locally measured fields.

title: Absence Of Absolutely Continuous Spectrum For One-Dimensional Capacitance Operators With Critical Long-Range Interactions
authors: Jiayu Qiu Habib Ammari
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09582v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we establish the absence of absolutely continuous spectrum for scalar one-dimensional Laurent operators with multiplicative disorder and critical long-range hoppings. In particular, the requirement of at least quartic off-diagonal decay rate in the existing theory is bypassed by exploiting the finite-difference bound of the convolution kernel, which is available even when the interaction decays only as [MATH] with [MATH]. We then apply the abstract main result to a concrete physical model, the capacitance operator in subwavelength physics. For a chain of three-dimensional resonators with one resonator per period, we verify the required decay and finite-difference estimates and conclude the absence of absolutely continuous spectrum. These results leave open the distinction between pure point and singular continuous spectrum, but constitute a key step in proving Anderson localization in wave systems with critical long-range interactions.
tldr: The paper proves the absence of absolutely continuous spectrum for one-dimensional capacitance operators with critical long-range interactions, extending existing spectral theory for random Laurent operators.
motivation: Anderson localization in wave systems with long-range interactions is not fully understood, especially when off-diagonal decay is weaker than the quartic rate required by prior theory.
method: The authors exploit finite-difference bounds on convolution kernels to bypass the quartic decay condition, then verify the required estimates for a chain of three-dimensional resonators modeled by a capacitance operator.
result: They establish the absence of absolutely continuous spectrum for scalar one-dimensional Laurent operators with multiplicative disorder and critical long-range hoppings, including the concrete subwavelength resonator chain.
conclusion: This is a key step toward proving Anderson localization in wave systems with critical long-range interactions, though the distinction between pure point and singular continuous spectrum remains open.

title: Tightness And Error Exponents Of Sdp With Logarithmically Many Communities
authors: Shengtao Guo, Ethan X. Fang, Junwei Lu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation for community recovery when the number of communities grows logarithmically. In the balanced stochastic block model with [MATH] vertices, we consider the regime [MATH], with edge probabilities [MATH] within communities and [MATH] across them, for fixed [MATH]. We derive the sharp asymptotic tightness boundary away from critical cases. When rare vertices cause tightness to fail while the bulk remains spectrally stable, the normalized matrix error of every near-optimal solution still vanishes. We prove matching high-probability exponents for this error and the normalized optimal objective gain, governed by the same local correction that determines tightness. Throughout this spectrally stable region, a single SDP solve followed by explicit rounding and refinement achieves exact community recovery above the information-theoretic threshold. This guarantee holds even when the planted community matrix is not an optimal solution to the SDP.
tldr: This paper analyzes sharp tightness boundaries and high-probability error exponents for a semidefinite programming relaxation in balanced stochastic block models with a logarithmically growing number of communities.
motivation: Community recovery in stochastic block models is a fundamental statistical inference problem, and understanding when SDP relaxations achieve exact recovery is of theoretical interest.
method: The authors study an SDP relaxation under the regime with M communities growing logarithmically, derive the sharp asymptotic tightness boundary, and prove matching high-probability exponents for the normalized matrix error and objective gain.
result: They show that when rare vertices cause tightness to fail while the bulk is spectrally stable, the normalized matrix error of every near-optimal solution still vanishes, and a single SDP solve with explicit rounding and refinement achieves exact community recovery above the information-theoretic threshold.
conclusion: The guarantees hold even when the planted community matrix is not an optimal SDP solution, providing a tight characterization of SDP performance in the logarithmic-community regime.

title: Open Problem: Computing Bayes-Nash Equilibrium In Simple Security Games
authors: Vincent Conitzer
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08796v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This is an open problem originally posed during the program "Economics and Computation" held in the Fall 2015 semester at the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing. It asks whether a (Bayes-)Nash equilibrium can be computed in polynomial time for Bayesian simple security games.
tldr: This paper poses an open problem asking whether a Bayes-Nash equilibrium can be computed in polynomial time for Bayesian simple security games.
motivation: The problem originated from the Economics and Computation program at the Simons Institute, aiming to clarify the computational complexity of equilibrium computation in security games.
method: The paper is an open problem statement rather than a technical contribution, surveying the context and formulation of Bayesian simple security games.
result: No computational result is proven; the central question remains open regarding polynomial-time computability of Bayes-Nash equilibria in this game class.
conclusion: The work highlights a gap in algorithmic game theory and invites further research on the complexity of equilibrium computation in security settings.

title: Visible-Spectrum Optical Covert Channels In Commodity Smart Lighting
authors: David Noever
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Smart light-emitting diode (LED) bulbs are networked devices that produce information-carrying output. This study asks whether that light can carry digital data through changes small enough to be difficult for a person in the room to notice. To explore this covert communication channel, we tested an unmodified smart bulb (Philips WiZ A19) using a camera as the receiver. Binary data were encoded programmatically in nearly matched color and brightness changes. Because the differences were deliberately small across 16 million color steps, the receiver periodically measured known reference states and used them to compensate for changes in the camera and background room illumination. The color method successfully transmitted the short message 'hi' using a color difference (E) of 0.5, a standard measure of perceptual color distance. The receiver recovered 99% of the transmitted bits, and the complete message passed an integrity check. The brightness method remained decodable at the smallest nonzero integer difference tested, alternating between dimming settings 56 and 54, with 96.2% mean bit accuracy across two runs. When both binary symbols were assigned to the same brightness in a control experiment, accuracy fell to approximately chance. These results show that the visible output of an ordinary smart bulb can serve as a low-rate data channel without hardware modification. Camera color drift can overwhelm small signals unless the receiver is recalibrated during transmission, sudden changes in ambient light can disrupt decoding, and longer messages require stronger error correction. The color experiment operated at a difference below a conventional threshold for human color discrimination. The corresponding perceptual limit for the brightness method has not yet been established experimentally.
tldr: A commodity smart LED bulb can transmit digital data covertly through imperceptibly small color and brightness changes detected by a camera.
motivation: The study investigates whether the visible light output of networked smart bulbs can serve as a low-rate covert communication channel without hardware modification.
method: Binary data were encoded in nearly matched color and brightness variations using a Philips WiZ A19 bulb, with a camera receiver that periodically measured reference states to compensate for drift and ambient light changes.
result: The color method transmitted 'hi' with a perceptual color difference of 0.5 and 99% bit recovery, while the brightness method achieved 96.2% accuracy at the smallest nonzero integer difference; control runs degraded to chance.
conclusion: Ordinary smart bulbs can act as low-rate data channels, but reliable decoding requires recalibration, resilience to ambient light, and error correction for longer messages.

title: Understanding And Mitigating Token-Pruning-Induced Vulnerabilities In VLMs
authors: Shuailong Wang, Xinyu Lyu, Shengming Yuan, Jingkuan Song, Heng Tao Shen, Lianli Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09703v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Token-Pruning accelerates Vision-Language Models by removing redundant visual tokens, yet its safety implications remain underexplored. In this work, we present the first comprehensive safety evaluation of Token-Pruning mechanisms and find that: most pruning strategies significantly degrade safety as pruning ratios increase, whereas Query-based Compression shows the opposite, with extreme pruning (up to 99.8%), unexpectedly improves model safety. This sharp contrast prompts a key question: How do different Token-Pruning strategies reshape model safety behavior, and is it possible to enhance safety without sacrificing acceleration? To answer this, we identify an unrecognized mechanism, termed Pruning-Induced Malicious Amplification, where removal of background tokens triggers a side effect: forcing the model's attention to collapse onto a few retained malicious anchors within the foreground, inadvertently amplifying their toxic semantics under jailbreak. To address that, we propose an inference-time and plug-and-play Safety-Aware Pruning (SAP) mechanism that counteracts such dominance via three steps: (1) identifying malicious anchors, (2) restoring pruned benign tokens, and (3) reallocating excessive attention from malicious anchors to benign tokens. Extensive experiments across three safety and four utility benchmarks demonstrate that SAP mitigates pruning-induced vulnerabilities, i.e., reducing ASR by up to 62%, without compromising efficiency or utility.
tldr: This paper evaluates safety vulnerabilities introduced by token-pruning in vision-language models and proposes an inference-time safety-aware pruning mechanism to mitigate them.
motivation: Token-pruning is widely used to accelerate vision-language models, but its safety implications remain underexplored. The authors aim to understand how different pruning strategies affect model safety and whether safety can be enhanced without sacrificing efficiency.
method: They conduct a comprehensive safety evaluation across multiple pruning strategies and identify a mechanism called Pruning-Induced Malicious Amplification. To counter it, they propose Safety-Aware Pruning (SAP), which identifies malicious anchors, restores pruned benign tokens, and reallocates attention away from malicious anchors.
result: Experiments across three safety and four utility benchmarks show that SAP reduces attack success rate by up to 62% while maintaining efficiency and utility, and reveal that query-based compression can unexpectedly improve safety at high pruning ratios.
conclusion: Token-pruning can significantly affect model safety, and the proposed SAP effectively mitigates pruning-induced vulnerabilities without compromising acceleration or performance.

title: Trust A Few: The Weakest Assumptions A Protocol Needs
authors: Aalok Thakkar Bhumika Mittal
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09730v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protocol verifiers check whether a protocol meets a security goal under stated trust assumptions, such as that a key is never leaked, a value is fresh, or a channel is authentic. They do not say which of those assumptions the goal needs. Rowe, Guttman and Liskov asked for the weakest assumptions under which a protocol achieves a goal and left the question open. We answer it for assumptions about keys, values and channels. Call a run that violates the goal an attack, and the assumptions that would rule it out its stopping set. The least a protocol must trust to meet a goal is exactly the set of minimal ways to stop all of its minimal attacks. Several such sets may exist. The answer becomes unique once either/or assumptions are allowed, and it is a single set exactly when every minimal attack is stopped by a single assumption. A Galois connection between assumptions and goals explains why: a goal may end in "or", but its hypothesis may not. The same structure gives the trust needed by a conjunction of goals and an exact condition under which composed protocols need no extra trust. To compute the answer, a loop asks a verifier whether a candidate suffices, records what stops each attack it reports, and recomputes the candidates. Deciding whether some trust of at most k assumptions suffices is NP-hard. With a bounded analyser of our own and with CPSA, the loop finds the weakest trust for 18 goals over ten protocols and their variants, and on each it agrees with evaluating every trust using the same verifier. The answers include an assumption that our model of the adopted fix of Kerberos PKINIT states but the client's authentication of the server does not need, and channel assumptions under which Needham-Schroeder meets its goal in a bounded model.
tldr: This paper characterizes the weakest trust assumptions a security protocol needs to achieve a goal, using minimal stopping sets for attacks and a Galois connection, with NP-hardness and a loop-based verifier.
motivation: Protocol verifiers require trust assumptions but do not identify which assumptions are necessary for a security goal, a question left open by Rowe, Guttman, and Liskov.
method: The authors formalize attacks as runs violating a goal and define stopping sets of assumptions that rule them out, then compute minimal trust sets via a loop that queries a verifier, records stopping conditions, and recomputes candidates.
result: They show the weakest trust corresponds to minimal hitting sets of minimal attacks, prove the problem NP-hard, and demonstrate the loop on 18 goals over ten protocols including Kerberos PKINIT and Needham-Schroeder.
conclusion: The framework answers the weakest-assumptions question for key, value, and channel assumptions and clarifies when composed protocols need no extra trust, but it is a classical formal-methods contribution with no quantum information relevance.

title: Faster Pmns Multi-precision Multiplications Using Truncated Montgomery Technique
authors: Laurent-St\'ephane Didier, Alexy Dutois-Ruiz, Jean-Marc Robert
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Polynomial Modular Number Systems (PMNS) aim to represent elements of fields or rings of large characteristics using polynomials satisfying bounds on some parameters (degree, absolute values of the coefficients). Those PMNS, while some conditions are fulfilled, using convenient parameters and implementation features, allow some speed-ups in cryptographic computations. Recent works (Meloni ) propose better speed-ups by improving the parameter generation of the system, and by using multi-precision polynomial coefficients, i.e. coefficients stored using several machine words. In this work, we first present PMNS schoolbook software implementation better in some context than the Toeplitz state-of-the-art counterpart of , taking advantage of smaller memory cost by being free to choose a smaller [MATH] parameter, minimizing at the same time the complexity of the multiplication. This implementation for 4096 bit modulo size shows element size smaller by 11\% and 20 \% speed-up. We thus present a new improvement on the PMNS, applying to the an approach similar to the truncated Montgomery reduction technique presented by Didier in . In the context of software implementations using instruction set extension, and modulo size up to 8192 bits, this new approach allows speed-ups up to 15\% in modular multiplication computation, in comparison with conventional approaches.
tldr: The paper presents faster multi-precision modular multiplication in Polynomial Modular Number Systems using a truncated Montgomery reduction technique.
motivation: PMNS can speed up cryptographic computations, and improving parameter selection and multi-precision coefficient handling may yield better performance for large moduli.
method: The authors develop a schoolbook PMNS software implementation with smaller memory cost and then adapt a truncated Montgomery reduction approach for multi-precision polynomial coefficients.
result: For 4096-bit moduli, the implementation reduces element size by 11% and achieves 20% speed-up; for moduli up to 8192 bits, the truncated Montgomery technique yields up to 15% speed-up in modular multiplication.
conclusion: The proposed PMNS variants provide practical speed and memory improvements over conventional approaches for large-modulus cryptographic arithmetic.

title: Vector Beams For Real-time Monitoring Of Crystalline Symmetry On {\mu}m Length Scale
authors: Yongbo Lv, Zidu Yu, Haotian Zhang, Liejia Qian, Hao Chu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symmetry constrains and determines the physical properties of crystalline solids. Determining crystalline symmetry often requires large-scale diffraction facility and advanced analysis software and therefore cannot be realized with real-time feedback. Alternatively, optical anisotropy has also been exploited for elucidating the rotation, mirror and inversion symmetries of solids on smaller tabletop setups. Second harmonic generation, in particular, has demonstrated a remarkable sensitivity to subtle changes in these symmetries during phase transitions. To access the full nonlinear susceptibility of a crystal in a cryogenic or vacuum environment, angle-by-angle rotation of the scattering plane of an obliquely incident and outgoing beam in co-ordination with their polarization states is required. This typically results in a bulky and wobbly setup, significant feedback latency, and a focal spot size > 20 {\mu}m unsuitable for microscopic samples such as few-layer 2D materials. In this work, we make use of vector beams to realize a non-rotating oblique-incidence setup, demonstrating a real-time (> 10 fps) visualization of crystalline symmetry on a sample area of ~ 2 {\mu}m in diameter. Both the feedback latency and focal spot size represent more than an order of magnitude improvement over previous designs based on a Gaussian beam and mechanically-rotating stages. Here, the use of a vector beam greatly simplifies and reduces the cost of nonlinear optical anisotropy measurements, heralding widespread applications of this approach in both research and industrial settings, for example, for strain monitoring and crystal alignment. Our work may also promote broader integration of structured optical field into solid state and condensed matter research in the future.
tldr: Vector beams enable real-time visualization of crystalline symmetry on a ~2 µm scale via nonlinear optical anisotropy measurements.
motivation: Determining crystalline symmetry usually requires large-scale diffraction facilities, while tabletop optical anisotropy methods need bulky mechanically rotating setups that are slow and have large focal spots.
method: The authors use vector beams to implement a non-rotating oblique-incidence setup that accesses the full nonlinear susceptibility of a crystal without angle-by-angle rotation.
result: They demonstrate real-time (>10 fps) crystalline symmetry visualization over a ~2 µm diameter area, improving feedback latency and focal spot size by more than an order of magnitude over Gaussian-beam designs.
conclusion: This approach simplifies and reduces the cost of nonlinear optical anisotropy measurements, with potential applications in strain monitoring, crystal alignment, and broader integration of structured optical fields into condensed matter research.

title: A Unified Framework For Characterizing General Mimo Channels
authors: Zeyan Zhuang, Anzheng Tang, Xin Zhang, Dongfang Xu, Shenghui Song
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08932v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern MIMO systems are evolving toward higher-dimensional and more flexible architectures, such as distributed and holographic MIMO, offering substantial benefits while giving rise to increasingly complex channel correlation structures. This growing architectural diversity makes it difficult to characterize the fundamental limits of different MIMO systems on a case-by-case basis, motivating a unified analytical framework applicable across a broad range of architectures. This paper addresses this research gap by investigating a generally correlated Rayleigh channel whose vectorized form follows a general Gaussian distribution with an arbitrary covariance matrix. For that purpose, we first prove that the spectral norm of the channel matrix is bounded in the asymptotic regime where the numbers of transmit and receive antennas grow proportionally.
