To address this gap, we formulate red teaming for vision-grounded web agents as an end-to-end grounding-to-execution problem, and introduce WebMirage, a framework that crafts localized visual perturbations that cause agents to select attacker-controlled content and execute the corresponding browser action across varying webpage renderings. It uses a role-slot abstraction and webpage recomposition to capture competition among webpage elements, and dataflow analysis to align optimization with action post-processing. We evaluate WebMirage across four agent configurations and six VLM backbones on 2,250 tasks covering 13 public websites and a sandbox benchmark. WebMirage achieves an average attack success rate of 91.9%, compared with 17.4% for the strongest baseline, and remains effective against three agent-level defenses.
tldr: WebMirage is a red-teaming framework that crafts localized adversarial visual perturbations to make vision-language web agents select attacker-controlled UI elements and execute unintended browser actions end-to-end.
motivation: Existing visual red-teaming of web agents only targets model inference, ignoring structured input processing and action post-processing, so model-level attack success does not guarantee control over actual browser execution.
method: The framework formulates red teaming as an end-to-end grounding-to-execution problem, using a role-slot abstraction with webpage recomposition to model element competition and dataflow analysis to align perturbation optimization with downstream action post-processing.
result: Across four agent configurations and six VLM backbones on 2,250 tasks over 13 public websites plus a sandbox benchmark, WebMirage attains a 91.9% average attack success rate versus 17.4% for the strongest baseline, and remains effective against three agent-level defenses.
conclusion: The work shows that adversarial image perturbations can reliably hijack vision-grounded web agents through to browser execution, highlighting the need for end-to-end robustness evaluation and defenses at the agent level.

title: Package Hallucination Attacks On Coding Agents Through Prompt Injection In Rule Files
authors: Yupu Wang, Zhengyuan Jiang, Reachal Wang, Neil Zhenqiang Gong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09264v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern agentic coding frameworks increasingly rely on community-shared rule files (e.g., AGENTS.md or .cursorrules) to guide autonomous code generation, yet the security risks of this pipeline remain underexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce the package hallucination attack, where an attacker injects malicious prompts into benign rule files to induce coding agents to replace legitimate dependencies with attacker-controlled packages. To obtain effective malicious prompts injected into rule files, we propose PackHallu, an evolutionary optimization framework that iteratively rewrites these injected prompts using trajectory-level feedback and LLM-guided mutations. Evaluations across multiple benchmarks, LLMs, and agent frameworks show that PackHallu achieves high attack success rates and strong transferability across diverse models and agent combinations. Our findings demonstrate that coding agents are vulnerable to package hallucination attacks, highlighting the urgent need for stronger security safeguards in autonomous coding systems.
tldr: The paper introduces a 'package hallucination attack' in which malicious prompts injected into community-shared coding-agent rule files (e.g., AGENTS.md, .cursorrules) trick LLM coding agents into substituting attacker-controlled packages for legitimate dependencies.
motivation: Agentic coding frameworks increasingly rely on shared rule files to steer autonomous code generation, but the security risks of this supply-chain-like pipeline are underexplored.
method: The authors propose PackHallu, an evolutionary optimization framework that iteratively rewrites injected prompts using trajectory-level feedback and LLM-guided mutations to maximize attack success.
result: Evaluations across multiple benchmarks, LLMs, and agent frameworks show high attack success rates and strong transferability across diverse model and agent combinations.
conclusion: Coding agents are vulnerable to package hallucination attacks, underscoring the need for stronger security safeguards in autonomous coding systems.

title: Ask The Expert: LLM-Guided Reinforcement Learning For Autonomous Cyber Defense
authors: Fernando Martinez, Abhishek Satyam, Tao Li, Junaid Farooq, Ying Wang, Juntao Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09337v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Policy-based reinforcement learning (RL) approaches have produced promising results for autonomous cyber defense; however, they are sample-inefficient in settings where defenders must respond under delayed, partial observations with actions from large action spaces. While large language models (LLMs) may reason semantically about security state space, high latency and trust assumptions prevent attractive in-line deployment models. We introduce Ask the Expert, a training-time guidance framework which first summarizes hard cyber-defense states, then intermittently queries an LLM for host-level defensive recommendations via a constrained action interface, and finally transforms those recommendations into tiered reward shaping for use with PPO. Because the LLM is discarded after training, deployment is a pure RL policy. Across TTCP CAGE CC1 and CC2 and both attacker types, this asymmetric design improves sample efficiency over PPO and outperforms the evaluated potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) baselines, while retaining the strongest terminal mean and requiring no LLM dependency at deployment time.
tldr: The paper introduces 'Ask the Expert,' a training-time framework that uses an LLM to generate tiered reward shaping for a PPO-based autonomous cyber-defense policy, discarding the LLM at deployment.
motivation: Policy-based RL for autonomous cyber defense is sample-inefficient under delayed, partial observations and large action spaces, and in-line LLM deployment is impractical due to latency and trust issues.
method: The framework summarizes hard cyber-defense states, intermittently queries an LLM through a constrained action interface for host-level recommendations, and converts these into tiered reward shaping used to train a PPO agent.
result: On TTCP CAGE CC1 and CC2 across two attacker types, the asymmetric design improves sample efficiency over PPO and outperforms potential-based reward shaping baselines while retaining the strongest terminal mean.
conclusion: LLM guidance at training time can substantially improve RL sample efficiency for cyber defense without incurring any LLM dependency during deployment.

title: Correct Answers, Unsupported Findings: Evidence Binding In Forensic Reconstruction Of Llm Agent Logs
authors: Taehyeon Yun, Dongho Kim, Geonwoo Kim, Juyoung Seo, Minseok Hur, Moohong Min
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09581v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forensic reconstruction of LLM-agent actions requires not only recovering the correct value, but establishing which preserved record supports that finding. Tool logs, generated explanations, and local citation identifiers capture different parts of this evidence, yet a citation identifier does not establish a source unless its binding to a record is preserved. We audit this distinction using 64 mechanically checkable cases from saved AgentDojo Banking executions. Two LLM readers reconstruct source relationships under controlled variations in visible evidence and identifier-to-record bindings. We separately evaluate complete-record agreement, evidence-grounded findings, justified abstention, and unsupported assertions. With original identifiers and no binding table, Sonnet recovered every literal source location but made unsupported citation-source assertions in 26 of 28 cases requiring the missing relation; 22 nevertheless matched the complete reference. Adding explicit bindings improved grounded reconstruction for both readers, whereas identifier renaming alone provided no consistent remedy. A deterministic same-packet comparator correctly resolved the bounded task or abstained throughout. These results show that factual agreement alone is insufficient for evaluating forensic reconstruction of agent logs and motivate preserving explicit record bindings to distinguish supported findings from correct guesses.
tldr: The paper audits whether LLM readers reconstructing forensic evidence from agent tool logs can distinguish genuinely supported findings from correct guesses, showing that factual agreement alone is insufficient without explicit identifier-to-record bindings.
motivation: Forensic reconstruction of LLM-agent actions requires not only recovering correct values but establishing which preserved record supports each finding, yet citation identifiers do not establish sources unless their bindings to records are preserved.
method: The authors audit 64 mechanically checkable cases from saved AgentDojo Banking executions, using two LLM readers under controlled variations of visible evidence and identifier-to-record bindings, plus a deterministic same-packet comparator, evaluating complete-record agreement, evidence-grounded findings, justified abstention, and unsupported assertions.
result: With original identifiers and no binding table, Sonnet recovered every literal source location yet made unsupported citation-source assertions in 26 of 28 cases needing the missing relation, with 22 still matching the complete reference; explicit bindings improved grounded reconstruction, whereas renaming identifiers alone did not help.
conclusion: Factual agreement alone is insufficient to evaluate forensic reconstruction of agent logs; explicit record bindings should be preserved to distinguish supported findings from correct guesses.

title: Convergence Of Roberts Flow Dynamos In Eulerian And Lagrangian Codes
authors: Nikyta Shchutskyi, Axel Brandenburg, Matthieu Schaller
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08996v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard benchmark tests for numerical magnetohydrodynamics codes focus on one- and two-dimensional problems that ignore the possibility of dynamos, i.e., an exponential instability converting kinetic energy into magnetic energy. They also tend to ignore magnetic helicity conservation that can have dramatic effects in periodic domains. The existence of magnetic diffusion is crucial for dynamos, as was exemplified by the impossi- bility of finding dynamo solutions when using Euler potentials, which is a perfectly valid approach in the absence of magnetic diffusion. The Roberts flows I, II, III, and IV are two- dimensional flows that support three-dimensional dynamos, all of which are also large- scale dynamos in the sense that their planar averages are of significant strengths, even though flow II is pointwise non-helical. Here we demonstrate the numerical convergence properties of solutions obtained using discretisation schemes of second, sixth, and tenth order in the mesh width in the Pencil Code, compare the results with the SPH- based SWIFT code, and present a list of averaged quantities that facilitate their use in characterising the solutions as benchmarks. In addition, we present a procedure to obtain two-dimensional time-independent magnetic field visualisation for all Roberts flows, and perform per-pixel comparison between the Pencil and SWIFT codes. The rich combination of features makes Roberts flows an excellent dynamo benchmark for the direct numerical simulations of magnetohydrodynamics equations.
tldr: The paper benchmarks numerical convergence of Roberts flow dynamo solutions across Eulerian (Pencil Code) and Lagrangian (SPH-based SWIFT) magnetohydrodynamics codes.
motivation: Standard MHD code benchmarks rely on one- and two-dimensional problems that omit dynamo instabilities and magnetic helicity conservation, leaving a gap for robust three-dimensional dynamo test problems.
method: Solutions for Roberts flows I–IV are computed with second-, sixth-, and tenth-order discretisation schemes in the Pencil Code and compared against the SPH-based SWIFT code, including per-pixel comparisons of time-independent 2D magnetic field visualisations.
result: The authors establish convergence properties of the dynamo solutions and compile a list of averaged quantities that serve as benchmark diagnostics for the Roberts flow configurations.
conclusion: Roberts flows constitute an excellent dynamo benchmark for direct numerical simulations of MHD equations, combining dynamo action, helicity effects, and cross-code comparability.

title: Reliable Uncertainty Estimation For Machine-Learned Multigroup Cross Sections Without Retraining
authors: Joshua Nichols, Andrew Osborne, Valerio Mascolino
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Uncertainty quantification in machine learning models is essential for nuclear energy applications. While machine learning models can make both uncertainty and point predictions, these models are often significantly more difficult to train jointly than models that make point predictions alone. Split conformal prediction is a family of methods for computing distribution-free prediction intervals by calculating nonconformity scores corresponding to a target quantile in a calibration dataset. Although conformal prediction only guarantees marginal coverage, normalizing nonconformity scores enables predictive interval widths to be calculated on a per-sample basis, providing an approximation to conditional coverage. In this work, we connect uncertainty predicting neural networks to pre-trained networks that estimate shielding factors in multigroup neutron cross sections. We train the uncertainty models on the same OpenMC data used by the pre-trained models, whose weights and biases remain fixed. The outputs of the uncertainty models are the standard deviations of the residual, separated into contributions from the model and tally uncertainty. Their corresponding variances are combined in quadrature to provide a normalizing factor for conformal prediction, providing interval widths that are adaptive on a per-sample basis. Baselines for comparison are established using Mondrian conformal prediction, and by using the ground truth OpenMC uncertainties as normalizers in the conformal framework. We use predicted uncertainty interval widths and the severity of predictions that overshoot the interval widths as bases for comparing our normalizer with the baselines. We find that our method dramatically reduces both interval widths and the degree to which predictions fall outside these widths.
tldr: This paper develops a method for reliable uncertainty estimation in machine-learned multigroup neutron cross sections using conformal prediction without retraining the underlying models.
motivation: Uncertainty quantification is important for nuclear energy applications, but jointly training models for both point predictions and uncertainty estimates is often more difficult than training point-prediction models alone.
method: The authors connect uncertainty-predicting neural networks to pre-trained shielding-factor estimators, training uncertainty models on OpenMC data while keeping the pre-trained weights fixed. They use the predicted residual standard deviations to normalize conformal prediction scores, yielding per-sample adaptive interval widths.
result: The proposed normalizer dramatically reduces interval widths and the severity of predictions falling outside those widths compared to Mondrian conformal prediction and ground-truth OpenMC uncertainty baselines.
conclusion: The approach provides a practical way to obtain adaptive, distribution-free uncertainty estimates for machine-learned multigroup cross sections without retraining, improving upon standard conformal prediction baselines.

title: Sum Of Squares And Non Sum Of Squares Regimes For The Toeplitz Bottcher Wenzel Form
authors: Ping Nie Wenqi Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Toeplitz matrices are among the simplest structured models of translation invariance, arising naturally in convolution, stationary covariance models, and discretizations of translation-invariant operators. For a pair of real matrices, the B\"ottcher--Wenzel form (BW form) is a nonnegative quartic measuring the gap in the corresponding commutator inequality. L\'aszl\'o conjectured that, when both matrices are Toeplitz, this quartic is a sum of squares for every matrix order. We show that the conjecture is false. More precisely, we identify an explicit family of corner-supported Toeplitz pairs, retaining only the outermost diagonals on the two sides, for which the associated BW form is not a sum of squares at all sufficiently large orders. The proof reduces the complete family of Gram representations to a finite complex test: its Gram-invariant part develops a strictly negative limiting direction, while the remaining Gram-dependent contribution vanishes. We also give an explicit sufficient threshold for the matrix order. The negative result is complemented by two positive regimes. If either Toeplitz factor is symmetric or skew-symmetric, then the corresponding BW form is SoS for every order, with the other factor allowed to be an arbitrary real Toeplitz matrix. For unrestricted Toeplitz pairs, we further prove SoS representability for every [MATH], with formal Lean 4 verification through order 20.
tldr: The paper disproves Lászlo's conjecture by constructing Toeplitz matrix pairs whose Böttcher–Wenzel quartic form is not a sum of squares at sufficiently large orders.
motivation: To determine whether nonnegative quartic forms arising from commutator inequalities for Toeplitz matrices always admit a sum-of-squares representation.
method: Reduce the complete family of Gram representations to a finite complex test, analyze a strictly negative limiting direction, and complement the negative result with positive SoS proofs and Lean 4 verification.
result: An explicit corner-supported Toeplitz family yields non-SoS BW forms for large orders; SoS holds when one factor is symmetric or skew-symmetric, and for unrestricted Toeplitz pairs up to a threshold with Lean verification through order 20.
conclusion: Lászlo's conjecture is false in general, but positive SoS regimes exist, giving a refined algebraic characterization of the Böttcher–Wenzel form.

title: Jaxiga - A Software Framework For GPU-enabled And Differentiable Isogeometric Analysis
authors: Yongjie Jessica Zhang Cosmin Anitescu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09083v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we present JAXIGA, an open-source library for isogeometric analysis based on JAX. The library separates the construction of the mesh from the computations which are traced for compilation and differentiation. This allows geometry evaluation, assembly and the supported solvers to be combined in a just-in-time compiled program, for which first-order reverse-mode derivatives can be computed. We consider three numerical methods obtained from a single pointwise energy density. The Galerkin and energy-minimization methods use the same discrete potential and have the same stationary points, while collocation enforces the corresponding strong form. The sensitivities of a converged solution are obtained by solving one adjoint problem, and their accuracy depends on the tolerances of both the primal and adjoint problems. We also describe hierarchical extraction for local refinement of the variational methods and the use of smooth spline spaces for fourth-order problems. The numerical results are compared with analytical solutions and independent FEniCSx and JAX-FEM computations. For the reported GPU benchmark with 36,448 unknowns, assembly is twenty-four times faster than on the host CPU. When the conjugate-gradient solver is also run on the GPU, the total solution time is reduced from 31.8 to 1.38 seconds, and the result agrees with the direct solution to [MATH]. These results show that the choice of solver and the reuse of compilation are important for obtaining an overall reduction in computational cost.
tldr: JAXIGA is an open-source JAX-based software framework for GPU-accelerated and differentiable isogeometric analysis.
motivation: The paper aims to provide a flexible and efficient computational framework for isogeometric analysis that leverages automatic differentiation and GPU acceleration for sensitivity analysis and large-scale simulations.
method: The library separates mesh construction from computation, traces operations for JIT compilation, supports Galerkin, energy-minimization, and collocation methods, and computes sensitivities via an adjoint problem.
result: Numerical benchmarks show up to 24x faster assembly on GPU versus CPU, and total solution time reduced from 31.8 to 1.38 seconds for a problem with 36,448 unknowns.
conclusion: The choice of solver and reuse of compiled code are crucial for achieving significant computational cost reductions in differentiable isogeometric analysis.

title: Improving Learning Of Green's Functions Through Kernel Decomposition
authors: Beiji Chen, Qiang Du, Kui Ren, Tian-Yi Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work analyzes a framework for learning the solution operator, or equivalently, the Green's function, of a general self-adjoint second-order elliptic operator [MATH]. Subtracting the singular part of the Green's function, either known analytically or supplied by an explicit Laplace parametrix, recasts the learning of [MATH] as learning an [MATH]-harmonic extension operator on the boundary. We formulate the process as operator learning between reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) to show that the kernel decomposition strategy raises the algebraic input rate by two orders and, under uniform analytic regularity of the induced boundary data together with compatible output spaces, upgrades the output rate from algebraic to exponential. We extend the framework further to semilinear problems via an iterative decomposition in which the only learned object remains a linear operator, ensuring that the improved linear rates translate directly to the nonlinear iteration. Numerical experiments are provided to validate the theoretical development.
tldr: The paper analyzes a kernel decomposition framework for learning Green's functions of second-order elliptic operators, improving input/output approximation rates via RKHS operator learning.
motivation: Learning solution operators and Green's functions for PDEs is challenging because of the singular part of the Green's function; a better theoretical framework can improve learning rates.
method: Subtracting the known singular part recasts the problem as learning an harmonic extension operator, formulated as operator learning between reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, and extended to semilinear problems via iterative decomposition.
result: The strategy improves the algebraic input rate by two orders and, under analytic regularity and compatible output spaces, upgrades the output rate from algebraic to exponential; numerical experiments validate the theory.
conclusion: Kernel decomposition provides a principled way to improve learning of Green's functions, with theoretical rate guarantees and practical numerical validation.

title: Local Asymptotic Normality For Spectral-tail Likelihoods Under Fixed-domain Sampling
authors: Jonas Wallin Alexandre B. Simas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09105v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish local asymptotic normality (LAN) for joint inference on scale and roughness in stationary Gaussian random fields observed on increasingly dense regular grids in a fixed domain. Scale and roughness are represented by the coefficient and decay exponent of the leading spectral tail. Under spectral regularity conditions, we identify the joint normalization governing the LAN expansion and prove consistency and asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimators. For \(N\) observations, the estimation errors are of order \(N^{-1/2}\) for roughness and \((\log N)/\sqrt N\) for scale. After componentwise normalization, the errors converge to a perfectly correlated Gaussian pair. Knowing either parameter improves the convergence rate for estimating the other by a logarithmic factor. The analysis uses generalized locally Toeplitz (GLT) theory, for which we develop a truncation principle accommodating nonintegrable limiting symbols and quantitative bounds on the contribution from low frequencies. We verify the assumptions for Mat\'ern and generalized Wendland covariance families, establishing uniform spectral bounds for the latter. We also show that consistency and the limiting distributions persist under covariance misspecification when the true and fitted spectra share the same leading tail and their difference decays sufficiently rapidly. This includes misspecification between Mat\'ern and generalized Wendland models under explicit parameter restrictions.
tldr: The paper establishes local asymptotic normality for joint inference of scale and roughness parameters in stationary Gaussian random fields under fixed-domain sampling.
motivation: The authors aim to provide a rigorous asymptotic theory for spectral-tail likelihood inference when observing dense regular grid samples in a fixed domain, which is relevant for spatial statistics models like Matérn and generalized Wendland.
method: They use generalized locally Toeplitz (GLT) theory, develop a truncation principle for nonintegrable limiting symbols, and derive quantitative bounds on low-frequency contributions to prove LAN and asymptotic normality.
result: They show consistency and asymptotic normality of maximum likelihood estimators, with errors scaling as N^{-1/2} for roughness and (log N)/√N for scale, converging to a perfectly correlated Gaussian pair after normalization.
conclusion: The results extend to covariance misspecification when spectra share the same leading tail, and the assumptions are verified for Matérn and generalized Wendland families.

title: Sharp And Adaptive Cluster Recovery In Slowly Mixing Gaussian Hidden Markov Models
authors: Mohamed Ndaoud Ibrahim Kaddouri
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study cluster recovery in a two-state Gaussian hidden Markov model in the slowly mixing regime, where the transition probability [MATH] may vanish with the sample size. Temporal persistence creates long homogeneous segments and fundamentally changes the recovery problem relative to the i.i.d. Gaussian mixture benchmark. Rather than being purely adverse, label dependence provides exploitable structure: the statistical difficulty becomes concentrated near the rare transition points, giving rise to recovery regimes governed explicitly by their frequency [MATH]. We first characterize, up to universal constants, the oracle Bayes risk for offline and online clustering. Both problems exhibit a nonstandard polynomial risk regime, but the sequential constraint induces an additional logarithmic localization cost, yielding a genuine online/offline gap. We also study fixed lag prediction with delayed label feedback and identify the effective memory horizon beyond which past labels no longer improve the optimal rate. When the signal direction is unknown and possibly high dimensional, the problem is governed by the effective signal strength \[ r_n^2 = {\|\theta\|^2/\sigma^2+d/n}. \] We derive minimax lower bounds and construct fully adaptive polynomial time procedures attaining the sharp recovery rates. In particular, almost full recovery is possible precisely when [MATH]. If [MATH], adaptation to both the signal [MATH] and the transition probability [MATH] incurs no first order loss, and the sharp exact recovery threshold (under the Hamming loss) is \[ r_n^2 = 2\log(n\delta)\,(1+o(1)). \] Thus the effective complexity of the problem is governed by the number of latent transitions, rather than by the sample size itself.
tldr: The paper studies cluster recovery in slowly mixing two-state Gaussian hidden Markov models, deriving sharp oracle Bayes risks, minimax lower bounds, and adaptive polynomial-time procedures.
motivation: Temporal persistence in hidden Markov models creates long homogeneous segments and changes the recovery problem relative to the i.i.d. Gaussian mixture benchmark, with label dependence providing exploitable structure.
method: The authors characterize oracle Bayes risk for offline and online clustering, derive minimax lower bounds, and construct fully adaptive polynomial-time procedures that attain sharp recovery rates.
result: They identify a nonstandard polynomial risk regime, an online/offline gap due to logarithmic localization cost, a fixed-lag prediction memory horizon, and sharp exact recovery threshold r_n^2 = 2 log(nδ)(1+o(1)) when adaptation incurs no first-order loss.
conclusion: The effective complexity of the problem is governed by the number of latent transitions rather than the sample size itself.

title: A Family Of Hurwitz Polynomial Vector Fields In $\mathbb{R}^3$ Having Non-constant Periodic Orbits
authors: Salom\'on Rebollo-Perdomo \'alvaro Casta\~neda
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct a two-parameter family of polynomial vector fields in [MATH] and prove that, on a nonempty open set of parameter values, every member of the family is Hurwitz and possesses two non-constant periodic orbits, one of saddle type and one attracting. This answers Problem 19 in Gasull's list of open problems on low-dimensional dynamical systems concerning the existence of non-constant periodic orbits in Hurwitz smooth vector fields on [MATH]. This also provides counterexamples to the expected non-existence of non-constant periodic orbits for Hurwitz polynomial vector fields; a question that arose from the first counterexamples to the Markus-Yamabe conjecture in the late 1990s and that was stated by Meisters in his featured MathSciNet review of the Bernat-Llibre counterexample.
tldr: The paper constructs a two-parameter family of polynomial vector fields in R^3 that are Hurwitz and possess non-constant periodic orbits, answering an open problem and providing counterexamples to a previously expected non-existence result.
motivation: The work is motivated by Gasull's list of open problems on low-dimensional dynamical systems, specifically Problem 19 concerning the existence of non-constant periodic orbits in Hurwitz smooth vector fields on R^3, and by questions arising from counterexamples to the Markus-Yamabe conjecture.
method: The authors explicitly construct a two-parameter family of polynomial vector fields and prove that on a nonempty open set of parameter values, every member is Hurwitz and has two non-constant periodic orbits (one saddle, one attracting).
result: They establish the existence of a family of Hurwitz polynomial vector fields in R^3 with non-constant periodic orbits, thereby solving Gasull's Problem 19 and disproving the expected non-existence of such orbits.
conclusion: The findings provide a definitive answer to an open problem in dynamical systems and highlight counterexamples relevant to the Markus-Yamabe conjecture, with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Regret-Optimal Linear-Quadratic Control Under Distributional Drift
authors: Jose Blanchet Lukas-Benedikt Fiechtner
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study finite-horizon LQR with independent disturbances whose laws may drift over time. We address uncertainty in this evolution through ex-ante distributionally robust regret optimization (DRRO), which minimizes worst-case excess expected cost relative to the optimal causal controller that knows the law sequence. To specify the admissible law sequences, we introduce a temporally coupled moment ambiguity set with a Gelbrich kinetic-energy budget and a second budget limiting departures from reference moments and persistent cumulative mismatch. Despite the coupling of moments across time, affine disturbance-feedback synthesis reduces exactly to a semidefinite program. An optimal policy uses past disturbances to predict the correction to nominal LQR determined by current and future disturbance means. The SDP solution also yields worst-case moment paths and corresponding laws. For standard distributionally robust optimization (DRO), the analogous SDP relaxation can have a duality gap. Portfolio liquidation experiments show substantially lower worst-case regret over the drifting ambiguity set than common-law DRRO and nominal control.
tldr: The paper develops a distributionally robust regret-optimal control framework for finite-horizon LQR when disturbance distributions drift over time, reducing affine disturbance-feedback synthesis to a semidefinite program.
motivation: To address uncertainty in evolving disturbance laws in LQR by minimizing worst-case excess expected cost relative to a clairvoyant causal controller that knows the law sequence.
method: Introduces a temporally coupled moment ambiguity set with a Gelbrich kinetic-energy budget and a second budget controlling departures from reference moments and cumulative mismatch, then solves affine disturbance-feedback synthesis exactly via an SDP.
result: The optimal policy uses past disturbances to predict corrections to nominal LQR based on current and future disturbance means; the SDP also yields worst-case moment paths and corresponding laws, and portfolio liquidation experiments show substantially lower worst-case regret than common-law DRRO and nominal control.
conclusion: Provides a tractable robust control framework for distributional drift, with exact SDP for DRRO, while the analogous SDP relaxation for standard DRO can have a duality gap.

title: Embeddings Of Generalized Weighted Morrey Spaces
authors: Zhen Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study continuous embeddings from two classes of generalized weighted Morrey spaces into generalized Morrey spaces. The Komori--Shirai-type spaces use the weighted measure of cubes in their normalization, whereas the Samko-type spaces use the Lebesgue measure. We first consider generalized Morrey spaces on bounded domains. In the non-radial setting, we establish embedding results under local radial comparability assumptions on the Morrey functions. As a consequence, we characterize the corresponding embeddings in the radial setting for the full range [MATH]. We then study embeddings from generalized Komori--Shirai-type weighted Morrey spaces associated with piecewise power weights and general Muckenhoupt weights. For the Samko-type scale, we treat both generalized and classical weighted Morrey spaces, again considering piecewise power weights and general Muckenhoupt weights. Finally, assuming that the weight is comparable to a positive constant on some cube or ball, we show that the continuous embeddings under consideration are not compact.
tldr: The paper studies continuous embeddings between generalized weighted Morrey spaces, including Komori–Shirai-type and Samko-type scales, and shows non-compactness under certain weight comparability conditions.
motivation: The author aims to characterize embedding relations for generalized weighted Morrey spaces, extending known results to non-radial and weighted settings with piecewise power weights and Muckenhoupt weights.
method: The analysis uses local radial comparability assumptions on Morrey functions, treats bounded domains, and works with piecewise power weights and general Muckenhoupt weights, with separate treatments for Komori–Shirai and Samko-type spaces.
result: Embedding results are established for non-radial and radial settings, and it is shown that the continuous embeddings are not compact when the weight is comparable to a positive constant on some cube or ball.
conclusion: The paper provides a systematic characterization of embeddings into generalized Morrey spaces for weighted settings, with non-compactness results under natural conditions.

title: Beyond Nominal Equilibria: Risk-Averse Multi-Population Mean-Field Games
authors: Bhavini Jeloka, Siddhartha Ganguly, Panagiotis Tsiotras
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09244v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in mean-field games and its multi-population variants enable large-scale heterogeneous multi-agent systems to be modeled through representative agents and their associated mean-field distributions. However, existing approaches do not explicitly account for uncertainty in the behavior of other populations. To this end, we introduce a new paradigm: risk-averse multi-population mean-field games, where each population optimizes a worst-case expected reward over dynamically feasible ambiguity sets of mean-field flows of a subset of the other populations. Employing an occupation-measure formulation along with tools from set-valued analysis, we establish, under mild assumptions, several theoretical properties of the multi-population game, including the geometric properties of the ambiguity sets and the existence of a novel risk-averse multi-population mean-field equilibrium. Further, we derive contractivity results of the fixed-point operator under entropy regularization and show that it can be utilized to learn the equilibrium. Finally, we propose a risk-averse fictitious-play scheme and show that exploitability decays to zero, despite the additional nonlinearity introduced by the worst-case objective. We report several numerical experiments to illustrate convergence and risk-averse behavior.
tldr: The paper introduces risk-averse multi-population mean-field games where each population optimizes a worst-case expected reward over ambiguity sets of other populations' mean-field flows.
motivation: Existing mean-field game approaches for large-scale heterogeneous multi-agent systems do not explicitly account for uncertainty in the behavior of other populations.
method: The authors use an occupation-measure formulation and set-valued analysis to study ambiguity sets and equilibrium existence, then derive contractivity under entropy regularization and propose a risk-averse fictitious-play learning scheme.
result: They establish geometric properties of ambiguity sets, existence of a risk-averse multi-population mean-field equilibrium, contractivity of the fixed-point operator under entropy regularization, and convergence of exploitability to zero.
conclusion: Numerical experiments illustrate convergence and risk-averse behavior, showing the proposed framework can model and learn equilibria beyond nominal mean-field games.

title: Convergence Of Repeated-pole Rational Approximation Of The Exponential On Infinite Sectors
