motivation: Understanding sharp error bounds for rational approximations to the exponential is important for numerical methods such as Krylov subspace approximations to matrix exponentials and related shift-and-invert Arnoldi computations.
method: The authors use a Möbius map to reduce the problem to polynomial approximation on a compact lens, then employ an exact boundary Faber integral, global fractional-power contour deformation, and a two-saddle expansion to derive sharp asymptotics.
result: They obtain the sharp two-sided order uniformly on compact subsets of a noncoalescing interval, identify a unique minimizer for the exponential factor, and derive matrix dimension-independent upper bounds via numerical-range estimates.
conclusion: The work characterizes a sector-uniform convergence law for repeated-pole rational approximation of the exponential and distinguishes it from individual matrix computation behavior, with implications for projected shift-and-invert Arnoldi methods.

title: Shifted Tapered-pole Approximation On Finite Sectors: An Exact Asymptotic And Dimension Control
authors: Tianqi Zhang Fei Xue
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study explicit lightning-plus-polynomial (LP) approximation of [MATH] on a closed unit-radius sector, where [MATH], [MATH] is fixed, and [MATH] is analytic nearby. Since the basic sector root-exponential rate is already known, we address three finer questions. First, a one-sided Abel--Poisson formula and a pole-free notched contour give a branchwise error bound that is uniform for grid shifts in compact subsets of [MATH] and valid for every fixed logarithmic power. Second, for [MATH] in the dense and balanced regimes, an exact vertex-scale rescaling identifies a positive finite leading constant for a specified shifted sequence. Third, a rate-matched band of additional representation poles followed by polynomial compression gives the explicit representation dimension [MATH] while leaving the first [MATH] tapered poles unchanged. A slightly overresolved hybrid sequence also preserves the exact leading constant. Matched-dimension experiments, including reentrant sectors, illustrate the allocation. These exact-asymptotic and dimension statements concern the stated constructions, not sector minimax approximation or total computational complexity.
tldr: The paper provides an exact asymptotic analysis and dimension control for shifted tapered-pole approximation on finite sectors.
motivation: To address finer questions about lightning-plus-polynomial approximation of a function on a unit-radius sector, including uniform error bounds and representation dimension.
method: Uses one-sided Abel-Poisson formula, pole-free notched contour, vertex-scale rescaling, and representation poles with polynomial compression.
result: Derives branchwise error bounds, identifies positive finite leading constants, and determines explicit representation dimension while preserving tapered poles.
conclusion: These exact-asymptotic and dimension statements apply to the stated constructions, not to sector minimax approximation or computational complexity.

title: Convergence Of Kernel And Neural-network Methods For Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman Equations On Unbounded Domains
authors: Yumiharu Nakano
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive error bounds from empirical squared residuals for two non-monotone, mesh-free approximations of Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equations on unbounded spatial domains: collocation with Wendland kernels under a native space norm constraint, and physics-informed neural networks with smooth activations under a Sobolev-norm constraint. The main step is to recover the pointwise residual control needed for viscosity-solution error estimates from the empirical loss, while quantifying the discretization or sampling error. For the kernel method, we prove uniform convergence on compact sets under classical and native space regularity and derive an a posteriori quantitative error bound for the unique bounded continuous viscosity solution. For the neural-network method, we prove uniform convergence on compact sets in probability and give a quantitative high-probability error bound under classical Sobolev regularity. The bounds are governed by the fill distance for kernels and by the network and sample sizes for neural networks. The proofs combine empirical-to-population estimates, an interpolation inequality that turns an [MATH] residual into a sup norm bound, and a controlled diffusion estimate for the error caused by truncating the domain. The regularity assumptions used to obtain convergence from approximation properties are additional to viscosity wellposedness. Numerical experiments in one and two space dimensions illustrate the methods and the estimates.
tldr: The paper derives error bounds for kernel collocation and physics-informed neural network approximations of Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equations on unbounded domains.
motivation: Mesh-free numerical solvers for HJB equations lack rigorous convergence guarantees on unbounded domains, which are common in stochastic control and reinforcement learning.
method: The authors combine empirical-to-population estimates, an interpolation inequality converting residual control into sup-norm bounds, and a controlled diffusion estimate for domain truncation, for Wendland kernels under native-space norms and for PINNs under Sobolev constraints.
result: Uniform convergence on compact sets is proven for both methods, with quantitative a posteriori bounds governed by fill distance and by network/sample size, illustrated numerically in one and two dimensions.
conclusion: Both kernel and neural-network approaches admit rigorous residual-based error control for viscosity solutions of HJB equations on unbounded domains.

title: Exact And Efficient Methods For Identifying Carcinogenic Multi-Hit Gene Combinations
authors: Rick S. H. Willemsen, Teresa L. F. Ho, Tenindra Abeywickrama
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09420v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cancer is driven by an estimated two to nine gene mutations, known as multi-hit combinations. Due to the large number of genes, identifying these multi-hit combinations presents a computationally challenging problem, which has previously required supercomputers to enumerate all or most gene combinations. Recent work formulated this classification task as the Multi-Hit Cancer Driver Set Cover Problem (MHCDSCP) and solved it via column generation on a single commodity CPU, where a pricing problem identifies promising gene combinations (arXiv:2602.22551). The main bottleneck is the pricing problem that has to be solved repeatedly. To solve the pricing problem to optimality, we propose a dedicated depth first search method that enumerates all possible gene combinations. Although enumerating gene combinations with depth first search have been performed on supercomputers with around 150,000 CPU cores (arXiv:2603.16721), our depth first search algorithm solves the pricing problem to optimality within seconds on a single CPU by leveraging dual information to prune large parts of the search space. By eliminating this bottleneck, our approach yields the first exact method for the MHCDSCP, which is guaranteed to find a global optimal solution.
tldr: A depth-first-search-based exact algorithm solves the pricing problem of the Multi-Hit Cancer Driver Set Cover Problem on a single CPU within seconds, yielding the first exact method for identifying multi-hit carcinogenic gene combinations.
motivation: Identifying the two-to-nine gene mutation combinations that drive cancer is combinatorially intractable at scale, and prior enumerations required supercomputers or suffered from a pricing-problem bottleneck in column generation.
method: The authors formulate the task as the Multi-Hit Cancer Driver Set Cover Problem and replace the repeated pricing-problem bottleneck with a dedicated depth-first search that uses dual information to prune large parts of the combinatorial search space.
result: The algorithm solves the pricing problem to optimality in seconds on a single commodity CPU, versus roughly 150,000 CPU cores for earlier supercomputer enumerations, and produces the first guaranteed globally optimal solutions for the MHCDSCP.
conclusion: The work delivers an exact and efficient combinatorial optimization method for cancer driver discovery, but it lies entirely in computational biology and operations research with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, or quantum hardware.

title: A Remark On Projection Outer Volume Ratio
authors: A. E. Litvak
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09562v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the projection outer volume ratio [MATH] introduced by D. Galicer, A.E. Litvak, M. Merzbacher, and D. Pinasco. When [MATH], we provide sharp bounds in the general case, namely \[ {\rm povr}_k(K)\leq C \max\Big\{1, {\ln(2n/k)}}\Big\}, \] where the maximal order is obtained for [MATH]. Moreover, in the important particular case [MATH] we show that [MATH] is bounded by an absolute constant whenever [MATH] and \[ {\rm povr}_k(B_2^n)\leq C{n-k}}\, \ln\left(1+{n-k}\right) \] for [MATH]. The latter bound is sharp up to a logarithmic term.
tldr: The paper studies the projection outer volume ratio of convex bodies and provides sharp asymptotic bounds in general and for the Euclidean ball.
motivation: The projection outer volume ratio was recently introduced as a geometric parameter, and the paper aims to establish sharp bounds for it, especially in the regime k ≤ n/2.
method: The work uses methods from asymptotic convex geometry, including volumetric estimates and comparison with the Euclidean ball, to derive upper and lower bounds.
result: It proves povr_k(K) ≤ C max{1, ln(2n/k)} in general and sharp bounds for B_2^n, including povr_k(B_2^n) ≤ C (n-k)^{-1} ln(1+n-k), sharp up to a logarithmic term.
conclusion: The bounds characterize the projection outer volume ratio in the general case and for the Euclidean ball, resolving order-optimal behavior up to logarithmic factors.

title: Adversarial Rl For Port-Scan Evasion: Attacker Feature Visibility In Edge-Deployed Ids
authors: Logan Andrew North, Priya Sanjay Kaluskar, Shasi Kumar Ramachandran Prabhu, Peilong Li, Suman Saha
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning-based intrusion detection systems (IDS) are increasingly used in resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) environments, yet their robustness is often evaluated against static attacks rather than adversaries that adapt to detection feedback. This paper investigates adaptive port-scan evasion against ML-based IDS models deployed on a Raspberry Pi 3B+. We implement a live Zeek-based IDS pipeline with XGBoost, a multi-layer perceptron, and a 1D convolutional neural network trained on TON_IoT telemetry, and use a Deep Q-Network (DQN) adversary to learn evasive combinations of probe timing, TCP flags, and payload size under black-box, gray-box, and white-box feature-visibility settings. Although the deployed IDS models detect conventional port scans at 91.1--99.8%, DQN final-50-episode evasion rates range from 61.9% to 98.3% across feature-visibility settings. Greater feature visibility does not monotonically improve evasion, and its effect is model-dependent: against XGBoost, the black-box agent achieves 92.9% evasion, compared with 61.9% and 76.9% for gray-box and white-box agents, respectively, whereas 1D-CNN is most vulnerable under white-box access at 98.1%. Because standard DQN can overestimate action values, we additionally spot-check representative conditions using Double DQN. The gray-box condition remains unstable in this check, providing no evidence that overestimation bias alone explains the observed instability. These results show that limited feature knowledge can still enable effective adaptive evasion against static edge-deployed IDS models, motivating more robust defenses for IoT edge environments.
tldr: The paper studies adaptive port-scan evasion against ML-based intrusion detection systems deployed on edge IoT hardware using deep reinforcement learning.
motivation: ML-based IDS for IoT are often evaluated against static attacks, not adaptive adversaries that learn from detection feedback, leaving robustness against evasion insufficiently understood.
method: The authors implement a live Zeek-based IDS pipeline with XGBoost, MLP, and 1D-CNN models on a Raspberry Pi 3B+, and train DQN adversaries under black-box, gray-box, and white-box feature-visibility settings to learn evasive scan timing, TCP flags, and payload sizes.
result: Conventional scans are detected at 91.1–99.8%, but DQN evasion rates reach 61.9–98.3%; greater feature visibility does not monotonically improve evasion and effects are model-dependent, with Double DQN spot-checks showing instability in the gray-box condition.
conclusion: Limited feature knowledge can enable effective adaptive evasion against static edge-deployed IDS, motivating more robust defenses for IoT edge environments.

title: A Deployment-Aware Feasibility Framework For Machine Learning-Based IoT Intrusion Detection Across Edge, Fog, And Cloud Architectures
authors: Munther Abualkibash Shaker Nawasra
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid growth and heterogeneity of Internet of Things (IoT) environments have exposed fundamental limitations in traditional rule-based and signature-based intrusion detection systems. This paper presents a quantitative deployment-aware analysis of machine learning (ML)-based intrusion detection approaches across edge, fog/gateway, and cloud architectures. Unlike prior surveys that primarily emphasize detection accuracy, this work defines representative quantitative deployment capability envelopes extracted from experimental and system-level studies and introduces a structured Deployment Feasibility Score (DFS) model. The proposed framework maps ML techniques to architectural layers based on computational demand, memory footprint, and latency sensitivity using a weighted ordinal scoring mechanism. The analysis demonstrates that lightweight statistical and linear models are most suitable for edge deployment, ensemble and clustering-based methods align with fog/gateway environments, while deep and optimization-driven models are best suited for cloud infrastructures. By formalizing deployment feasibility through quantitative grounding and structured evaluation, this work provides practical guidance for selecting intrusion detection solutions under real-world architectural constraints, supporting more informed and deployment-conscious IoT security design.
tldr: The paper proposes a quantitative Deployment Feasibility Score (DFS) framework for mapping machine learning-based IoT intrusion detection models to edge, fog, and cloud architectural layers.
motivation: Traditional rule-based and signature-based intrusion detection systems struggle with the rapid growth and heterogeneity of IoT environments, and prior surveys focus on detection accuracy while ignoring real-world deployment constraints.
method: The authors define representative quantitative deployment capability envelopes from experimental and system-level studies and introduce a weighted ordinal scoring mechanism to map ML techniques to architectural layers based on computational demand, memory footprint, and latency sensitivity.
result: The analysis finds that lightweight statistical and linear models suit edge deployment, ensemble and clustering-based methods align with fog/gateway environments, and deep and optimization-driven models are best suited for cloud infrastructures.
conclusion: The framework provides practical, deployment-conscious guidance for selecting IoT intrusion detection solutions under real-world architectural constraints.

title: Separating Comb Inequalities Is NP-hard
authors: Victor Drouin-Touchette Yohan Finet
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Comb inequalities are important cutting planes for the symmetric travelling salesman problem, yet the complexity of their exact separation has remained a longstanding question in polyhedral combinatorics. We present a reduction from 3-SAT proving that deciding whether a comb inequality is violated is NP-complete and that the corresponding separation problem is NP-hard. This result holds even when the input vector belongs to the subtour elimination polytope, every edge value is zero, one half or one and the support graph is nonplanar with maximum degree four. The reduction constructs a graph in which six-vertex ladder gadgets encode Boolean relations and cubic graphs enforce consistency among occurrences of each logical variable. For a propositional logic formula with [MATH] variables and [MATH] clauses, the constructed graph has [MATH] vertices and a linear number of positive edges. The reduction also proves hardness when every permitted tooth has two or four vertices with half of the tooth in the handle. We discuss consequences for approximating the maximum comb violation, optimization over the comb relaxation and explain why hardness of separation does not automatically transfer to larger inequality families.
tldr: The paper proves that separating comb inequalities for the symmetric travelling salesman problem is NP-hard via a reduction from 3-SAT.
motivation: Comb inequalities are important cutting planes for TSP, but the complexity of exactly separating them had been a longstanding open question in polyhedral combinatorics.
method: A reduction from 3-SAT constructs a graph with six-vertex ladder gadgets encoding Boolean relations and cubic graphs enforcing variable consistency, showing that deciding violation of a comb inequality is NP-complete.
result: Separation is NP-hard even when the input lies in the subtour elimination polytope, edge values are restricted to {0, 1/2, 1}, and the support graph is nonplanar with maximum degree four.
conclusion: The authors discuss consequences for approximating maximum comb violation and note that hardness of separation does not automatically transfer to larger inequality families.

title: Fine-Grained Hardness Of Approximating Dynamic Time Warping
authors: Jihan Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09233v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove conditional lower bounds for approximating dynamic time warping (DTW) over the uniform metric on three symbols. Let [MATH] be the two string lengths and [MATH] their respective numbers of runs. Under the Gap Block Disjointness (GBD) hypothesis, for every fixed [MATH] and [MATH], no deterministic algorithm [MATH]-approximates DTW on two explicit strings of length [MATH] in [MATH] time. This matches the known tradeoff between approximation and running-time exponents for deterministic algorithms within any fixed factor greater than six in the approximation exponent. For run-length encoded strings, the Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis (OVH) rules out any constant-factor approximation in [MATH] time for every constant [MATH]. More generally, for every fixed [MATH], it rules out [MATH]-approximation in the same running time. These bounds extend to every fixed metric with at least three points, including absolute distance on [MATH]. Both reductions use long runs to force equal-symbol matches in low-cost alignments. For explicit strings, we combine Boolean gadgets with deterministic gap amplification to obtain a polynomial approximation gap. For run-length encoded strings, an encoding of regular-expression membership gives accepting instances an alignment whose cost does not increase as selected runs grow. Rejecting instances have distance at least the chosen run length, while the number of runs stays fixed.
tldr: The paper proves conditional lower bounds for approximating dynamic time warping over small metrics, showing no efficient deterministic approximation under Gap Block Disjointness or Orthogonal Vectors hypotheses.
motivation: Dynamic time warping is a fundamental sequence alignment method, but its fine-grained approximability under popular complexity hypotheses was not fully understood.
method: The author uses reductions from Gap Block Disjointness and Orthogonal Vectors, combining Boolean gadgets, deterministic gap amplification, and run-length encoded regular-expression membership encodings to force equal-symbol matches in low-cost alignments.
result: Under GBD, no deterministic algorithm approximates DTW on explicit strings within certain running-time exponents; under OVH, no constant-factor approximation is possible for run-length encoded strings, with extensions to any fixed metric of at least three points.
conclusion: The work establishes tight tradeoffs between approximation ratio and running time for DTW, closing gaps in fine-grained hardness and extending lower bounds beyond the uniform metric.

title: Constitution-Guided Watermarking
authors: Toluwani Aremu, Samuele Poppi, Nils Lukas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Watermarking enables language model providers to identify text generated by their models. However, its desired properties can conflict (\ie~stronger watermark signals can degrade text quality), while designs that resist editing may also facilitate forgery. Providers address these trade-offs by choosing configurations that balance competing objectives or prioritize particular properties. Either approach imposes a shared operating point on requests with different requirements, potentially sacrificing quality where wording preservation matters or robustness where reliable attribution is essential. To allow flexible and adaptable designs, we introduce , a framework that selects request-appropriate trade-offs from provider requirements, listed as natural-language principles. , a pretrained reasoning agent examines constitutional rules alongside watermark implementations and iteratively refines rule-specific configurations using empirical feedback. , a separate monitor identifies applicable rules and retrieves the corresponding policy, including watermarking exemptions, without modifying the serving model. Furthermore, our framework supports offline parallel optimization and refinement of rule-specific configurations based on evolving provider requirements without affecting deployment, and binds each deployed configuration to its evaluation evidence, making deployment decisions auditable. In a proof-of-concept evaluation using KGW and a five-rule constitution, our framework selects configurations responsive to provider priorities and improves post-paraphrase detection on robustness-prioritized requests by up to [MATH] percentage points over fixed configurations, while matching or exceeding all baselines in aggregate quality and clean detection at a nominal [MATH] false-positive rate.
tldr: The paper introduces a constitution-guided framework for selecting request-appropriate language-model watermarking trade-offs via a reasoning agent and monitor.
motivation: Watermarking schemes face conflicting requirements such as robustness, text quality, and forgeability, and fixed operating points cannot adapt to different deployment needs.
method: It uses natural-language constitutional rules, a pretrained reasoning agent that iteratively refines rule-specific configurations with empirical feedback, and a separate monitor that retrieves applicable policies or exemptions.
result: In a proof-of-concept with KGW and a five-rule constitution, the framework improves post-paraphrase detection on robustness-prioritized requests while matching or exceeding baselines in aggregate quality and clean detection.
conclusion: The framework enables flexible, auditable, and offline-optimizable watermarking configurations without modifying the serving model, though it remains outside quantum information research.

title: Envy-free Allocations With Individual Payments
authors: Robert Bredereck, Eva Deltl, Tanmay Inamdar, Pallavi Jain, Pranjal Pandey
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an envy-free allocation of indivisible goods does not exist, monetary transfers can restore envy-freeness. Existing work on fair division with subsidies, however, typically assumes that these payments are provided by an external source, an assumption that may be unrealistic in many applications. We address this limitation by allowing only monetary transfers between agents, with each agent's payments constrained by their individual budget. We show that while it is polynomial-time tractable to determine whether a given allocation can be made envy-free by payments under individual budgets, the general problem of computing such an allocation from scratch is NP-hard, even when agents have relatively large budgets. Motivated by this intractability, we conduct a parameterized complexity analysis, establishing fixed-parameter tractability with respect to the number of goods or to the joint parameter number of agents and good types, and we provide efficient algorithms in several special cases. For explicitly listed items, our type-based algorithm answers the envy-freeness part of an open question of T. T. Nguyen and J. Rothe, "Complexity Results and Exact Algorithms for Fair Division of Indivisible Items: A Survey.".
tldr: The paper studies envy-free allocations of indivisible goods when monetary transfers are only allowed between agents under individual budget constraints, establishing tractability, NP-hardness, and parameterized complexity results.
motivation: Existing fair-division-with-subsidies work assumes payments come from an external source, which is unrealistic in many settings; the authors instead restrict transfers to occur among agents subject to individual budgets.
method: The authors give a polynomial-time algorithm to check whether a given allocation can be made envy-free via budget-constrained payments, prove NP-hardness of computing such allocations from scratch, and perform a parameterized complexity analysis plus special-case algorithms.
result: Verification is tractable, but finding an envy-free budget-constrained allocation is NP-hard even with large budgets; the problem is fixed-parameter tractable in the number of goods or in the joint parameter (agents, good types), and a type-based algorithm resolves part of an open question by Nguyen and Rothe.
conclusion: Budget-constrained envy-free allocation is a computationally hard but occasionally tractable fair-division problem, with the type-based approach answering an open question for explicitly listed items.

title: Optimal Regret For Online Market Making With Limit Order Book
authors: Maria Elena Vischi, Francesco Emanuele Stradi, Alberto Marchesi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study online learning in market making, where, at each round, a market maker posts bid and ask prices before observing the market price and the private valuation of an incoming trader. In this setting, Maran et al. 2026 introduce a feedback model motivated by limit order books, in which the trader's valuation is revealed only if no transaction occurs. Assuming that trader valuations are drawn i.i.d. from an unknown distribution while market prices are chosen adversarially, they establish an expected regret bound of [MATH]. In this work, we improve upon this guarantee by establishing a high-probability regret bound of [MATH]. As a warm-up, we first consider the full-feedback setting. We introduce a discretization of the bid-ask space based on two coupled grids and combine it with Hedge to achieve the desired regret rate. Building on these ideas, we then address the substantially weaker feedback induced by a limit order book and develop an algorithm that achieves the same guarantee. Finally, we investigate the limits of learnability in fully adversarial environments, where the valuations may vary arbitrarily as well. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that when both market prices and trader valuations are chosen adversarially, sublinear regret is impossible even under full feedback, thereby motivating our stochastic assumption on the valuations.
tldr: The paper studies online market making with limit order book feedback, improving regret bounds and showing impossibility of sublinear regret under fully adversarial prices and valuations.
motivation: Market making in limit order books requires learning pricing strategies under partial feedback, where trader valuations are only revealed when no transaction occurs.
method: The authors use discretization of the bid-ask space with two coupled grids combined with Hedge, first for full feedback and then for limit order book feedback; they also analyze fully adversarial settings.
result: They establish a high-probability regret bound improving prior expected regret, and prove that sublinear regret is impossible when both market prices and trader valuations are adversarial even with full feedback.
conclusion: The stochastic assumption on trader valuations is necessary for learnability, and the proposed algorithm achieves the desired regret rate under limit order book feedback.

title: Automotive Hardware Attacks: An Architect's Guide To Tara
authors: Xiaolu Hou Jakub Breier
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Threat analysis and risk assessment (TARA) according to ISO/SAE 21434 treats implementation-level hardware attacks inconsistently. We show that two of the three attack-feasibility approaches exemplified in the standard rate every attack path that requires physical access as very low by construction, independent of the implementation, while the third can assign the same path any of the four ratings, depending on the assumed state of attacker knowledge and on the attacker profile. This paper presents a hardware-aware extension of the TARA that covers side-channel analysis (SCA), fault-injection attacks (FIA), and abuse of debug and test interfaces. It adds an attacker model for physical access over the vehicle lifecycle; a path-dominance relation on the attack-potential factors that identifies when a simpler path makes a sophisticated one irrelevant; a three-level hardware relevance gate (H0 to H2) with an explicit decision rule that fixes whether resistance of a hardware step may be argued, must be documented, or must be demonstrated by test; and a rating rule under which a hardware step receives no credit for implementation-specific resistance until the required evidence exists. The gate is positioned relative to cybersecurity assurance levels and targeted attack feasibility. The method is applied to a reference gateway architecture, and its structural inputs are examined on ten published attacks on automotive components. In seven of the ten studies, the demonstrated attack included a debug, programming, boot, diagnostic, or update mechanism, whereas only four studies included an attack on a cryptographic computation.
tldr: The paper proposes a hardware-aware extension of Threat Analysis and Risk Assessment (TARA) for automotive cybersecurity, addressing side-channel analysis, fault injection, and debug/test interface attacks.
motivation: The ISO/SAE 21434 standard treats implementation-level hardware attacks inconsistently, rating physical-access attack paths as very low by construction and allowing variable ratings depending on attacker knowledge.
method: The authors add an attacker model for physical access over the vehicle lifecycle, a path-dominance relation on attack-potential factors, a three-level hardware relevance gate (H0–H2), and a rating rule requiring evidence for implementation-specific resistance.
result: The method is applied to a reference gateway architecture and ten published automotive attacks; seven of ten studies involved debug, programming, boot, diagnostic, or update mechanisms, while only four included an attack on a cryptographic computation.
conclusion: A hardware-aware TARA can more consistently assess physical and implementation-level attacks in automotive systems, but the work is outside the scope of quantum information research.

title: Formal Runtime Verification For Tool-Using Llm Agents: An Offline Same-Benchmark Study On AgentDojo And Stac
authors: Nikolaos Kekatos, Stylianos Basagiannis, Marinelio Chintri, Alexios Lekidis, Tom Nianios, Ioannis Seitoglou, Anastasios Temperekidis, Panagiotis Katsaros
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Guardrails for tool-using LLM agents are usually application-specific rules, which makes multi-step, data-dependent safety policies hard to specify, audit and reuse. As a declarative alternative, we evaluate metric first-order temporal logic (MFOTL), replaying the recorded trajectories that AgentDojo, STAC and R-Judge already ship through the unmodified MonPoly monitor, offline and without running an agent. On these corpora, five generic obligations flag 71.8% of STAC attack chains and 70.1% of successful AgentDojo attacks, but also fire on 29.3% of benign runs. This imprecision stems from the corpora rather than the logic: they rarely record approvals and never record timestamps, so history-dependent obligations reduce to detecting risky action types. Where the trace does carry relational context, provenance-aware policies discriminate better; that context, however, is itself attackable, and one planted line defeats a naive provenance check on 94-99% of the runs it would otherwise flag. Binding provenance to the lookup that produced it closes this evasion at no cost in detection or benign firing. Taken together, these results show that formal temporal monitoring adds value exactly when the trace exposes trustworthy history. We therefore quantify how far current benchmarks are from that point and propose a twelve-field enforcement-ready trace schema.
tldr: This paper evaluates metric first-order temporal logic (MFOTL) for offline runtime verification of tool-using LLM agent trajectories using AgentDojo, STAC, and R-Judge benchmarks.
motivation: Guardrails for tool-using LLM agents are typically application-specific and brittle; the authors seek a declarative, reusable monitoring approach based on formal temporal logic.
method: They replay recorded agent trajectories through the unmodified MonPoly monitor, testing five generic obligations and provenance-aware policies, including a planted-line evasion attack and a binding fix.
result: The generic obligations flag 71.8% of STAC attack chains and 70.1% of successful AgentDojo attacks but also fire on 29.3% of benign runs; provenance-aware policies improve discrimination, and binding provenance to the lookup closes an evasion that otherwise defeats naive checks on 94–99% of flagged runs.
conclusion: Formal temporal monitoring is valuable only when execution traces expose trustworthy history; the authors quantify benchmark gaps and propose a twelve-field enforcement-ready trace schema.

title: The Adaptive Lasso With Weighted Ipw Factor And Krr Penalty Function
authors: Zeen Song
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we first consider a Lasso estimator incorporating a weighted IPW factor,and obtain certain conditions for the Lasso variable selection to be consistent or inconsistent. Then we provide a modified version of the adaptive Lasso equipped with a weighted IPW factor and a KRR penalty function, establishing that the proposed adaptive Lasso possesses the Oracle property. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed adaptive Lasso exhibits near-minimax optimality in performance.
tldr: The paper develops an adaptive Lasso estimator with a weighted inverse probability weighting (IPW) factor and a kernel ridge regression (KRR) penalty, proving oracle properties and near-minimax optimality.
motivation: Variable selection in high-dimensional settings with missing data or covariate shift requires estimators that remain consistent and attain oracle-like behavior; classical Lasso penalization alone is often insufficient.
method: The authors analyze a Lasso estimator augmented with a weighted IPW factor to characterize conditions for selection consistency, then introduce an adaptive Lasso variant combining the weighted IPW factor with a KRR penalty function.
result: The proposed adaptive Lasso is shown to possess the Oracle property, and numerical simulations indicate near-minimax optimal performance.
conclusion: The weighted IPW plus KRR-penalized adaptive Lasso provides a theoretically sound and empirically competitive approach to high-dimensional variable selection.

title: Finite-dimensional Normed Spaces Without Small-norm Hyperplane Projections
authors: Tomasz Kobos
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that there exists an absolute constant [MATH] such that for every [MATH] there exists an [MATH]-dimensional real normed space [MATH] for which every linear projection [MATH] onto a hyperplane satisfies [MATH]. More generally, for every integer [MATH] there exists a constant [MATH] such that for every [MATH] there exists an [MATH]-dimensional real normed space [MATH] such that every projection [MATH] onto a subspace of codimension at most [MATH] satisfies [MATH]. The proof is based on an idea of Gleit and Lazar, who established an analogous result for the space of real [MATH] matrices equipped with either the trace-class norm or the operator norm.
tldr: The paper constructs finite-dimensional real normed spaces in which every linear projection onto a hyperplane (or low-codimension subspace) must have large norm.
motivation: Understanding lower bounds on the norm of projections onto hyperplanes and low-codimension subspaces is a classical question in the local theory of Banach spaces, extending earlier constructions of Gleit and Lazar for matrix spaces.
method: The author gives an explicit construction of n-dimensional normed spaces using an idea of Gleit and Lazar, and proves the existence of absolute constants bounding the projection norms from below.
result: For every n there is an n-dimensional real normed space such that every projection onto a hyperplane has norm at least c (absolute constant), and more generally every projection onto a subspace of codimension at most k exceeds a constant depending on k.
conclusion: The results generalize the Gleit–Lazar phenomenon to arbitrary finite dimensions and codimensions, showing that small-norm hyperplane projections cannot exist in general.

title: Open Problem: Computing The Optimal Deterministic Budget-balanced Mechanism
authors: Vincent Conitzer
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This is an open problem originally posed during the program "Economics and Computation" held in the Fall 2015 semester at the Simons Institute for the Theory of Computing. It asks whether, in automated mechanism design, it is possible to compute the optimal deterministic budget-balanced mechanism in polynomial time. Some variants, also open to my knowledge, are also discussed.
tldr: This open problem asks whether the optimal deterministic budget-balanced mechanism can be computed in polynomial time in automated mechanism design.
motivation: The problem was originally posed during the Simons Institute program on Economics and Computation and remains open, with several variants also unresolved.
method: The paper states the open problem and discusses related variants, without providing a solution or computational method.
result: No polynomial-time algorithm is given; the question of tractability remains open along with the variants considered.
conclusion: The work highlights a fundamental open question in algorithmic mechanism design and calls for further investigation.

title: SwarmReconGuard: Black-Box Detection Of Distributed Collective Reconnaissance By Individually Benign-Looking Agent Populations
authors: Vahid Tavakkoli, Kabeh Mohsenzadegan, Kyandoghere Kyamakya
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous and agentic clients can distribute reconnaissance across many identities so that each request remains valid, low-rate, and benign-looking while the population collectively acquires broad system knowledge. We formalize this threat as Distributed Collective Reconnaissance (DCR) and present SwarmReconGuard, a reproducible black-box benchmark in which the defender observes only service-boundary telemetry. The Docker-isolated study evaluates 11 benign and attack behaviors across 10-10,000 virtual identities, comprising 440 test runs and 3,666,300 requests, with complete telemetry integrity. We compare semantic, Gaussian, conditional, graph, kernel, hybrid, and CUSUM-based detectors. Gaussian likelihood-ratio detection achieves 100[MATH] detection with 0[MATH] observed false positives on known attacks but only 3[MATH] on unseen policies. CUSUM yields 36.1[MATH] overall detection at 1.25[MATH] false positives, while hybrid CUSUM reaches 85.7[MATH] detection with 0[MATH] observed false positives at 10,000 identities. Results expose a major policy-generalization gap and motivate exposure-aware, scale-aware defenses.
tldr: SwarmReconGuard is a black-box benchmark for detecting distributed collective reconnaissance (DCR), where many agentic clients individually issue benign-looking requests that collectively reveal system knowledge.
motivation: Autonomous and agentic clients can split reconnaissance across thousands of identities so each request stays valid and low-rate, evading per-identity anomaly detection while the population aggregates broad system intelligence.
method: The authors formalize DCR and build a Docker-isolated benchmark with 11 benign and attack behaviors across 10–10,000 virtual identities (440 runs, 3,666,300 requests), comparing semantic, Gaussian, conditional, graph, kernel, hybrid, and CUSUM-based detectors using only service-boundary telemetry.
result: Gaussian likelihood-ratio detection achieves 100% detection with zero observed false positives on known attacks but only 3% on unseen policies; CUSUM reaches 36.1% detection at 1.25% FPs, while hybrid CUSUM reaches 85.7% detection with zero observed FPs at 10,000 identities.
conclusion: The findings expose a major policy-generalization gap in collective-detection approaches and motivate exposure-aware, scale-aware defenses for swarm-based reconnaissance.

title: A New Method For Proving Confluence On Abstract Reduction Systems --- Confluence Of non-E-overlapping Weakly-shallow TRSs ---
authors: Masahiko Sakai, Mizuhito Ogawa, Michio Oyamaguchi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09572v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper proposes a new method for proving the confluence of an abstract reduction system (ARS) by clarifying the sufficient conditions, called compatibility and edge commutativity, for expanding a given finite sub-ARS into a confluent one by adding rewrite edges. This method can be regarded as an extension of our earlier work, which showed that a weakly non-overlapping, shallow, and non-collapsing term rewriting system (TRS) is confluent. Furthermore, we apply our method to demonstrate that a non-[MATH]-overlapping and weakly shallow TRS is confluent. Here, a term is weakly shallow if each defined function symbol occurs either at the root or in the ground subterms, and a TRS is weakly shallow if both sides of all its rewrite rules are weakly shallow. This drops the non-collapsing condition assumed in our previous work on weakly shallow TRSs. Moreover, since a weakly shallow TRS is non-[MATH]-overlapping whenever it is non-[MATH]-overlapping, and the latter property is decidable, we also obtain a decidable sufficient condition for confluence: non-[MATH]-overlapping and weakly shallow TRSs are confluent.
tldr: The paper introduces a new method for proving confluence in abstract reduction systems via compatibility and edge commutativity, applying it to weakly shallow term rewriting systems.
motivation: Confluence is a fundamental property in rewriting systems, and existing sufficient conditions often rely on restrictive assumptions like non-collapsing or shallow terms.
method: The authors define sufficient conditions—compatibility and edge commutativity—for expanding a finite sub-ARS into a confluent one, and apply this framework to non-E-overlapping weakly shallow TRSs.
result: They show that non-E-overlapping and weakly shallow TRSs are confluent, dropping the non-collapsing condition required in previous work, and obtain a decidable sufficient condition for confluence.
conclusion: The proposed method generalizes earlier results and provides a more permissive, decidable criterion for confluence in weakly shallow TRSs.

title: Black-Box Adversarial Patch Attacks On VLAs Via Ancestor Vlm Exploitation
authors: Xiaoyi Pang, Haoyue Feng, Quanxin Shou, Yikun Miao, Zhengyang Yan, Song Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical physical environments, yet their adversarial robustness remains poorly understood. Existing attacks typically assume white-box access or rely on surrogate VLAs, which rarely holds in real-world deployments. Our key insight is that most VLAs are adapted from a publicly released pretrained vision-language model (VLM), inheriting two capabilities essential for action generation: visual perception and instruction-conditioned grounding. Therefore, this paper explores a previously unaddressed question: can an adversary attack deployed VLAs using only their ancestor VLMs? To this end, we propose three adversarial patch attacks that disrupt the inherited capabilities: a vision disruption attack that corrupts the projected visual tokens through relative and absolute terms, an instruction-grounded semantic evidence suppression attack that removes the visual evidence required for instruction-grounded concepts, and a joint attack that unifies both objectives under a two-phase curriculum. Experiments across different VLA families on both simulation and static real-world images show that patches optimized on the ancestor VLM cause substantial degradations in VLA task success rates, demonstrating that VLAs inherit adversarial vulnerabilities alongside their foundational capabilities. This effect is not uniform: it is strongest on tasks that require precise instruction-grounded localization, and nearly vanishes on policies whose adaptation rewrites the shared visual-semantic representation or whose action head iteratively smooths perturbations away. By characterizing the boundary conditions of vulnerability inheritance and providing analysis of why the inheritance effect holds or fails, we advance the understanding of safety for VLA-involved systems.
tldr: The paper introduces three black-box adversarial patch attacks against Vision-Language-Action models by exploiting their publicly available ancestor VLMs to disrupt inherited visual perception and instruction-grounding capabilities.
motivation: VLAs are increasingly deployed in safety-critical physical settings, yet their adversarial robustness is poorly understood and existing attacks assume unrealistic white-box or surrogate-model access.
method: The authors design a vision disruption attack corrupting projected visual tokens, an instruction-grounded semantic evidence suppression attack, and a joint two-phase curriculum attack, all optimized on the ancestor VLM rather than the deployed VLA.
result: Patches optimized on the ancestor VLM substantially degrade VLA task success rates across multiple VLA families in simulation and static real-world images, with the strongest effect on tasks requiring precise instruction-grounded localization.
conclusion: VLAs inherit adversarial vulnerabilities alongside foundational capabilities from their ancestor VLMs, and the inheritance effect exhibits clear boundary conditions depending on adaptation and action-head smoothing.

title: Convergence Of Isoparametric Bgn Methods For Mean Curvature Flow Of Closed Surfaces With High-order Finite Elements
authors: Yifei Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove the convergence of the isoparametric Barrett--Garcke--N\"urnberg (BGN) method for mean curvature flow of closed surfaces. For finite elements of degree [MATH] and time steps [MATH], the numerical surfaces converge to the exact surfaces in the manifold distance with order [MATH]. The proof relies on two ingredients. First, we construct approximation flows by an expansion in time, whose interpolations satisfy the BGN method with an improved defect. Second, we derive a refined estimate for the tangential error from an algebraic identity for tangential test functions.
tldr: The paper proves convergence of high-order finite element isoparametric BGN methods for mean curvature flow of closed surfaces.
motivation: Mean curvature flow is a fundamental geometric evolution equation, and BGN-type methods are widely used for its numerical approximation, but convergence for high-order finite elements needed rigorous analysis.
method: The proof constructs approximation flows via time expansion satisfying the BGN method with improved defect, and derives a refined tangential error estimate from an algebraic identity for tangential test functions.
result: Numerical surfaces converge to exact surfaces in manifold distance with order related to finite element degree and time step size.
conclusion: The isoparametric BGN method is proven convergent for closed surface mean curvature flow with high-order finite elements.

title: An Energy--stable Ale--fem With Compensated Tangential Velocity For Navier--Stokes Free--boundary Flows
authors: Nuo Lei, Weiying Zheng, Na Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an energy-stable arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) finite element formulation for incompressible Navier-Stokes flows with surface-tension-driven free boundaries. The key ingredient is a multiplier-free compensated tangential velocity formulation, which redistributes boundary nodes via the discrete tangential curvature residual. The relaxation parameter governing the artificial tangential velocity is scaled according to the viscous-capillary balance, yielding the natural choice [MATH], where [MATH] is the surface tension coefficient and [MATH] is the dynamic viscosity. We prove that the fully discrete scheme is well-posed, energy-dissipative, and temporally consistent with its semi-discrete counterpart. Numerical results confirm the robustness of the proposed method across a range of [MATH] and [MATH] values. Furthermore, the method exhibits superior mesh quality preservation compared with the BGN method, particularly in the small-time-step regime.
tldr: The paper develops an energy-stable arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) finite element scheme for incompressible Navier-Stokes flows with surface-tension-driven free boundaries.
motivation: Simulating free-boundary flows requires robust mesh motion that preserves mesh quality and numerical stability, which standard ALE approaches like the BGN method struggle to maintain, especially at small time steps.
method: The authors introduce a multiplier-free compensated tangential velocity formulation that redistributes boundary nodes using the discrete tangential curvature residual, with a relaxation parameter scaled by the viscous-capillary balance (surface tension over dynamic viscosity).
result: They prove the fully discrete scheme is well-posed, energy-dissipative, and temporally consistent with its semi-discrete counterpart, and numerical experiments show improved mesh quality preservation over the BGN method, particularly in the small-time-step regime.
conclusion: The proposed ALE formulation offers a stable and accurate numerical method for free-boundary Navier-Stokes problems with surface tension, though it lies entirely outside quantum information science.

title: Nonmonotone Coderivative-Based Newton Methods For Nonsmooth Optimization With Machine Learning Applications
authors: Sina Kazemdehbashi, Yanchao Liu, Boris S. Mordukhovich
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Newton-type algorithms are among the most effective methods for solving optimization problems because of their rapid local convergence. However, extending these methods to nonsmooth optimization is challenging due to the difficulty of incorporating second-order information. To address this issue, we propose a coderivative-based Newton framework for solving both unconstrained and constrained nonsmooth optimization problems using tools from variational analysis and generalized differentiation. The proposed method employs generalized Hessians, defined as coderivatives of the subgradient mapping, and is applicable to both [MATH] functions and convex composite optimization problems with extended-real-valued components. To enhance robustness, the algorithm incorporates an adaptive regularization strategy that enables it to handle problems whose generalized Hessians are positive semidefinite. In addition, a Hybrid Adaptive Nonmonotone (HAN) line search scheme is developed as a globalization technique to improve global convergence and practical performance. Under standard assumptions, both the exact and inexact versions of the algorithm are globally convergent and achieve local superlinear convergence when the associated subgradient mapping satisfies the semismooth* property. The proposed framework is further extended to convex composite optimization through the forward-backward envelope, allowing it to handle problems with or without strong convexity in the smooth component of the objective function. Numerical experiments on Lasso, logistic Lasso, and support vector machine (SVM) problems demonstrate the efficiency and robustness of the proposed algorithm. Comparisons with several well-established first-order and second-order methods for nonsmooth optimization show that the proposed approach is computationally competitive while maintaining strong convergence properties.
tldr: The paper proposes coderivative-based Newton methods with adaptive regularization and nonmonotone line search for nonsmooth optimization, with applications to Lasso, logistic Lasso, and SVM problems.
motivation: Extending Newton-type algorithms to nonsmooth optimization is challenging because second-order information is difficult to incorporate, and existing methods often lack robust globalization strategies.
method: The authors develop a coderivative-based Newton framework using generalized Hessians (coderivatives of the subgradient mapping), an adaptive regularization strategy, and a Hybrid Adaptive Nonmonotone (HAN) line search, with extensions to convex composite optimization via the forward-backward envelope.
result: The exact and inexact versions are globally convergent and achieve local superlinear convergence under semismooth* assumptions, and numerical experiments on Lasso, logistic Lasso, and SVM show competitive performance against established first-order and second-order methods.
conclusion: The proposed framework provides a theoretically sound and computationally efficient approach for nonsmooth optimization, though it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Contextualization Of Third-Party Cloud Security Findings
authors: Gal Engelberg Leon Goldberg
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08895v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finding severity is the main driver of how security teams prioritize remediation. For third-party cloud security findings, that severity is static: the rule that raised the finding assigns it before the rule meets any environment, so it reflects the risk of the condition in general rather than the risk the finding poses to the concrete environment where it lives. Scoring standards define where environment-specific context belongs. How far that context changes finding severities in production, where the deciding evidence lies, and whether it holds against the live environment have not been measured. We address this gap with contextualization, re-deriving each finding's severity from evidence in the environment where the finding lives. A deep research agent over a precomputed cross-signal asset graph investigates each finding against the resource's state, its graph neighborhood, and other products' signals, and returns an adjusted severity with an evidence trace. We evaluate it in a production field study of 9,967 vendor HIGH findings from two commercial cloud security platforms across eight real production environments, on three criteria: the faithfulness of the facts behind each verdict to the live environment, the dependence of each decision on context beyond the flagged resource, and the regularity of the reasoning. Three in four findings are re-graded, mostly downward, and the same rule often moves in opposite directions inside a single environment. About half of the decisive evidence lies beyond the flagged resource, and read-only probes of live infrastructure confirm the decisive fact for 99.4% of decided findings.
tldr: The paper proposes context-aware re-scoring of third-party cloud security findings using a deep research agent over an asset graph, validated in production.
motivation: Static severity scores for cloud security findings do not reflect environment-specific risk, and the extent to which contextual evidence changes severity in practice has not been measured.
method: A deep research agent investigates each finding against a precomputed cross-signal asset graph, using resource state, graph neighborhood, and other product signals to produce adjusted severity with evidence traces.
result: In a production study of 9,967 HIGH findings across eight environments, three in four findings are re-graded mostly downward, about half of decisive evidence lies beyond the flagged resource, and read-only probes confirm the decisive fact for 99.4% of decided findings.
conclusion: Environment-specific contextualization substantially changes cloud security finding severity, demonstrating the value of graph-based evidence and live validation for remediation prioritization.

title: TwinGuard-Lite: A Rule-Based State-Admission Gateway For Generative Patient Digital Twins
authors: Sheikh Rabiul Islam Wenhui Chu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Future generative patient digital twins may combine longitudinal health records with language-model agents and keep information across sessions. The wording of a proposed update does not reveal whether it comes from an allowed source, conflicts with the patient's record, or belongs to someone else. We present TwinGuard-Lite, a rule-based gateway that admits an update to a twin's persistent state only if it passes checkable approximations of two integrity properties. Grounded state consistency (GSC) is approximated by a provenance check and a contradiction check; cross-patient noninterference (CPN) is approximated by a namespace check against trusted transport metadata. We evaluate three attack families over 20 seeded person-level splits of a semi-synthetic stream built from the openly licensed eICU database demo, with 29,131 [MATH] 2706 candidate updates per seed. A keyword filter and an anomaly detector detect 16% and 24% of attacks, respectively; a provenance-only ablation detects 59.9% but misses every cross-patient attack. Combining GSC and CPN yields 99.1% precision, 90.5% recall, a 94.6% F1 score, and a 0.033% false-positive rate. Every attack the full gateway admits falsely claims a trusted source; when the retrieval channel does so, 92.9% of retrieval attacks are admitted. The results hold under stated trust assumptions, and no language model, agent, or retriever is executed: TwinGuard-Lite is a mechanism-level proof of concept that motivates authenticated, patient-bound ingestion, not a clinical safeguard.
tldr: TwinGuard-Lite is a rule-based state-admission gateway for generative patient digital twins, enforcing provenance, contradiction, and namespace checks to achieve high attack detection on semi-synthetic eICU data.
motivation: Future generative patient digital twins may persist language-model-agent updates across sessions, but update wording alone cannot reveal whether an update is unauthorized, contradictory, or belongs to another patient.
method: The gateway approximates grounded state consistency via provenance and contradiction checks and cross-patient noninterference via a namespace check against trusted transport metadata, evaluated on three attack families over 20 seeded person-level splits of a semi-synthetic eICU stream.
result: Combining GSC and CPN yields 99.1% precision, 90.5% recall, a 94.6% F1 score, and a 0.033% false-positive rate, while provenance-only detection reaches 59.9% but misses every cross-patient attack.
conclusion: Under stated trust assumptions, TwinGuard-Lite is a mechanism-level proof of concept that motivates authenticated, patient-bound ingestion rather than serving as a clinical safeguard; no language model, agent, or retriever is executed.

title: Structural Analysis Of Hybrid-Trace Nets: An Optimization Approach
authors: Nguyen Cong Nhat Le, Claire N. Bonial, John G. Rogers, Neil T. Dantam
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault and error detection is crucial for ensuring the correctness of safety-critical systems. Safety verification often addresses reachability of bad system states, where exhaustive state inspection may be intractable due to the large state spaces of complex systems. We propose a reachability relaxation for hybrid trace nets, a useful mathematical model for analyzing concurrent event systems, to efficiently verify system safety. We further use our relaxation to effectively identify invariants, expressions that hold in all reachable states, allowing state-space reduction for efficient verification. Empirically, our approach proves unsafe states unreachable in 1.5x more instances, generates 2.5x more invariants with up to 2 orders of magnitude faster generation times than the baselines in the tested problems.
tldr: The paper proposes a reachability relaxation for hybrid-trace nets to efficiently verify safety and generate invariants in concurrent event systems.
motivation: Fault and error detection in safety-critical systems requires verifying reachability of bad states, but exhaustive state inspection is intractable for large state spaces.
method: The authors introduce a reachability relaxation for hybrid trace nets and use it to identify invariants, enabling state-space reduction and efficient verification.
result: Empirically, the approach proves unsafe states unreachable in 1.5x more instances and generates 2.5x more invariants with up to two orders of magnitude faster generation than baselines.
conclusion: The relaxation-based approach improves safety verification and invariant generation for hybrid-trace nets, though it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Consumption And Investment When Welfare Floors Change Over Time
authors: Gugyum Ha, Junkee Jeon, Takwon Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study consumption and investment over a finite horizon when continuation utility must stay above a welfare floor that changes over time, and the floor at the horizon acts as a terminal wealth floor. A cumulative multiplier reduces the problem to a parabolic obstacle problem. When relative risk aversion exceeds one, the intervention boundary exists at every interior date. When it is below one, the boundary exists exactly at the dates where a discounted transformation of the floor is locally increasing and sets a strict running record, so it can disappear and later reenter. We prove local regularity of the boundary, construct the dual value from the obstacle solution, and verify the optimal cumulative multiplier, whose moments are controlled through its representation as a running supremum. Strong duality identifies the exact lower endpoint of feasible wealth. With stochastic income in a complete market, the floor becomes the value of an outside option, which links the boundary to limited commitment and endogenous borrowing capacity.
tldr: The paper studies consumption and investment over a finite horizon when continuation utility must remain above a time-varying welfare floor, reducing the problem to a parabolic obstacle problem.
motivation: Welfare floors that change over time and act as terminal wealth floors are relevant to limited commitment and endogenous borrowing capacity in financial economics.
method: A cumulative multiplier is used to transform the constrained problem into a parabolic obstacle problem, with dual value constructed from the obstacle solution and strong duality identifying the lower endpoint of feasible wealth.
result: For relative risk aversion above one, the intervention boundary exists at every interior date; for below one, it exists exactly when a discounted floor transformation sets a strict running record, so it can disappear and later reenter.
conclusion: The analysis links the welfare floor to an outside option in a complete market with stochastic income, thereby connecting the boundary to limited commitment and endogenous borrowing capacity.

title: CredLeakBench: Evaluating Credential Leakage And Recovery In Llm Agents
authors: Rafid Ahmed, Joseph Fioresi, Mubarak Shah, Yuzhang Shang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language model agents are increasingly deployed to automate everyday digital chores from managing emails and social media to handling banking and bills allowing users to step away from supervision. However, this capability also exposes sensitive information to phishing. Safe execution requires distinguishing malicious requests from genuine ones without simply refusing to act. Despite its practical importance, this problem remains underexplored and it is unclear whether current agents or existing defenses can achieve it. To study this problem, we first propose CredLeak-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate how effectively and securely agents automate human workflows when confronted with phishing and identity verification. The benchmark covers both user-directed authentication and autonomous inbox monitoring, where agents are not explicitly instructed to log in. It systematically varies deceptive cues and pairs phishing scenarios with legitimate counterparts, enabling joint evaluation of information leakage and utility on genuine tasks. Within a sandboxed environment, leakage is measured through actual submissions of information rather than agents' self-reported behavior. Our evaluation reveals that all tested models are vulnerable to leakage. Agents also disclose sensitive information during autonomous inbox monitoring, demonstrating that phishing can induce disclosure without a user request to authenticate. Furthermore, most evaluated mitigations that reduce leakage also impair performance on genuine tasks, exposing a security utility trade off in existing defenses. These findings show why reducing leakage alone is insufficient: effective defenses must prevent unauthorized disclosure while preserving legitimate task completion. CredLeak-Bench provides a controlled framework for measuring both objectives and evaluating progress toward secure, useful agents.
tldr: CredLeak-Bench is a benchmark for evaluating credential leakage and recovery in LLM agents exposed to phishing and identity verification tasks.
motivation: LLM agents are increasingly used for sensitive digital chores, but their vulnerability to phishing and the trade-off between security and utility remain underexplored.
method: The authors introduce a sandboxed benchmark that varies deceptive cues and pairs phishing scenarios with legitimate tasks, measuring actual information submission rather than self-report.
result: All tested models leak credentials, including during autonomous inbox monitoring, and most mitigations reduce leakage at the cost of impaired performance on genuine tasks.
conclusion: Current defenses face a security-utility trade-off, and effective solutions must prevent unauthorized disclosure while preserving legitimate task completion.

title: Towards Verifying Neural Networks Against Multi-Parameter Bit-Flip Perturbations
authors: Hai Duong, Thanh Le, Ho Nguyen, Thanhvu Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hardware faults can flip bits in the stored weights of a quantized neural network, potentially compromising its predictions. While such faults typically affect multiple parameters simultaneously, existing verifiers are limited to single-parameter perturbations due to the combinatorial explosion of possible flip locations in large networks. We present mBFV (m-BitFlip Verifier), an efficient verification framework that proves robustness against simultaneous bit flips across multiple parameters without explicitly enumerating these combinations. mBFV achieves this via a novel multi-parameter bound propagation technique that directly aggregates the m worst-case contributions. To further tighten these bounds, mBFV employs a branch-and-bound mechanism over perturbation locations, partitioning the potential flips to smaller groups of neurons. Evaluated on 625 instances, mBFV successfully verifies 293, significantly outperforming a prior single-parameter verifier (38 verified instances) and an exact mixed-integer linear programming baseline (0 verified instances). Notably, while these baselines are restricted to single-parameter flips on small networks (up to 13k parameters), mBFV scales to verify networks with up to 1.15M parameters against up to four simultaneous parameter flips.
tldr: The paper introduces mBFV, a verification framework that proves robustness of quantized neural networks against simultaneous bit-flip faults across multiple parameters.
motivation: Hardware faults can flip multiple stored weights in quantized neural networks, but existing verifiers are limited to single-parameter perturbations due to the combinatorial explosion of possible multi-flip locations in large networks.
method: mBFV uses a novel multi-parameter bound propagation technique that directly aggregates the worst-case contributions of multiple bit flips without enumerating combinations, and employs a branch-and-bound mechanism over perturbation locations to tighten bounds.
result: Evaluated on 625 instances, mBFV verifies 293, significantly outperforming a prior single-parameter verifier (38 verified) and an exact MILP baseline (0 verified), scaling to networks with up to 1.15M parameters against up to four simultaneous flips.
conclusion: mBFV efficiently verifies multi-parameter bit-flip robustness beyond prior methods, but it is a classical neural network verification contribution with no connection to quantum information theory or the other research directions.

title: Proceedings Seventeenth International Symposium On Games, Automata, Logics, And Formal Verification
authors: Giorgio Bacci (aalborg University, Denmark), Micka\"el Randour
abstract: ArXiv:2610.08898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This volume contains the proceedings of GandALF 2026, the Seventeenth International Symposium on Games, Automata, Logics, and Formal Verification. The symposium was held in Aalborg, Denmark, on September 15-17, 2026. The aim of GandALF 2026 is to bring together researchers from academia and industry who are actively working in the fields of Games, Automata, Logics, and Formal Verification. The idea is to cover an ample spectrum of themes, ranging from theory to applications, and stimulate cross-fertilisation.
tldr: This is the proceedings volume of the GandALF 2026 symposium on games, automata, logics, and formal verification, unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: The symposium aims to bring together researchers working on games, automata, logics, and formal verification to stimulate cross-fertilisation across theory and applications.
method: The volume collects papers presented at the Seventeenth International Symposium on Games, Automata, Logics, and Formal Verification (GandALF 2026).
result: It provides a broad spectrum of contributions in formal verification and related theoretical computer science areas.
conclusion: The proceedings serve as a reference for recent developments in games, automata, logics, and formal verification, with no direct relevance to quantum information research.

title: Mars: Malware Analysis With Rule-Based Scoring Of Llm Claims
authors: Hyeongjun Choi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09553v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models can triage malware through direct verdicts or behavioral claims scored by an external policy. We present MARS, a malware triage framework, and compare direct classification with single-pass claim scoring using the same evidence collector and identical static evidence bundles for each model. The evaluation covers 1,195 PE and ELF binaries grouped into 1,001 near-duplicate clusters and six language models, with deterministic rules providing a baseline. Direct classification is more accurate for all six models. On samples with usable outputs from both paths, its accuracy advantage ranges from 3.7 to 20.9 percentage points, with all 95% cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals for the differences above zero. It also achieves higher malicious alert recall in ten of twelve platform and model combinations. Claim mediation provides no consistent reduction in performance variation across models. Separate subset studies find more consistent alert decisions for direct classification and a larger recall loss for the claim path when predefined indicator fields are removed. In a family identification probe, claims yield higher accuracy than verdict labels but lower accuracy than evidence text. Retained claims expose the inputs to verdict computation and permit policy revision without another model call. We reproduce archived verdicts exactly and apply a revised policy to the same records, including outputs from two additional models withdrawn by their provider. Under the evaluated claim taxonomy and additive policy, these results favor direct classification when only a verdict is required, while demonstrating that retained claims support explicit policy inspection and revision.
tldr: MARS compares direct LLM malware classification with rule-based scoring of LLM-generated behavioral claims on a dataset of PE and ELF binaries, finding that direct classification is generally more accurate.
motivation: Large language models can triage malware either by direct verdicts or by generating behavioral claims that an external policy scores, and it is unclear which approach is more reliable.
method: The study evaluates six language models on 1,195 binaries grouped into 1,001 near-duplicate clusters, using identical static evidence bundles and deterministic rule-based baselines, with comparisons of accuracy, recall, and variation across platform/model combinations.
result: Direct classification outperforms claim scoring for all six models, with accuracy advantages of 3.7 to 20.9 percentage points and higher malicious alert recall in ten of twelve combinations, while claim mediation does not consistently reduce performance variation.
conclusion: For verdict-only malware triage, direct classification is favored, but retained claims still allow explicit policy inspection and revision without additional model calls.

title: Heating And Escape Of Confined Atoms Subject To Colored Noise
authors: Joseph M. Ryan, Katherine Jonas, Christopher Monroe
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The motion of a particle in a finite-depth confining potential, such as that of an electromagnetically trapped atom or ion, is approximately harmonic at low energy and softens as the escape energy is approached. When the particle is driven by a stochastic force, the heating and escape times depend sensitively on the noise power spectrum. We study escape times of particles in softening potentials driven by power-law colored noise. We identify two nested conditions for weak noise: the particle must execute many oscillations before escape, and noise forces must be small relative to forces exerted by the trap so as not to tilt the potential appreciably. In this regime, we derive expressions for the mean escape time using stochastic averaging techniques and compare them with Monte Carlo simulations of the full equations of motion. We also examine the crossover to regimes where these conditions are not met and large quasi-static forces give rise to additional escape mechanisms. Applying these results to an experimental measurement of lifetimes in a microfabricated ion trap, we find that spectral color alone cannot account for the rapid escape rates observed, whereas quasi-static barrier tilting by a stray field of plausible magnitude could. These results are relevant to the heating and escape of trapped atoms due to noisy force fields, as well as to other nonlinear oscillators subject to colored noise.

title: Particle-Number-Preserving Quantum Signal Processing For Thermal Properties: Canonical-Ensemble Estimation And Grand-Canonical Reconstruction
authors: Taehee Ko, Sungbin Lim, Sangkook Choi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.09373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop an end-to-end framework for estimating canonical thermal properties of particle-number-conserving second-quantized Hamiltonians using quantum simulations. The framework integrates initial state preparation with mixed Dicke states, particle-number-preserving Trotterized simulation, and generalized quantum signal processing to estimate canonical partition functions and observables. Building on this canonical scheme, we introduce a grand-canonical reconstruction scheme in which the same quantum measurement data can be reused for arbitrary chemical potentials through classical reweighting, thereby avoiding repeated quantum circuit executions as the chemical potential is varied. We prove the existence of system-size-independent temperature regimes in which both the canonical and reconstructed grand-canonical schemes have lower asymptotic time complexity than classical Lanczos methods, up to polynomial factors, for physically relevant Hamiltonians. We numerically validate our theoretical results for the two-dimensional Hubbard model in both weak- and intermediate-coupling regimes.
